title: Bun.RedisClient.subscribe() (fork)
text: subscribe(channel: string, listener: RedisClient.StringPubSubListener): Promise ; — Subscribe to a Redis channel. Subscribing disables automatic pipelining, so all commands are received immediately. Subscribing moves the channel to a dedicated subscription state which prevents most other commands from being executed until unsubscribed. Only ping, subscribe, and unsubscribe can be called while subscribed. @example ```ts await client.subscribe("my-channel", (message, channel) => { console.log(`Received message on ${channel}: ${message}`); });

title: Bun.RedisClient.subscribe() (fork)

Subscribing disables automatic pipelining, so all commands are received immediately. Subscribing moves the channels to a dedicated subscription state in which only a limited set of commands can be executed.

title: Bun.RedisClient.unsubscribe() (fork)
text: unsubscribe(channel: string): Promise ; — Unsubscribe from a single Redis channel. If there are no more channels subscribed to, the client automatically re-enables pipelining if it was previously enabled. Once all channels have been unsubscribed from, the client leaves the subscription state. For further details on the subscription state, see subscribe.

title: Bun.WebView.Backend
text: type Backend = — Browser backend selection. - `"webkit"` (default): WKWebView. macOS only. Zero external dependencies — uses the system WebKit.framework. - `"chrome"`: Chrome/Chromium via DevTools Protocol over `--remote-debugging-pipe`. Works anywhere Chrome is installed. Auto-detects the binary in standard locations; override with `backend.path` or the `BUN_CHROME_PATH` environment variable. The object form accepts extra launch flags. Chrome switches are last-wins for duplicates, so `argv` can override the defaults. **Chrome is spawned once per process** — the first `new Bun.WebView()` …

title: Bun.WebView.url
text: url: string; — Connect to an existing Chrome's DevTools WebSocket directly. Get the URL from Chrome's `DevToolsActivePort` file (`<port>\n<path>`, in the profile directory) — the full URL is `ws://127.0.0.1:<port><path>`. Enable remote debugging in Chrome at `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`, or launch with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. Both write `DevToolsActivePort`. **Note**: The `chrome://inspect` toggle shows an "Allow remote debugging?" dialog on **every** new connection. Mutually exclusive with `path`/`argv` — you're connecting to a Chrome that's already running, not spawning one.

title: Bun.WebView.url
text: url?: false; — Controls the connect-vs-spawn choice: - `false` — skip auto-detect, always spawn a fresh Chrome. Executable path still auto-found unless `path` is set. - `undefined` (default) — **auto-detect**: if a `DevToolsActivePort` file exists (Chrome with remote debugging is running), connect to it; else spawn. Auto-detect falls back to spawn if the connect fails (stale file from a dead Chrome). The WebSocket auto-closes when the last `WebView` is closed. For unattended automation, pass `url: false`.

title: Bun.WrapAnsiOptions.trim
text: trim?: boolean; — If `true`, trim leading and trailing whitespace from each line. If `false`, preserve whitespace.

title: Bun.WebView.path
text: path?: string; — Path to the Chrome/Chromium executable. Overrides auto-detection and forces Bun to spawn a fresh Chrome subprocess (skipping the existing-Chrome auto-connect). **Auto-connect**: when neither `path` nor `url` is set, Bun checks Chrome's `DevToolsActivePort` file — if a Chrome with remote debugging is already running, Bun connects to it over WebSocket instead of spawning. Pass `path` (or `argv`) to force spawn-mode.

title: Bun.markdown
text:
namespace markdown — Markdown related APIs. Parses and renders markdown with four output modes: - `html()` — render to an HTML string - `ansi()` — render to an ANSI-colored string for terminals - `render()` — render with custom callbacks for each element - `react()` — parse to React-compatible JSX elements Supports GFM extensions (tables, strikethrough, task lists, autolinks) and component overrides to replace default HTML tags with custom components. @example ```tsx // Render markdown to HTML const html = Bun.markdown.html("# Hello **world**"); // "

Hello world

\n" // …

title: Bun.BuildConfig.splitRequire
text: splitRequire?: boolean; — With `splitting` and `target: "bun"`, every `require()` of a bundled ES module is a chunk boundary too. The call stays synchronous: it is emitted as `import.meta.require("./chunk-…js")` and the chunk is evaluated when the call runs, so a `require()` inside a function that never runs costs nothing at startup. Set to `false` to keep such modules inlined in the calling chunk. No effect for other targets.

text: type int32 = number & { readonly "bun.int32"?: true }; — A whole number from -2147483648 to 2147483647. To TypeScript, and under `bun run`, this is a `number`. With `--aot`, a variable, field, parameter or return value of this type takes four bytes, and arithmetic on it skips the checks for fractions. The build must prove that every value stored in an `int32` is one, and reports an error where it can't. `| 0` turns any number into an int32. ```ts class Cursor { line: int32 = 0; column: int32 = 0; } function advance(cursor: Cursor, by: int32) { cursor.column = (cursor.column + by) | 0; // …

text: minChunkSize?: number; — With `splitting`, chunks that are always loaded together are folded into one (for example, code shared by an entry point and a module it `import()`s lives in the entry point's chunk). This option additionally folds chunks whose combined source size is below this many bytes and whose modules have no top-level side effects into a chunk loaded by a superset of their importers, so fewer modules are loaded at runtime. Nothing lazy becomes eager and no side effect runs earlier; the chunk that absorbs a folded chunk exports the symbols other chunks import from it. Requires …

title: Bun.BuildConfig.modulePreload

title: Bun.TrimOptions.allow
text: allow?: Bun.Build.TrimFeature[]; — Features to keep even if your code never uses them, along with the features they need. Use it when something the compiler can't see uses an API: a string passed to `eval()`, a native addon, or a module loaded at run time.

title: Bun.TrimOptions.remove
text: remove?: Bun.Build.TrimFeature[]; — Features to remove even if your code uses them. Every import, global and property is still there, so `typeof` and `in` answer as before. A call throws an `Error` whose `code` is `"ERR_FEATURE_REMOVED"`. Use it to make sure that an executable can't do something, such as load native code: `remove: ["native-code"]`. A name can't be in both `allow` and `remove`.

title: Bun.TrimOptions.locales
text: locales?: string[]; — The only locales to keep, such as `"en"` or `"de-AT"`. Without it, Bun keeps the locales your code passes to `Intl` as constants, and every locale if one of them isn't a constant. If the program asks for a locale that was removed, the process exits with code 70. It has no effect on macOS, where Bun uses the system's ICU. Equivalent CLI flag: `--trim-locales`, which implies `--trim`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.trim
text: trim?: boolean | TrimOptions; — Remove the Bun and Node.js APIs your code never calls from the executable. With `aot`, the compiler knows which APIs the program uses, and Bun removes every other feature. Without `aot`, Bun only removes the command-line tools. An object does what `true` does, with the options in TrimOptions. Removing a feature removes its code, not its names: every global, constructor, prototype, property and constant is still there. title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.functionSource
text: functionSource?: boolean; — With `aot`: embed each function's source code in the executable. With `false`, `fn.toString()` returns `function name() { [native code] }` and the executable is smaller. `--preload` in `BUN_OPTIONS` is an error at startup, with `inspector` too. `obfuscate` and `sourcemap: "external"` imply `false`. Equivalent CLI flag: `--no-compile-function-source`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.allowCodeFromDisk
text: allowCodeFromDisk?: boolean; — With `aot`: let a dynamic `import()`, `require()` or `new Worker()` load code that isn't in the executable from disk when the program runs, such as a plugin or a config file. Bun interprets that code. Without it, the executable only runs code that was compiled into it, and such a load throws. The option keeps Bun's transpiler and the source code of Bun's built-in modules in the executable, and the compiler can prove less about the program, so the executable is larger and can run slower. Equivalent CLI flag: `--aot-allow-code-from-disk`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.autoloadBunfig

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.autoloadTsconfig

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.autoloadPackageJson

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.aot
text: aot?: boolean; — Compile the program's JavaScript and TypeScript to machine code at build time. It cannot be combined with `bytecode`. The executable has no JIT. Code that only exists at run time, such as a string passed to `eval()` or `new Function()`, runs in the interpreter. Built-in objects such as `Object.prototype`, `Array.prototype` and `Promise` are read-only in the executable. Assigning to one throws a `TypeError`. Breakpoints aren't available. Requires a `target` that matches the platform and Bun version running the build. `format` has no effect: each file keeps the module format it …

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.obfuscate
text: obfuscate?: boolean; — With `aot`: strip function names and file names from the executable and write a source map next to it. `sourcemap: "external"` does the same for stack traces and leaves the `name` of functions and classes alone. With `obfuscate` it is `""`. Equivalent CLI flag: `--obfuscate`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.inspector
text: inspector?: boolean; — With `aot`: let a debugger attach to the executable through `BUN_INSPECT`, or `--inspect`, `--inspect-wait` and `--inspect-brk` in `BUN_OPTIONS`. A debugger can run any code in any scope, so the compiler can prove less about the program. The executable is larger and slower. Equivalent CLI flag: `--compile-inspector`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.aotExplain
text: aotExplain?: AotReport | AotReport[]; — With `aot`: reports to add to `BuildOutput.logs`, at level `"verbose"`. - `"text"`: the code that compiled to a slow path, one entry per cause with a fix, worst first - `"json"`: the same, one JSON object per line - `"guards"`: every type guard that can fail at run time, why the compiler couldn't remove it, and how to fix it - `"guards-json"`: the same, one JSON object per line - `"trim"`: which Bun and Node.js APIs the program uses, and why `trim` kept or removed each feature - `"allocations"`: where each object is allocated (stack, heap or removed), …

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.aotHarden
text: aotHarden?: string | string[]; — With `aot`: add run-time checks, so that a bug in the compiler is harder to turn into a memory bug. Each name costs speed, and none is on unless it is listed here. - `"proof-checks"`: check the type that the compiler has proven of a value again at each read, and check again what the compiler remembers from earlier code. Objects stay on the heap, not on the stack. The build also runs the compiler's own verifier. - `"ignore-told-ranges"`: check every index against the length, where the index is used. A check that fails aborts the process. Takes a list of names, …

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.aotOrder
text: aotOrder?: string | string[] | false | null; — Lay the executable out by the order in which a run of it entered its functions. Requires `aot: true`. Run an executable built with `aotRecordOrder: true` with `BUN_AOT_ORDER_OUT=<path>` to record a start, then build again with that file. A file from an older build of the app still applies. With several files, list the most important one first. A function lies where the first file that lists it places it. `false` and `null` mean no file, so `aotOrder: haveProfile && path` works. Equivalent CLI flag: `--aot-order <file>[,<file>...]`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.aotRecordOrder
text: aotRecordOrder?: boolean; — Build an executable that writes what `aotOrder` takes when it runs with `BUN_AOT_ORDER_OUT=<path>`. Other executables have no recorder. Requires `aot: true`. Equivalent CLI flag: `--aot-record-order`

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.bytecodeOrder
text: bytecodeOrder?: string | string[] | false | null; — Profile-guided layout for the executable's bytecode. Requires `bytecode: true`. Run an executable built with `bytecode: true` with `BUN_BYTECODE_ORDER_OUT=<path>` to record which functions it uses, then build again with that file. Bun places the bytecode the run used together at the front, so the executable starts faster and uses less memory. A profile from an older build of the app still applies. With several files, list the most common way of starting the app first. `false` and `null` mean no profile, so `bytecodeOrder: haveProfile && path` …

title: Bun.CompileBuildOptions.jitPolicy
text: jitPolicy?: number; — The JIT policy the executable starts with (see Bun.unsafe.setJITPolicy). `1` is the normal policy. A value `> 1` multiplies JavaScriptCore's tier-up thresholds so code that only runs during startup stays in the interpreter longer; the app should call `Bun.unsafe.setJITPolicy(1)` once it is interactive. Equivalent CLI flag: `--compile-jit-policy <n>`

text: windowBits?: — The base 2 logarithm of the window size (the size of the history buffer). Larger values of this parameter result in better compression at the expense of memory usage. The following value ranges are supported: - `9..15`: The output has a zlib header and footer (Deflate) - `-9..-15`: The output does **not** have a zlib header or footer (Raw Deflate) - `25..31` (16+`9..15`): The output has a gzip header and footer (gzip) The gzip header has no file name, no extra data, no comment, no modification time (set to zero) and no header CRC.

title: Bun.ZlibCompressionOptions.strategy
text: strategy?: number; — Tunes the compression algorithm. One of these `constants` of `node:zlib`; any other value throws. - `Z_DEFAULT_STRATEGY` (`0`): For normal data **(Default)** - `Z_FILTERED` (`1`): For data produced by a filter or predictor - `Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY` (`2`): Force Huffman encoding only (no string match) - `Z_RLE` (`3`): Limit match distances to one (run-length encoding) - `Z_FIXED` (`4`): Prevents the use of dynamic Huffman codes `Z_RLE` is designed to be almost as fast as `Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY`, but give better compression for PNG image data. `Z_FILTERED` forces more Huffman coding and …

title: Bun.PluginConstraints.filter
text: filter: RegExp; — Only apply the plugin when the import specifier matches this regular expression @example ```ts // Only apply the plugin when the import specifier matches the regex Bun.plugin({ setup(builder) { builder.onLoad({ filter: /node_modules\/underscore/ }, (args) => { return { contents: "throw new Error('Please use lodash instead of underscore.')" }; }); } })

text: namespace?: string; — Only apply the plugin when the import specifier has a namespace matching this string Namespaces are prefixes in import specifiers. For example, `"bun:ffi"` has the namespace `"bun"`. The default namespace is `"file"` and it can be omitted from import specifiers.

title: Bun.OnLoadResult
text: type OnLoadResult = OnLoadResultSourceCode | OnLoadResultObject | undefined | null | void; — Return `undefined` or `null` to skip the module. The next matching `onLoad` callback runs instead. If every callback skips it, the module is loaded as if no plugin had matched it.

title: Bun.OnResolveArgs.path

title: Bun.OnResolveResult.path
text: path: string; — The destination of the import In a runtime plugin, a path without a `namespace` is resolved from the importing module like any other import, without running `onResolve` callbacks on it. If nothing is found there, it is used as it is when an `onLoad` callback matches it. A bare name could also be a package in the registry, so `onResolve` callbacks run on it once more. If one of them returns a path, the name is the plugin's own and is never auto-installed.

title: Bun.OnResolveResult.namespace

title: Bun.PluginBuilder.onStart()

With hot module reloading, it runs at the start of each incremental rebuild. @example ```ts Bun.plugin({ setup(builder) { builder.onStart(() => { console.log("bundle just started!!") }); }, }); @returns `this` for method chaining

title: Bun.BunPlugin.target

This field is not read by Bun.plugin, only Bun.build and `bun build`

title: Bun.BunPlugin.setup()

title: Bun.BunRegisterPlugin
text: interface BunRegisterPlugin — Extend Bun's module resolution and loading behavior Plugins are applied in the order they are defined. There are two kinds of hooks: - `onLoad` returns source code or an object that becomes the module's exports - `onResolve` redirects a module specifier to another module specifier. It does not chain. Plugin hooks must define a `filter` RegExp and only match when the ES Module resolution semantics mean that plugins may be initialized _after_ a module is resolved. You might need to load plugins at the very beginning of the application and then use a dynamic import …

Default: `process.env`.

title: Bun.Socket
text: interface Socket extends Disposable — A TCP or TLS socket connection. Sockets are created with `Bun.connect()` or accepted by a `Bun.listen()` server.

title: Bun.WorkerOptions.credentials
text: credentials?: import("undici-types").RequestCredentials | undefined; — In Bun, this does nothing.

title: Bun.Socket.write()
text: write(data: string | BufferSource, byteOffset?: number, byteLength?: number): number; — Writes `data` to the socket. This method is unbuffered and non-blocking. It uses the `sendto(2)` syscall internally. For best performance with many small writes, batch them into a single `socket.write()` call. @example ```ts // Send a string const bytesWritten = socket.write("Hello, world!\n"); // Send binary data const buffer = new Uint8Array([0x01, 0x02, 0x03]); socket.write(buffer); // Send part of a buffer const largeBuffer = new Uint8Array(1024); // ... fill largeBuffer ... socket.write(largeBuffer, …

title: Bun.Socket.data
text: data: Data; — The user-defined data associated with this socket instance. Set it when the socket is created with `Bun.connect({ data: ... })`. It can be read or updated at any time. @example ```ts // In a socket handler function open(socket: Socket<{ userId: string }>) { console.log(`Socket opened for user: ${socket.data.userId}`); socket.data.lastActivity = Date.now(); // Update data }

title: Bun.Socket.end()
text: end(data?: string | BufferSource, byteOffset?: number, byteLength?: number): number; — Sends the final data chunk and initiates a graceful shutdown of the socket's write side. After calling `end()`, no more data can be written using `write()` or `end()`. The socket remains readable until the remote end also closes its write side or the connection is terminated. This sends a TCP FIN packet after writing the data. @example ```ts // send some data and close the write side socket.end("Goodbye!"); // or close write side without sending final data socket.end();

title: Bun.Socket.end()
text: end(): void; — Close the socket immediately

title: Bun.Socket.ref()
text: ref(): void; — Keep Bun's process alive at least until this socket is closed After the socket has closed, the socket is unref'd, the process may exit, and this becomes a no-op

title: Bun.Socket.timeout()
text: timeout(seconds: number): void; — Set a timeout until the socket automatically closes. To reset the timeout, call this function again. When a timeout happens, the `timeout` callback is called and the socket is closed.

title: Bun.Socket.terminate()
text: terminate(): void; — Forcefully closes the socket connection immediately. This is an abrupt termination, unlike the graceful shutdown initiated by `end()`. It uses `SO_LINGER` with `l_onoff=1` and `l_linger=0` before calling `close(2)`. Consider using close or end for graceful shutdowns. In the `handshake` callback of a TLS 1.3 client, this refuses the server before the client certificate is sent. @example ```ts socket.terminate();

title: Bun.Socket.shutdown()
text: shutdown(halfClose?: boolean): void; — Shuts down one half of the connection. With no argument, sends a FIN: the socket can still receive data but can no longer send it. With `true`, stops receiving data. Calls the `shutdown(2)` syscall internally. @example ```ts // Stop sending data, but allow receiving socket.shutdown(); // Stop receiving data socket.shutdown(true);

title: Bun.Socket.readyState
text: readonly readyState: -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2; — The ready state of the socket. A positive value means the socket is open and usable - `-2` = Shutdown - `-1` = Detached - `0` = Closed - `1` = Established - `2` = Else

title: Bun.Socket.unref()
text: unref(): void; — Allow Bun's process to exit even if this socket is still open After the socket has closed, this function does nothing.

title: Bun.Socket.flush()
text: flush(): void; — Flush any buffered data to the socket This attempts to send the data immediately, but success depends on the network conditions and the receiving end. It might be necessary after several `write` calls if immediate sending is critical, though the OS often handles flushing efficiently. `write` calls outside `open`/`data`/`drain` might benefit from manual `cork`/`flush`.

title: Bun.Socket.reload()
text: reload(options: Pick , "socket">): void; — Reset the socket's callbacks. This is useful with `bun --hot` for hot reloading. This applies to all sockets from the same Listener. It is per socket only for Bun.connect.

title: Bun.WorkerOptions.preload
text: preload?: string[] | string | undefined; — An array of module specifiers to preload in the worker. These modules load before the worker's entry point is executed. Equivalent to passing the `--preload` CLI argument, but only for this Worker.

title: Bun.Socket.listener
text: readonly listener?: SocketListener; — The server that created this socket This is `undefined` if the socket was created by Bun.connect or if the listener has already closed.

title: Bun.Socket.remoteFamily
text: readonly remoteFamily: "IPv4" | "IPv6"; — IP protocol family used for the remote endpoint of the socket @example "IPv4" | "IPv6"

title: Bun.Socket.remoteAddress
text: readonly remoteAddress: string; — Remote IP address connected to the socket @example "192.168.1.100" | "2001:db8::1"

title: Bun.Socket.remotePort
text: readonly remotePort: number; — Remote port connected to the socket @example 8080

title: Bun.Socket.localFamily
text: readonly localFamily: "IPv4" | "IPv6"; — IP protocol family used for the local endpoint of the socket @example "IPv4" | "IPv6"

title: Bun.Socket.localAddress
text: readonly localAddress: string; — Local IP address connected to the socket @example "192.168.1.100" | "2001:db8::1"

title: Bun.Socket.localPort
text: readonly localPort: number; — Local port connected to the socket @example 8080

title: Bun.Socket.authorized
text: readonly authorized: boolean; — `true` if the peer certificate was signed by one of the CAs specified when creating the `Socket` instance, otherwise `false`

title: Bun.Worker.onmessage
text: onmessage: ((this: Worker, ev: MessageEvent) => any) | null; — [MDN Reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Worker/message_event)

title: Bun.Socket.alpnProtocol
text: readonly alpnProtocol: string | false | null; — The selected ALPN protocol. Before a handshake has completed, this value is always `null`. When a handshake has completed but no ALPN protocol was selected, this is `false`.

title: Bun.Socket.disableRenegotiation()
text: disableRenegotiation(): void; — Disables TLS renegotiation for this `Socket` instance. Once called, attempts to renegotiate will trigger an `error` handler on the `Socket`. Bun does not support renegotiation as a server. (Attempts by clients result in a fatal alert so that ClientHello messages cannot be used to flood a server and escape higher-level limits.)

title: Bun.Worker.onmessageerror
text: onmessageerror: ((this: Worker, ev: MessageEvent) => any) | null; — [MDN Reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Worker/messageerror_event)

title: Bun.Socket.exportKeyingMaterial()
text: exportKeyingMaterial(length: number, label: string, context: Buffer): Buffer; — Keying material is used for validations to prevent different kinds of attacks in network protocols, for example in the specifications of IEEE 802.1X. @example ```js const keyingMaterial = socket.exportKeyingMaterial( 128, 'client finished'); // Example return value of keyingMaterial: // <Buffer 76 26 af 99 c5 56 8e 42 09 91 ef 9f 93 cb ad 6c 7b 65 f8 53 f1 d8 d9 // 12 5a 33 b8 b5 25 df 7b 37 9f e0 e2 4f b8 67 83 a3 2f cd 5d 41 42 4c 91 // 74 ef 2c ... 78 more bytes> @param length number of bytes to retrieve from …

title: Bun.Socket.getAuthorizationError()
text: getAuthorizationError(): Error | null; — Returns the reason why the peer's certificate was not verified. This is only set when `socket.authorized === false`.

title: Bun.Socket.getCertificate()
text: getCertificate(): import("tls").PeerCertificate | object | null; — Returns an object representing the local certificate. The returned object has some properties corresponding to the fields of the certificate. If there is no local certificate, an empty object is returned. If the socket has been destroyed, `null` is returned.

title: Bun.Socket.getCipher()
text: getCipher(): import("tls").CipherNameAndProtocol; — Returns an object containing information on the negotiated cipher suite. For example, a TLSv1.2 protocol with AES256-SHA cipher: ```json { "name": "AES256-SHA", "standardName": "TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA", "version": "SSLv3" }

title: Bun.Socket.getEphemeralKeyInfo()
text: getEphemeralKeyInfo(): import("tls").EphemeralKeyInfo | object | null; — Returns an object representing the type, name, and size of parameter of an ephemeral key exchange in `perfect forward secrecy` on a client connection. It returns an empty object when the key exchange is not ephemeral. This is only supported on a client socket; `null` is returned if called on a server socket. The supported types are `'DH'` and `'ECDH'`. The `name` property is available only when type is `'ECDH'`. For example: `{ type: 'ECDH', name: 'prime256v1', size: 256 }`.

title: Bun.Worker.postMessage()
text: postMessage(message: any, transfer: Transferable[]): void; — Clones message and transmits it to worker's global environment. transfer can be passed as a list of objects that are to be transferred rather than cloned. [MDN Reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Worker/postMessage)

title: Bun.Socket.getPeerCertificate()
text: getPeerCertificate(): import("node:tls").PeerCertificate; — Returns an object representing the peer's certificate. If the peer does not provide a certificate, an empty object is returned. If the socket has been destroyed, `null` is returned. If the full certificate chain was requested, each certificate includes an `issuerCertificate` property containing an object representing its issuer's certificate.

title: Bun.Socket.getSharedSigalgs()
text: getSharedSigalgs(): string[]; — See [SSL\_get\_shared\_sigalgs](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man1.1.1/man3/SSL_get_shared_sigalgs.html) for more information.

title: Bun.Socket.getTLSFinishedMessage()
text: getTLSFinishedMessage(): Buffer | undefined; — As the `Finished` messages are message digests of the complete handshake (with a total of 192 bits for TLS 1.0 and more for SSL 3.0), they can be used for external authentication procedures when the authentication provided by SSL/TLS is not desired or is not enough.

title: Bun.Socket.getTLSPeerFinishedMessage()
text: getTLSPeerFinishedMessage(): Buffer | undefined; — As the `Finished` messages are message digests of the complete handshake (with a total of 192 bits for TLS 1.0 and more for SSL 3.0), they can be used for external authentication procedures when the authentication provided by SSL/TLS is not desired or is not enough.

title: Bun.Socket.getTLSTicket()
text: getTLSTicket(): Buffer | undefined; — For a client, returns the TLS session ticket if one is available, or `undefined`. For a server, always returns `undefined`. It may be useful for debugging. See `Session Resumption` for more information.

title: Bun.Socket.getTLSVersion()
text: getTLSVersion(): string; — Returns a string containing the negotiated SSL/TLS protocol version of the current connection. The value `unknown` is returned for connected sockets that have not completed the handshaking process. The value `null` is returned for server sockets or disconnected client sockets. Protocol versions are: * `'SSLv3'` * `'TLSv1'` * `'TLSv1.1'` * `'TLSv1.2'` * `'TLSv1.3'`

title: Bun.Worker.terminate()
text: terminate(): void; — Aborts worker's associated global environment. [MDN Reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Worker/terminate)

title: Bun.Socket.isSessionReused()
text: isSessionReused(): boolean; — **TLS only:** Checks if the current TLS session was resumed from a previous session. See `Session Resumption` for more information.

title: Bun.Socket.setMaxSendFragment()
text: setMaxSendFragment(size: number): boolean; — Sets the maximum TLS fragment size. Returns `true` if setting the limit succeeded; `false` otherwise. Smaller fragment sizes decrease the buffering latency on the client: larger fragments are buffered by the TLS layer until the entire fragment is received and its integrity is verified; large fragments can span multiple roundtrips and their processing can be delayed due to packet loss or reordering. However, smaller fragments add extra TLS framing bytes and CPU overhead, which may decrease overall server throughput.

title: Bun.Socket.setNoDelay()
text: setNoDelay(noDelay?: boolean): boolean; — Enable/disable the use of Nagle's algorithm. Only available for already connected sockets; returns `false` otherwise

title: Bun.Socket.setKeepAlive()
text: setKeepAlive(enable?: boolean, initialDelay?: number): boolean; — Enable/disable keep-alive functionality, and optionally set the initial delay before the first keepalive probe is sent on an idle socket. Set `initialDelay` (in milliseconds) to set the delay between the last data packet received and the first keepalive probe. Setting `0` for `initialDelay` (the default) will leave the value unchanged from the default (or previous) setting. Only available for already connected sockets; returns `false` otherwise. Enabling the keep-alive functionality sets the following socket options: …

title: Bun.Socket.bytesWritten

title: Bun.Socket.renegotiate()

title: Bun.Socket.setVerifyMode()

title: Bun.Socket.exportKeyingMaterial()
text: exportKeyingMaterial(length: number, label: string, context?: string | BufferSource): void; — Exports the keying material of the socket.

title: Bun.Socket.close()
text: close(): void; — Closes the socket. This is a wrapper around `end()` and `shutdown()`.

title: Bun.Socket.getServername()
text: getServername(): string; — Returns the servername of the socket.

title: Bun.Socket.setServername()
text: setServername(name: string): void; — Sets the servername of the socket.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.open()
text: open?(socket: Socket ): void | Promise ; — Called when the socket connects. For TLS sockets with no `handshake` handler, this is called only after the handshake completes.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.error()
text: error?(socket: Socket , error: Error): void | Promise ; — Called when a handler throws, and when an established TLS session fails (a record that does not decrypt, a fatal alert from the peer). After a TLS failure the socket closes, with or without this handler.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.handshake()
text: handshake?(socket: Socket , success: boolean, authorizationError: Error | null): void; — Called when the TLS handshake completes.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.end()
text: end?(socket: Socket ): void | Promise ; — Called when the other end shuts down its side of the socket by sending a TCP FIN packet.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.connectError()
text: connectError?(socket: Socket , error: Error): void | Promise ; — Called when the socket fails to be created. The promise returned by `Bun.connect` rejects **after** this function is called. When `connectError` is specified, the rejected promise is not added to the promise rejection queue (so it isn't reported as an unhandled promise rejection, since `connectError` handles it). When `connectError` is not specified, the rejected promise is added to the promise rejection queue.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.timeout()
text: timeout?(socket: Socket ): void | Promise ; — Called when a message times out.

title: Bun.SocketHandler.binaryType

text: headers?: HeadersInit | undefined; — Custom headers to send to the proxy server. These headers are sent in the CONNECT request (for HTTPS targets) or in the proxy request (for HTTP targets).

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.tls
text: tls?: BunFetchRequestInitTLS | undefined; — TLS options for the connections of this session. A request that passes its own `tls` uses that instead, as a whole. A `checkServerIdentity` given here runs once per connection, and the connection is then shared by the requests of this session.

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.proxy
text: proxy?: FetchProxyOption | undefined; — The proxy for the requests of this session. The constructor throws for a value that names no proxy, such as a number or an object without a `url`. Only `undefined`, `null` and `""` mean no option. On a request, `fetch()` ignores such a value.

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.keepAlive
text: keepAlive?: — Connection reuse. `false` closes every connection after its response. The limits do not apply to HTTP/3 connections.

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.idleTimeout
text: idleTimeout?: number | undefined; — Seconds an idle connection stays in the pool before it is closed. The socket timer is coarse: it moves in 4 second steps up to four minutes, and in whole minutes beyond that. Bun rounds the value up to the timer, so a connection is never closed before `idleTimeout`, and it can stay open for up to two steps longer. The longest is 238 minutes (14280), and a larger value means that.

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.maxIdleSockets
text: maxIdleSockets?: number | undefined; — Most idle connections this session keeps per kind of connection (plain, TLS, each distinct `tls` configuration, Unix socket). When one more is released, the longest-idle one is closed. Without it the session has no limit of its own. The idle connections of all sessions and of plain `fetch()` share one bounded pool per kind, and when it is full Bun closes the longest-idle connection in it. A value above the size of that pool has no effect.

title: Bun.FetchSessionInit.unix
text: unix?: string | undefined; — Send the requests of this session over a Unix socket.

title: Bun.FetchSession
text: class FetchSession — Connection settings shared by the `fetch()` calls that name it, and the keep-alive connection pool they share. Connections are never shared between two sessions, or between a session and plain `fetch()`. @example ```ts const session = new Bun.FetchSession({ proxy: { url: "http://proxy.internal:8080", respectNoProxy: false }, tls: { ca: await Bun.file("corp-ca.pem").text() }, }); const response = await session.fetch("https://example.com"); // the same request, as an option of the global fetch(): await fetch("https://example.com", { session });

title: Bun.FetchSession.fetch
text: readonly fetch: (input: string | URL | Request, init?: BunFetchRequestInit) => Promise ; — `fetch()` with this session. The function is bound: hand it to anything that takes a `fetch`. A `session` in `init` does not replace this one. It has no `preconnect`, so where an option is typed `typeof fetch` (which in Bun includes `fetch.preconnect`), pass `session.fetch as typeof fetch`. @example ```ts const client = new SomeClient({ fetch: session.fetch });

Branch on these instead of parsing the message. - `ERR_IMAGE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED` — the requested format isn't available on this *machine* (HEIC/AVIF without the OS codec, TIFF on Linux). Catch this to fall back to a portable format. - `ERR_IMAGE_TOO_MANY_PIXELS` — header dimensions or resize output exceed `maxPixels`, a row of a PNG takes 4 GiB or more, or a path or `Bun.file()` input is over the 256 MiB cap. - `ERR_IMAGE_DECODE_FAILED` / `ERR_IMAGE_ENCODE_FAILED` — codec error. title: Bun.Image.ConstructorOptions.maxPixels
text: maxPixels?: number; — Reject inputs whose `width × height` exceeds this many pixels. The check runs after the header is read but before any pixel buffer is allocated, so a tiny file claiming a huge canvas is refused cheaply. A decoded image takes 4 bytes per pixel, which is 1 GiB at the default. A PNG of 32 KiB can decode to that size. Decoding a PNG that is one very wide row needs up to 20 bytes of memory per pixel, 5 GiB at the default. For untrusted input, set this to the largest image you accept.

title: Bun.Image
text: WebP codecs; resize and rotate are SIMD kernels — no native module install, no `sharp`. The constructor and every chainable method only *record* settings; the decode → transform → encode pipeline runs on a worker thread when a terminal (`bytes`, `buffer`, `blob`, `toBase64`, `metadata`) is awaited. Chainables overwrite (calling `.resize()` twice keeps the second). Order of execution is fixed regardless of call order: `autoOrient → rotate → flip/flop → resize → modulate`. The source ICC colour profile (Display P3, Adobe RGB, Jpegli XYB, etc.) is preserved through re-encode to JPEG, PNG, and …

title: Bun.Image.backend

Byte-identical to a Linux build; HEIC/AVIF reject with `ERR_IMAGE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED`. Set before awaiting a pipeline; in-flight tasks read the value as of when they were scheduled.

title: Bun.__internal.BunEventTarget.addEventListener()
text: addEventListener( — Adds a new handler for the `type` event. Any given `listener` is added only once per `type` and per `capture` option value. If the `once` option is true, the `listener` is removed after the next time a `type` event is dispatched. The `capture` option is not used by Node.js in any functional way other than tracking registered event listeners per the `EventTarget` specification. Specifically, the `capture` option is used as part of the key when registering a `listener`. Any individual `listener` may be added once with `capture = false`, and once with `capture = true`.

title: heapSize()
text: function heapSize(): number; — Returns the size of the JavaScript heap in bytes: the objects that survived the most recent garbage collection, plus the memory they own outside the heap (string contents, `ArrayBuffer` contents). Objects allocated since the last collection are not included, so call fullGC first for an up-to-date number. This is the `heapSize` field of heapStats without the rest of the statistics. For the memory usage of the whole process, use memoryUsage.

title: heapStats()
text: function heapStats(): HeapStats; — Returns statistics about the JavaScript heap, including a count of the live objects of each type. See HeapStats for what each field measures. Counting walks the whole heap, so this is much slower than heapSize. To find out what is leaking, compare `objectTypeCounts` from before and after the code you suspect, calling fullGC before each snapshot so that garbage that has not been collected yet does not show up in the difference. @example ```ts fullGC(); const before = heapStats().objectTypeCounts; await runSuspectedLeak(); fullGC(); const after = …

title: memoryUsage()
text: function memoryUsage(): MemoryUsage; — Returns memory statistics for the whole Bun process: resident set size, committed memory, and page faults. See MemoryUsage for what each field measures. Unlike heapSize and heapStats, this includes memory that is not part of the JavaScript heap.

title: bytecodeOrderStats()
text: function bytecodeOrderStats(): BytecodeOrderStats | null; — For an executable built with `bun build --compile --bytecode --bytecode-order`: how many functions this thread has loaded from each part of the bytecode the order file arranged. Returns `null` in any other process. See BytecodeOrderStats. @example ```ts const stats = bytecodeOrderStats(); if (stats) console.log(stats.cold / (stats.hot + stats.unknown + stats.cold));

title: getRandomSeed()
text: function getRandomSeed(): number; — Returns the seed of the pseudo-random number generator behind `Math.random()`. The seed is chosen at random when Bun starts; see setRandomSeed.

title: bun:jsc
text: declare module "bun:jsc" — Low-level access to JavaScriptCore, the engine Bun runs JavaScript on: garbage collection, heap and memory statistics, JIT controls, a sampling profiler, and structured-clone serialization. Most of these functions exist for debugging Bun itself and for benchmarks. The numbers they return describe JavaScriptCore internals. @example ```ts fullGC(); console.log(heapStats().objectTypeCounts.Promise ?? 0, "live promises");

title: setRandomSeed()
text: function setRandomSeed(value: number): void; — Reseeds the pseudo-random number generator behind `Math.random()`, making the values it returns reproducible: after setting the same seed, `Math.random()` returns the same sequence of values. The generator belongs to the current global object, so this does not affect `node:vm` contexts, and it has no effect on `node:crypto` or Web Crypto. @example ```ts setRandomSeed(42); const a = Math.random(); setRandomSeed(42); Math.random() === a; // true

title: isRope()
text: function isRope(input: string): boolean; — Returns whether a string is currently stored as a "rope". JavaScriptCore represents the result of string concatenation as a rope, a tree pointing at the pieces, and only copies the pieces into one contiguous buffer ("flattens" the rope) when something needs the characters, such as a comparison, `charCodeAt`, using the string as a property key, or passing it to native code. Once flattened, a string stays flat. Returns `false` for anything that is not a string. @example ```ts const s = "a".repeat(100) + "b".repeat(100); isRope(s); // true …

title: callerSourceOrigin()
text: function callerSourceOrigin(): string | null; — Returns the URL of the source file containing the code that called this function, such as `"file:///home/me/app/index.ts"`. Code created with `eval` or `new Function` reports the file that created it. Returns `null` when no JavaScript caller is on the stack, for example when this function itself is passed as a callback to `Promise.prototype.then`. JavaScriptCore performs proper tail calls in strict mode code, which includes every ES module, so a helper that does `return callerSourceOrigin()` reports the file of the helper's caller rather than its …

title: noFTL()
text: function noFTL(func: (...args: any[]) => any): void; — Prevents a function from ever being compiled by the FTL JIT, JavaScriptCore's highest optimization tier. The function can still reach the baseline and DFG tiers. Use it to check whether a bug or a performance difference is specific to FTL-compiled code. Only affects compilations that happen after the call, so call it before `func` gets hot. Does nothing if `func` is not a JavaScript function.

title: noOSRExitFuzzing()
text: function noOSRExitFuzzing(func: (...args: any[]) => any): void; — Excludes a function from OSR exit fuzzing. OSR exit fuzzing is a JavaScriptCore testing mode, enabled with the `BUN_JSC_useOSRExitFuzz=1` environment variable, in which optimized code randomly bails out ("OSR exits") to the baseline tier in order to test that bailing out is always correct. Has no effect unless fuzzing is enabled, and does nothing if `func` is not a JavaScript function.

title: optimizeNextInvocation()
text: function optimizeNextInvocation(func: (...args: any[]) => any): void; — Makes JavaScriptCore start optimizing a function (compiling it with the DFG JIT) the next time it is called, instead of waiting for the function to become hot on its own. Optimization happens on a background thread, so the optimized code is installed shortly after that call; poll numberOfDFGCompiles to find out when. Has no effect until the function has been called enough times to be compiled by the baseline JIT, and does nothing if `func` is not a JavaScript function.

title: numberOfDFGCompiles()
text: function numberOfDFGCompiles(func: (...args: any[]) => any): number; — Returns how many times a function has been optimized: `1` if the function currently has DFG- or FTL-compiled code, plus one for each time its optimized code has been thrown away (reoptimizationRetryCount). Returns `0` while the function is still running in the interpreter or the baseline JIT, and `1000000` when the JIT is disabled. @example ```ts function add(a: number, b: number) { return a + b; } // Run until the optimizing compiler has picked up `add` while (numberOfDFGCompiles(add) === 0) add(1, 2);

title: releaseWeakRefs()
text: function releaseWeakRefs(): void; — Releases the targets of `WeakRef`s so that a garbage collection can collect them immediately. As the JavaScript specification requires, creating a `WeakRef` or calling its `deref()` keeps the target alive until the end of the current job (the current synchronous run of script). That is why a `WeakRef` created in the same script as a fullGC call still holds its target afterwards; calling this first lets the collection clear it. @example ```ts let target: object | null = {}; const ref = new WeakRef(target); target = null; fullGC(); ref.deref(); // still the …

title: totalCompileTime()
text: function totalCompileTime(): number; — Returns the total time in milliseconds this process has spent JIT-compiling JavaScript, across the baseline, DFG, and FTL tiers. JavaScriptCore only records compile times when it is started with the `BUN_JSC_reportTotalCompileTimes=1` environment variable; otherwise this returns `0`.

title: reoptimizationRetryCount()
text: function reoptimizationRetryCount(func: (...args: any[]) => any): number; — Returns how many times JavaScriptCore has thrown away a function's optimized code because the assumptions it was compiled with turned out to be wrong (for example, a function that was only ever called with integers is called with a string), forcing the function to be optimized again. Each retry doubles how long the function has to run before it is optimized again, so a function with a high count is being deoptimized repeatedly. Returns `0` for functions that have not been compiled by the baseline JIT yet.

title: jscDescribe()
text: function jscDescribe(value: any): string; — Returns JavaScriptCore's debug description of a value: how the value is represented (`Int32`, `Double`, `String`, `Object`, and so on) and, for values on the heap, its address and its `Structure` (hidden class). Renamed from "describe" to avoid confusion with the test runner. @example ```ts jscDescribe(1); // "Int32: 1" jscDescribe({ a: 1 }); // "Object: 0x... with butterfly (nil) (Structure 0x...:[..., Object, (1/2, 0/0){a:0}, NonArray, ...]), StructureID: ..."

title: drainMicrotasks()
text: function drainMicrotasks(): void; — Runs every pending microtask right now: promise reactions, `queueMicrotask()` callbacks, and `process.nextTick()` callbacks. The event loop does not run: the callbacks of completed I/O, messages, and timers wait until the current callback returns. Microtasks normally run only after the current script or callback finishes; this lets synchronous code observe their effects immediately. @example ```ts let resolved = false; Promise.resolve().then(() => { resolved = true; }); drainMicrotasks(); resolved; // true

title: setTimeZone()
text: function setTimeZone(timeZone: string): string; — Sets the time zone used by `Intl`, `Date`, and other date and time APIs. You can also set the time zone with the `TZ` environment variable, and read the current one with `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`.

title: HeapStats
text: interface HeapStats — Statistics about the JavaScript heap, returned by heapStats. Sizes are in bytes. `heapSize` and `objectCount` only count the objects that survived the most recent garbage collection, while `objectTypeCounts` includes everything currently allocated, so call fullGC before taking a snapshot you intend to compare.

title: HeapStats.heapSize
text: heapSize: number; — Size of the objects that survived the most recent garbage collection, plus `extraMemorySize`. The same number heapSize returns.

title: HeapStats.heapCapacity
text: heapCapacity: number; — Memory the heap has reserved for holding objects, plus `extraMemorySize`. At least `heapSize`; the difference is space that new objects can be allocated into without growing the heap.

title: HeapStats.extraMemorySize
text: extraMemorySize: number; — Memory owned by objects in the heap but allocated outside of it, such as the contents of strings and `ArrayBuffer`s. Included in both `heapSize` and `heapCapacity`.

title: HeapStats.objectCount
text: objectCount: number; — Number of cells that survived the most recent garbage collection. Every garbage-collected allocation is a cell: objects, strings, functions, and JavaScriptCore's internal structures alike.

title: HeapStats.protectedObjectCount
text: protectedObjectCount: number; — Number of cells that native code has protected from being garbage collected. getProtectedObjects returns them.

title: HeapStats.globalObjectCount
text: globalObjectCount: number; — Number of global objects in the heap: one for the main script, plus one for each `node:vm` context.

title: HeapStats.protectedGlobalObjectCount
text: protectedGlobalObjectCount: number; — How many of the global objects are protected by native code.

title: HeapStats.objectTypeCounts
text: objectTypeCounts: Record ; — Number of live cells of each type, keyed by JavaScriptCore's name for the type: JavaScript classes such as `Object`, `Array`, `Promise`, and `Function`, engine-internal types such as `Structure` and `FunctionExecutable`, and `string` for primitive strings. Ordered from most to least common; types with no live instances are omitted. Unlike `objectCount`, this includes cells allocated since the last garbage collection.

title: HeapStats.protectedObjectTypeCounts
text: protectedObjectTypeCounts: Record ; — Like `objectTypeCounts`, but counting only the cells included in `protectedObjectCount`.

title: BytecodeOrderStats
text: interface BytecodeOrderStats — Returned by bytecodeOrderStats. Counts are per thread: a `Worker` has its own. A function whose bytecode was discarded and loaded again counts again. Sizes are in bytes.

title: BytecodeOrderStats.hot
text: hot: number; — Functions loaded that the order file's run had used.

title: BytecodeOrderStats.unknown
text: unknown: number; — Functions loaded that the build the order file was recorded from did not have.

title: BytecodeOrderStats.cold
text: cold: number; — Functions loaded that the order file's run had not used.

title: BytecodeOrderStats.regions
text: regions: — The size of each part of the bytecode, in the order they are stored.

title: MemoryUsage
text: interface MemoryUsage — Memory statistics for the whole process, returned by memoryUsage. Sizes are in bytes.

title: MemoryUsage.current
text: current: number; — The physical memory the process is using right now. The same measurement as `process.memoryUsage().rss`: the resident set size on Linux and Windows, and on macOS the memory footprint that Activity Monitor shows (`phys_footprint`, which also counts compressed pages and leaves out clean file-backed ones).

title: MemoryUsage.peak
text: peak: number; — The largest value `current` has had over the life of the process.

title: jscDescribeArray()
text: function jscDescribeArray(array: any[]): string; — Describes the storage behind an object's indexed elements: the address of its "butterfly" (the out-of-line buffer JavaScriptCore keeps elements in), the public `length`, and the "vector length" (the number of element slots allocated, which can exceed `length`). Returns `"<not object>"` for primitives. @example ```ts jscDescribeArray([1, 2, 3]); // "<Butterfly: 0x...; public length: 3; vector length: 3>"

title: MemoryUsage.currentCommit
text: currentCommit: number; — On macOS and Linux, the memory currently committed by [mimalloc](https://github.com/microsoft/mimalloc), the allocator Bun uses for memory outside the JavaScript heap. On Windows, the process's commit charge.

title: MemoryUsage.peakCommit
text: peakCommit: number; — The largest value `currentCommit` has had.

title: MemoryUsage.pageFaults
text: pageFaults: number; — On macOS and Linux, the number of major page faults (faults that had to read from disk) the process has taken. On Windows, the total number of page faults.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame
text: interface SamplingProfileStackFrame — One sampled stack frame in a SamplingProfileStackTraces trace.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.sourceID
text: sourceID: number; — Identifies the source file; matches the `sourceID` of an entry in SamplingProfileStackTraces.sources. `4294967295` for native functions, which have no source.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.name
text: name: string; — The function's name, `""` for anonymous functions, or `"(module)"` for a module's top-level code.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.location
text: location: string; — Where in the function the sample landed, as the function's code hash, the tier, and the bytecode index, for example `"#A4IKxq:Baseline:bc#78"`. This is the same notation SamplingProfile.bytecodes uses. `"#<nil>:None:<nil>"` for native functions.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.sourceURL
text: sourceURL?: string; — Path or URL of the source file (or the specifier of a built-in module, such as `"node:events"`), mapped through its source map when it has one. Absent for native functions.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.line
text: line: number; — 1-based line of the sampled location. `4294967295` when unknown, such as for native functions.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.column
text: column: number; — 1-based column of the sampled location. `4294967295` when unknown.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.category
text: category: string; — The tier the function was running in when sampled: `"LLInt"`, `"Baseline"`, `"DFG"`, or `"FTL"` for JavaScript functions, `"AOT"` for a function compiled ahead of time, or one of the other names from the tier breakdown in SamplingProfile.bytecodes (native functions show up as `"Unknown Executable"`).

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.flags
text: flags: number; — `1` if the function is part of the JavaScript built into Bun (JavaScriptCore's own builtins and Bun's built-in modules such as `node:events`), `0` if it is yours.

title: SamplingProfileStackFrame.inliner
text: inliner?: — Present when the function had been inlined into another function's optimized code: describes the function it was inlined into and the position in it.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces
text: interface SamplingProfileStackTraces — The raw samples collected by the sampling profiler, as SamplingProfile.stackTraces.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.interval
text: interval: number; — How often the stack was sampled, in seconds (`0.001` for the default interval of 1000 microseconds).

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.traces
text: traces: Array< — One entry per sample, in the order they were taken.

title: gcAndSweep()
text: function gcAndSweep(): number; — Runs a full garbage collection and then sweeps the heap, all synchronously, so the memory of every unreachable object has been freed by the time this returns. fullGC does the same collection but leaves the sweep to happen lazily afterwards.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.timestamp
text: timestamp: number; — When the sample was taken, in seconds on a monotonic clock. Only the differences between samples are meaningful.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.frames
text: frames: SamplingProfileStackFrame[]; — The stack at the time of the sample, innermost frame first.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.sources
text: sources: Array< — The source files the sampled frames belong to. Native functions have no source and are not listed.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.sourceID
text: sourceID: number; — The ID that SamplingProfileStackFrame.sourceID refers to.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.url
text: url?: string; — Path or URL of the file, or the specifier of a built-in module such as `"node:events"`. Absent for sources without one, such as code passed to `eval`.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.sourceURL
text: sourceURL?: string; — The file's `//# sourceURL=` directive, if it has one.

title: SamplingProfileStackTraces.sourceMappingURL
text: sourceMappingURL?: string; — The file's `//# sourceMappingURL=` directive, if it has one.

title: SamplingProfile
text: interface SamplingProfile — The result of profile: two human-readable reports plus the raw samples they were computed from.

title: SamplingProfile.functions
text: functions: string; — A formatted summary of the functions that were most often at the top of the stack when a sample was taken (that is, ranked by self time). Each entry shows the number of samples, the function name, its code hash, and the ID of its source file. Example output: ```js Sampling rate: 100.000000 microseconds. Total samples: 6858 Top functions as <numSamples 'functionName#hash:sourceID'> 2948 '#<nil>:8' 393 'visit#<nil>:8' 263 'push#<nil>:8' 164 'scan_ref_scoped#<nil>:8' 164 'walk#<nil>:8' 144 'pop#<nil>:8' 107 'extract_candidates#<nil>:8' 94 'get#<nil>:8' 82 …

title: SamplingProfile.bytecodes
text: bytecodes: string; — A formatted breakdown of the samples by execution tier, followed by the individual bytecode locations that were sampled most often. Useful for seeing which tier hot code is running in: time spent in `LLInt` or `Baseline` means the code has not been optimized (yet). Example output: ```js Tier breakdown: LLInt: 106 (1.545640%) Baseline: 2355 (34.339458%) DFG: 3290 (47.973170%) FTL: 833 (12.146398%) js builtin: 132 (1.924759%) Wasm: 0 (0.000000%) Host: 111 (1.618548%) RegExp: 15 (0.218723%) C/C++: 0 (0.000000%) Unknown Executable: 148 (2.158064%) Hottest bytecodes as …

title: SamplingProfile.stackTraces
text: stackTraces: SamplingProfileStackTraces; — The raw samples: the full stack captured at each sampling interval, which is what `functions` and `bytecodes` are computed from. Use this to build your own reports, such as a flame graph or inclusive timings.

title: fullGC()
text: function fullGC(): number; — Runs a full garbage collection synchronously: every object in the heap is visited, and everything unreachable becomes garbage. Compare edenGC, which only looks at recent allocations. The garbage's memory is reclaimed lazily as the heap is swept afterwards; gcAndSweep also does the sweep before returning. Unlike `Bun.gc(true)`, this does not release the targets of `WeakRef`s (releaseWeakRefs) and does not touch memory outside the JavaScript heap.

title: profile()
text: function profile any>( — Runs JavaScriptCore's sampling profiler on a function and returns the profile. The profiler records the JavaScript stack every `sampleInterval` microseconds while `callback` runs, then stops. The profile summarizes where the samples landed; see SamplingProfile. If `callback` throws, the profiler stops and the exception propagates. Tier names in the output: - LLInt ("Low Level Interpreter") is the interpreter that runs before any JIT compilation - Baseline is the first JIT compilation tier: the least optimized, but the fastest to compile - DFG ("Data Flow Graph") is the …

title: getProtectedObjects()
text: function getProtectedObjects(): any[]; — Returns objects that native code has explicitly protected from being garbage collected. Calling this function creates another reference to each object, which further prevents it from being garbage collected. This is mostly a debugging tool for Bun itself. Warning: not all of the returned objects are supposed to be observable from JavaScript.

title: startRemoteDebugger()
text: function startRemoteDebugger(host?: string, port?: number): void; — Starts a remote debugging socket server on the given port. This exposes JavaScriptCore's built-in debugging server. It is separate from Bun's debugger (`bun --inspect`). This is untested and may not be supported on macOS.

title: startSamplingProfiler()
text: function startSamplingProfiler(optionalDirectory?: string, sampleInterval?: number): void; — Starts JavaScriptCore's sampling profiler and leaves it running for the rest of the process. To profile one function and get the result back as a value, use profile instead.

title: estimateShallowMemoryUsageOf()
text: function estimateShallowMemoryUsageOf(value: object | CallableFunction | bigint | symbol | string): number; — Non-recursively estimates the memory usage of an object, excluding the memory usage of properties or other objects it references. For more accurate per-object memory usage, use Bun.generateHeapSnapshot. The estimate is best-effort. When it's wrong, the memory may be non-contiguous (such as a large array). Passing a primitive type that isn't heap allocated returns 0.

title: edenGC()
text: function edenGC(): number; — Runs an eden (young generation) garbage collection synchronously. JavaScriptCore's collector is generational: an eden collection only examines objects allocated since the previous collection, so it is much cheaper than fullGC, but it cannot free an object that survived an earlier collection.

title: StreamOptions.windowsHandle
text: windowsHandle?: bigint | undefined; — A raw Win32 `HANDLE` to read from or write to, in place of a path or `fd`. Use it for a handle that is not a CRT file descriptor, such as an anonymous pipe handle inherited from another process. The stream wraps the handle in a file descriptor that it owns and closes. Windows only: on other platforms the constructor throws `ERR_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE_ON_PLATFORM`. It cannot be combined with `fd` or `fs`.

title: BunConnectionOptions.ca
text: ca?: string | Buffer | NodeJS.TypedArray | Bun.BunFile | Array | undefined; — Override the trusted CA certificates. The default is the list of well-known CAs curated by Mozilla; setting this option replaces that list entirely.

title: BunConnectionOptions.cert
text: cert?: — Cert chains in PEM format. Provide one cert chain per private key. Each chain consists of the PEM certificate for its private key, followed by the PEM intermediate certificates (if any) in order, not including the root CA (the root CA must be pre-known to the peer, see `ca`). Multiple cert chains do not have to be in the same order as their private keys in `key`. Without the intermediate certificates, the peer cannot validate the certificate and the handshake fails.

title: BunConnectionOptions.key
text: key?: — Private keys in PEM format. PEM keys may be encrypted. Multiple keys using different algorithms can be provided either as an array of unencrypted key strings or buffers, or as an array of objects in the form `{pem: <string|buffer>[, passphrase: <string>]}`. The object form can only occur in an array, and `object.passphrase` is optional. Encrypted keys are decrypted with `object.passphrase` if provided, otherwise with `options.passphrase`.

title: Bun.RedisClient.bzmpop()
text: bzmpop( — Blocking version of ZMPOP. Blocks until a member is available or timeout expires. @example ```ts // Block for 5 seconds waiting for a member const result1 = await redis.bzmpop(5, 1, "myzset", "MIN"); // Returns: ["myzset", ["member1", 1]] or null if timeout // Block indefinitely (timeout 0) const result2 = await redis.bzmpop(0, 2, "zset1", "zset2", "MAX"); // Returns: ["zset1", ["member5", 5]] // Block with COUNT option const result3 = await redis.bzmpop(1, 1, "myzset", "MIN", "COUNT", 2); // Returns: ["myzset", [["member1", 1], ["member2", 2]]] or null if timeout

title: Bun.Server
text: interface Server extends Disposable — HTTP & HTTPS Server To start the server, see serve For performance, Bun pre-allocates most of the data for 2048 concurrent requests. That means starting a new server allocates about 500 KB of memory. Try to avoid starting and stopping the server often (unless it's a new instance of bun). Powered by a fork of [uWebSockets](https://github.com/uNetworking/uWebSockets).

title: Bun.Server.stop()
text: stop(closeActiveConnections?: boolean): Promise ; — Stop listening to prevent new connections from being accepted. By default, it does not cancel in-flight requests or websockets. Idle keep-alive connections are closed right away, and connections with a request in flight close as soon as their response completes. That means it may take some time before all network activity stops. The returned promise resolves once every connection is closed.

title: Bun.Server.closeIdleConnections()

title: Bun.ServerWebSocketSendStatus
text: type ServerWebSocketSendStatus = number; — A status that represents the outcome of a sent message. - if **0**, the message was **dropped**. - if **-1**, there is **backpressure** of messages. - if **>0**, it represents the **number of bytes sent**. Sending an empty payload (`ws.send("")`, `ws.ping()`, `ws.pong()`) succeeds but also returns **0**. @example ```js const status = ws.send("Hello!"); if (status === 0) { console.log("Message was dropped"); } else if (status === -1) { console.log("Backpressure was applied"); } else { console.log(`Success! Sent ${status} bytes`); }

The `message`, `open`, and `drain` callbacks are automatically corked, so you only need to call this if you are sending messages outside of those callbacks or in async functions. @example ```ts ws.cork((ctx) => { ctx.send("These messages"); ctx.sendText("are sent"); ctx.sendBinary(new TextEncoder().encode("together!")); });

The declared type of `message` is the one of the default `binaryType`.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.maxPayloadLength
text: maxPayloadLength?: number; — Sets the maximum size of a received message, in bytes, after decompression. Larger messages close the connection with code `1009`. An integer from `0` to `4294967295`. Larger values are clamped. `0` means only empty messages are accepted.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.backpressureLimit
text: backpressureLimit?: number; — Sets the maximum number of bytes that can be buffered on a single connection. Past the limit, `send()` drops the message and returns `0`. An integer from `0` to `4294967295`. Larger values are clamped. `0` means no limit.

text: idleTimeout?: number; — Sets the number of seconds to wait before timing out a connection due to no messages or pings. An integer from `0` to `960`. `0` disables the timeout and the automatic pings from `sendPings`. `1` to `7` round up to `8`.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.publishToSelf

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.sendPings
text: sendPings?: boolean; — Whether the server pings a client shortly before `idleTimeout` expires, which keeps idle connections open as long as the client responds. The server always replies to client pings with a pong.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.perMessageDeflate
text: perMessageDeflate?: — Enables the permessage-deflate extension, for clients that support it. `true` is the same as `{ compress: "shared", decompress: "shared" }`.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.compress
text: compress?: WebSocketCompressor | boolean; — The compressor for messages the server sends. - `"shared"` or `true`: one compressor for all sockets, reset after each message. - `"dedicated"` or a size: one compressor per socket that keeps context across messages. Compresses better, but uses that much memory per socket. `"dedicated"` is the same as `"256KB"`. - `"disable"` or `false`: never compress, even if `send()` passes `true`.

title: Bun.WebSocketHandler.decompress
text: decompress?: WebSocketCompressor | boolean; — The decompressor for messages the server receives. - `"shared"` or `true`: one decompressor for all sockets. Clients are told to reset their compressor after each message. - `"dedicated"` or a size: one decompressor per socket. The size is the window size, capped at 32 KB. `"dedicated"`, `"64KB"` and larger mean `"32KB"`. `"3KB"` means 2 KB. - `"disable"` or `false`: no per-socket decompressor. permessage-deflate can't stop a client from compressing, so this falls back to `"shared"` if `compress` is enabled.
