title: Bun.SQL.ColumnTransform.to
text: to?: ((name: string) => string) | undefined; — Renames a name that goes to the database: the keys of `sql(object)`, the columns picked in `sql(object, "a", "b")`, and every `sql("name")`, table names included.

title: Bun.SQL.Transform
text: interface Transform — The `transform` option @example ```ts const sql = new SQL({ transform: SQL.camel }); await sql`INSERT INTO users ${sql({ firstName: "Alice" })}`; // "first_name" const [user] = await sql`SELECT first_name FROM users`; console.log(user.firstName);

title: Bun.SQL.Transform.column
text: column?: ((name: string) => string) | ColumnTransform | undefined; — Renames columns. A function means ColumnTransform.from.

title: Bun.ReservedSQL.close()
text: close(options?: { timeout?: number }): Promise ; — Closes the connection instead of returning it to the pool.

title: Bun.SQL.Transform.undefined
text: undefined?: unknown; — The value that Bun sends for an `undefined` parameter. When it is set (`null` counts), the insert and update helpers leave no column out. Without it, `undefined` is `NULL`, and the helpers leave out a column that is `undefined`.

title: Bun.SQL.NameTransform
text: interface NameTransform — One of `SQL.toCamel`, `SQL.fromCamel` and the like. Call it to convert a name, or pass it as the `transform` option to rename in one direction.

title: Bun.SQL.camel
text: const camel: { readonly column: Required }; — `transform` preset: `user_id` in the database, `userId` in JavaScript

title: Bun.SQL.pascal
text: const pascal: { readonly column: Required }; — `transform` preset: `user_id` in the database, `UserId` in JavaScript

title: Bun.SQL.kebab
text: const kebab: { readonly column: Required }; — `transform` preset: `user_id` in the database, `user-id` in JavaScript

title: Bun.SQL.toCamel
text: const toCamel: NameTransform; — `"user_id"` to `"userId"`. As `transform`, renames the columns of results only.

title: Bun.SQL.toPascal
text: const toPascal: NameTransform; — `"user_id"` to `"UserId"`. As `transform`, renames the columns of results only.

title: Bun.SQL.toKebab
text: const toKebab: NameTransform; — `"user_id"` to `"user-id"`. As `transform`, renames the columns of results only.

title: Bun.SQL.fromCamel
text: const fromCamel: NameTransform; — `"userId"` to `"user_id"`. As `transform`, renames the names in `sql()` helpers only.

title: Bun.SQL.fromPascal
text: const fromPascal: NameTransform; — `"UserId"` to `"user_id"`. As `transform`, renames the names in `sql()` helpers only.

title: Bun.SQL.fromKebab
text: const fromKebab: NameTransform; — `"user-id"` to `"user_id"`. As `transform`, renames the names in `sql()` helpers only.

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.adapter
text: adapter?: "sqlite"; — Selects the SQLite adapter. Optional when filename is set, because a `filename` selects SQLite too.

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.filename
text: filename?: URL | ":memory:" | (string & {}) | undefined; — Path to the database file Examples: - `sqlite://:memory:` - `sqlite://./path/to/database.db` - `sqlite:///Users/bun/projects/my-app/database.db` - `./dev.db` - `:memory:` Everything from the first `?` is a query string, which can have `mode=`: `ro` (read-only), `rw` (read-write, the file must exist) or `rwc` (read-write and create, the default). `memory` has no effect, and any other mode throws. The `readonly` and `create` options take priority over it, and a read-only database ignores `create` and `readwrite`. Without a `filename`, …

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.url
text: url?: URL | string | undefined; — The same as filename, which takes priority. Needs `adapter: "sqlite"` unless the value is a `sqlite:` or `file:` URL.

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.bigint
text: bigint?: boolean | undefined; — Return every integer as a `BigInt`. The same as `safeIntegers`, under the name that the other adapters use. `safeIntegers` takes priority.

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.transform
text: transform?: Transform | NameTransform | undefined; — Renames columns between the database and JavaScript, for example SQL.camel

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.onconnect
text: onconnect?: ((err: Error | null) => void) | undefined; — SQLite: called once, when Bun has tried to open the database. Receives `null`, or the `Error` that kept it from opening (for example `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`).

title: Bun.SQL.SQLiteOptions.onclose
text: onclose?: ((err: Error | null) => void) | undefined; — SQLite: called when SQL.close closes the database. Receives an `Error` with the message `"Connection closed"`, not `null`.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.url
text: url?: URL | string | undefined; — Connection URL, for example `postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb`. For each setting, an option takes priority over the URL, and the URL over the environment. Without `url` and without a connection string, Bun reads a URL from the environment, such as `DATABASE_URL`, and the other options change single fields of it. With `adapter`, a `DATABASE_URL` that names another adapter's server is not used, except for the TLS mode it asks for when no other URL applies.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.host
text: host?: string | undefined; — Database server hostname

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.hostname
text: hostname?: string | undefined; — Database server hostname. For PostgreSQL, a value that starts with `/` is the directory of a unix socket.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.port
text: port?: number | string | undefined; — Database server port number

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.username
text: username?: string | undefined; — Database user for authentication

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.user
text: user?: string | undefined; — Database user for authentication (alias for username)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.password
text: password?: string | (() => MaybePromise ) | undefined; — Database password for authentication

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.pass
text: pass?: string | (() => MaybePromise ) | undefined; — Database password for authentication (alias for password)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.database
text: database?: string | undefined; — Name of the database to connect to. `PGDATABASE`, `MYSQL_DATABASE` and `MARIADB_DATABASE` take priority over the database in a URL.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.db
text: db?: string | undefined; — Name of the database to connect to (alias for database)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.adapter
text: adapter?: "postgres" | "mysql" | "mariadb"; — Database adapter/driver to use. Takes priority over the protocol of the URL. `"mariadb"` uses the MySQL driver and reads the `MARIADB_*` environment variables instead of `MYSQL_*`.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.idleTimeout
text: idleTimeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds a connection can sit idle before it is closed. A connection that runs a query, is reserved, or has an open transaction is not idle.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.idle_timeout
text: idle_timeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds a connection can sit idle before it is closed (alias for idleTimeout)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.connectionTimeout
text: connectionTimeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds to wait when establishing a connection. Does not limit how long a query runs.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.connection_timeout
text: connection_timeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds to wait when establishing a connection (alias for connectionTimeout)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.connectTimeout
text: connectTimeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds to wait when establishing a connection (alias for connectionTimeout)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.connect_timeout
text: connect_timeout?: number | undefined; — Maximum time in seconds to wait when establishing a connection (alias for connectionTimeout)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.maxLifetime
text: maxLifetime?: number | undefined; — Maximum lifetime in seconds of a connection. A connection that is busy at that moment finishes its queries, its transaction or its reservation first. It takes no new queries, and then closes.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.max_lifetime
text: max_lifetime?: number | undefined; — Maximum lifetime in seconds of a connection (alias for maxLifetime)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.tls
text: tls?: — Whether to use TLS/SSL for the connection. A string selects the SSL mode (`"disable"`, `"allow"`, `"prefer"`, `"require"`, `"verify-ca"`, `"verify-full"`). A `BunFile` is the CA certificate to verify the server against, the same as `{ ca: Bun.file(path) }`, and selects `"verify-full"`. `true` and an options object ask for at least `"require"`. An object with `ca`, `caFile`, `checkServerIdentity` or `rejectUnauthorized: true` raises a mode below `"verify-ca"` to `"verify-full"`. Without `rejectUnauthorized`, `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` turns certificate verification off in every …

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.ssl
text: ssl?: — Whether to use TLS/SSL for the connection (alias for tls)

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.path
text: path?: string | undefined; — Unix domain socket to connect through instead of TCP to `hostname:port`. For PostgreSQL, a directory resolves to `<path>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`. A path that does not exist fails the connection. Also the `?path=` parameter of the URL.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.socket
text: socket?: string | undefined; — Unix domain socket to connect through (alias for path). Also the `?socket=` parameter of the URL.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.onconnect
text: onconnect?: ((err: Error | null) => void) | undefined; — PostgreSQL and MySQL: called once for each connection that opens, always with `null`. Bun reports a failed connection attempt to onclose, not here.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.onclose
text: onclose?: ((err: Error | null) => void) | undefined; — PostgreSQL and MySQL: called once for each connection that closes or fails to connect, with the `Error` that says why. It is never `null`: after SQL.close the code is `ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_CLOSED` or `ERR_MYSQL_CONNECTION_CLOSED`. A failed attempt passes its own error, for example `ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_REFUSED`.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.connection
text: connection?: Record | undefined; — PostgreSQL only. Runtime configuration parameters that Bun sends when it opens a connection, for example `{ application_name: "api", search_path: "app" }`.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.max
text: max?: number | undefined; — Maximum number of connections in the pool

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.bigint
text: bigint?: boolean | undefined; — Return large integers as `BigInt`. By default they are returned as strings. PostgreSQL: every `int8`, whatever its value. MySQL: `BIGINT` values outside the 32-bit range, and a `lastInsertRowid` above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.prepare
text: prepare?: boolean | undefined; — PostgreSQL only. Use named prepared statements. Each connection keeps the 1,024 it used last. `false` throws for MySQL and does nothing for MariaDB.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.allowPublicKeyRetrieval
text: allowPublicKeyRetrieval?: boolean | undefined; — MySQL only. Allow the client to request the server's RSA public key during `caching_sha2_password` / `sha256_password` authentication when the connection is not protected by TLS. Disabled by default because a network attacker can substitute their own key and recover the plaintext password. Enable only for trusted local connections, or use TLS instead. Not needed over TLS, where Bun sends the password directly. `caching_sha2_password` does not need it over a unix socket either. `sha256_password` does.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.foundRows
text: foundRows?: boolean | undefined; — MySQL and MariaDB only. Report the rows that the `WHERE` clause of an `UPDATE` matched in `affectedRows`, as `mysql2`, the `mariadb` connector, PostgreSQL and SQLite do. Without it, the server counts only the rows whose values changed, so an `UPDATE` that sets a row to the values it already has reports `0`. Also the `?foundRows=` parameter of the URL.

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.channelBinding
text: channelBinding?: "disable" | "prefer" | "require" | undefined; — PostgreSQL only. Whether a SCRAM login over TLS is tied to the server's certificate (SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS), so that someone who terminates TLS between the client and the server cannot pass the login on. - `"prefer"`: binds the login when the connection uses TLS and the server offers it - `"require"`: only accepts a bound login. Otherwise the connection fails with `ERR_POSTGRES_CHANNEL_BINDING_REQUIRED`: without TLS, and when the server asks for an MD5 password, a clear text password, or none. - `"disable"`: never binds the login …

title: Bun.SQL.PostgresOrMySQLOptions.transform
text: transform?: Transform | NameTransform | undefined; — Renames columns between the database and JavaScript, for example SQL.camel

title: Bun.SQL.Options
text: type Options = SQLiteOptions | PostgresOrMySQLOptions; — Configuration options for SQL client connection and behavior @example ```ts const config: Bun.SQL.Options = { hostname: localhost, port: 5432, username: dbuser, password: secretpass, database: myapp, idleTimeout: 30, max: 20, onconnect: (err) => { if (!err) console.log('Connected to database'); } };

title: Bun.SQL.ListenSubscription
text: interface ListenSubscription extends AsyncDisposable — One registration made by SQL.listen.

title: Bun.SQL.ListenSubscription.unlisten()
text: unlisten(): Promise ; — Remove this registration. Resolves once the channel is no longer subscribed, or immediately when other registrations on it remain. Idempotent; `await using` calls it at the end of the scope.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn
text: interface ResultColumn — A column of a PostgreSQL or MySQL result, as the server described it @example ```ts const result = await sql`SELECT id, data FROM posts`; console.log(result.columns); // PostgreSQL: // [ // { name: "id", type: 23, table: 16388, number: 1 }, // int4 // { name: "data", type: 3802, table: 16388, number: 2 }, // jsonb // ]

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.name
text: name: string; — The name of the column in the result

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.type
text: type: number; — The type of the column. - PostgreSQL: the OID of the type, such as `23` for `int4`, `25` for `text`, `1009` for `text[]`, `3802` for `jsonb` - MySQL: the type code of the protocol, such as `3` for `INT`, `8` for `BIGINT`, `253` for `VARCHAR`, `245` for `JSON`

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.table
text: table: number | string; — The table that the column comes from. - PostgreSQL: the OID of the table. `0` for an expression. - MySQL: the name of the table, or its alias in the query. `""` for an expression.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.number
text: number?: number; — PostgreSQL only. The number of the column in its table, from `1`. `0` for an expression, negative for a system column such as `ctid`.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.length
text: length?: number; — MySQL only. The length of the column, as the server sent it

title: Bun.SQL.ResultColumn.flags
text: flags?: number; — MySQL only. The flags of the column, as the server sent them

title: Bun.SQL.ResultStatement
text: interface ResultStatement — The statement that produced a PostgreSQL or MySQL result. The runs of one prepared statement on one connection share one object. Treat it as read-only.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultStatement.string
text: string: string; — The text that Bun sent, with `$1` or `?` for each parameter

title: Bun.SQL.ResultStatement.types
text: types: number[]; — The types of the parameters, as the server reported them: OIDs on PostgreSQL, type codes on MySQL. MariaDB does not type parameters, so each one is `6`. Empty for a query without parameters.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultStatement.columns
text: columns: ResultColumn[]; — The same array as ResultMetadata.columns

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata
text: interface ResultMetadata — Properties of the array that a query resolves to, next to the rows. They are accessors on the prototype, not own properties, so `console.log`, `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` and spreading only see the rows. A query with several statements (`.simple()`, a MySQL `CALL`) resolves to a plain array of results. The metadata is on each inner array.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.count
text: count: number; — The number of rows returned, or the number of rows written when the statement returns none

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.affectedRows
text: affectedRows: number; — The number of rows that an `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE` wrote. `0` for a statement that writes nothing. PostgreSQL tags `CREATE TABLE AS`, and a `SELECT` whose CTE writes, as `SELECT`, so it is `0` for them. MariaDB reports `INSERT ... RETURNING` as a result set, so it is `0` there too.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.lastInsertRowid
text: lastInsertRowid: number | bigint | string | null; — The key that an `INSERT` generated. - PostgreSQL: `null`. Use `RETURNING`. - MySQL: the first `AUTO_INCREMENT` value of the statement, `0` if there is none. Above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` it is a string, or a `BigInt` with `bigint: true`. - SQLite: the `rowid` of the last inserted row, also after a statement that inserts nothing. `null` for a statement that only reads. A `BigInt` with `safeIntegers: true` or `bigint: true`.

title: Bun.SQLArrayParameter
text: interface SQLArrayParameter — An array parameter created by SQL.array

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.command
text: command: string | null; — The kind of statement. PostgreSQL: the command tag, such as `"INSERT"` or `"CREATE TABLE"`. SQLite: the first keyword. MySQL: `null`, because the protocol does not report it.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.columns
text: columns: ResultColumn[] | null; — The columns of the result, also when it has no rows and with `.values()` or `.raw()`. Empty for a statement that returns no rows, such as a plain `INSERT`. `null` on SQLite.

title: Bun.SQL.ResultMetadata.statement
text: statement: ResultStatement | null; — The text, the parameter types and the columns of the statement. `null` on SQLite.

title: Bun.SQLArrayParameter.serializedValues
text: serializedValues: string; — The array values, serialized into a single string

title: Bun.SQL.Query
text: interface Query extends Promise — A pending SQL query. Extends `Promise`, so it can be awaited, and adds methods to control how it runs. The array it resolves to also has ResultMetadata. A query is lazy. It starts in the call to `then()`, `catch()`, `finally()` or execute, and `await` calls `then()`. What `then()` and `catch()` return is a promise like any other: when it rejects with nothing to handle the rejection, that is reported as an unhandled rejection. So is an error that a `finally()` callback throws. The failure of a query that was only started, with `execute()` or `finally()`, is not …

title: Bun.SQL.Query.active
text: active: boolean; — True while a connection runs the query

title: Bun.SQL.Query.cancelled
text: cancelled: boolean; — True after cancel was called

title: Bun.SQL.Query.cancel()
text: cancel(): Query ; — Cancels the query. A query that Bun has not sent yet never runs. It rejects with `ERR_POSTGRES_QUERY_CANCELLED` (or the `MYSQL` / `SQLITE` code). PostgreSQL: Bun asks the server to stop a running query, on a second connection. The query rejects with the server's error, `errno` `"57014"`, or resolves if it ends first. A query that Bun sent behind another one, or that has another one sent behind it, rejects with `ERR_POSTGRES_QUERY_CANCELLED` and a `hint`, because the server may still run it. MySQL: a query that Bun has sent runs to the end and settles with its result.

title: Bun.SQL.Query.simple()
text: simple(): Query ; — Executes the query as a simple query. Parameters are not allowed, but the query can contain multiple commands separated by semicolons.

title: Bun.SQLArrayParameter.arrayType
text: arrayType: ArrayType | undefined; — The element type of the array, for example `"INT"`. `undefined` when no type was given: Bun adds no cast, and the server infers the type.

title: Bun.SQL.Query.readable()
text: readable(): ReadableStream >; — PostgreSQL only. Starts a `COPY ... TO STDOUT` query and returns the bytes that the server sends, in the format that the statement names. A chunk can end in the middle of a row. Call it before the query starts. The query takes no parameters, and resolves with the row count in `count` when the server has finished. A failure reaches the stream, so the query needs no handler of its own. @example ```ts await Bun.write("users.csv", new Response(sql`COPY users TO STDOUT (FORMAT csv)`.readable()));

title: Bun.SQL.Query.writable()
text: writable(): WritableStream ; — PostgreSQL only. Starts a `COPY ... FROM STDIN` query and returns a stream that takes the bytes for the server, in the format that the statement names. `close()` resolves when the server has stored the rows, and rejects with the server's error. `abort()` stores nothing. The connection runs nothing else until then, so always close or abort the stream. Bun aborts a stream that is still open when its transaction, savepoint or reservation ends. Call it before the query starts. The query takes no parameters, and resolves with the row count in `count`. @example ```ts …

title: Statement.columnTypes
text: readonly columnTypes: Array<"INTEGER" | "FLOAT" | "TEXT" | "BLOB" | "NULL" | null>; — The actual SQLite column types from the first row of the result set, as reported by `sqlite3_column_type()`. Useful for expressions and computed columns, which are not covered by declaredTypes. Returns an array of SQLite type constants as uppercase strings: - `"INTEGER"` for integer values - `"FLOAT"` for floating-point values - `"TEXT"` for text values - `"BLOB"` for binary data - `"NULL"` for null values - `null` for unknown/unsupported types Only available for read-only statements (SELECT queries). For …

title: Statement.declaredTypes
text: readonly declaredTypes: Array ; — The declared column types from the table schema, as reported by `sqlite3_column_decltype()`. Returns an array of: - The exact type string declared in the `CREATE TABLE` statement - `null` for columns without declared types, such as expressions and computed columns Available for both read-only and read-write statements, before and after they run. @example ```ts // For table columns: const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT id, name, weight FROM products"); console.log(stmt.declaredTypes); // => ["INTEGER", "TEXT", "REAL"] // For expressions (no declared types): const …

title: Statement.safeIntegers()
text: safeIntegers(enabled: boolean): this; — Set whether this statement returns integers as `bigint`. The default is the `safeIntegers` option of the Database. With `false`, integers are returned as `number`, and integers beyond 53 bits are rounded to the nearest `number`. The setting also decides the type of `lastInsertRowid` in the result of run. Database.query returns the same `Statement` for the same SQL, so the setting stays for its next caller. @example ```ts db.run("CREATE TABLE foo (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, big INTEGER)"); db.run("INSERT INTO foo (big) VALUES (?)", …

title: Statement.safeIntegers()
text: safeIntegers(): boolean; — Whether this statement returns integers as `bigint`.

title: Statement.finalize()
text: finalize(): void; — Finalize the prepared statement, freeing the resources used by the statement and preventing it from being executed again. This is called automatically when the prepared statement is garbage collected. It is safe to call this multiple times. Calling this on a finalized statement has no effect. Internally, this calls `sqlite3_finalize`.

title: Statement.toString()
text: toString(): string; — Return the expanded SQL string for the prepared statement. Internally, this calls `sqlite3_expanded_sql()` on the underlying `sqlite3_stmt`. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?", "baz"); console.log(stmt.toString()); // => "SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = baz" console.log(stmt); // => "SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = baz"

title: Statement.toJSON()
text: toJSON(): { sql: string; isFinalized: boolean; paramsCount: number; columnNames: string[] }; — What `JSON.stringify()` shows for the statement.

title: Statement.as()
text: as (Class: new (...args: any[]) => T): Statement ; — Make get and all return an instance of the provided `Class` instead of the default `Object`, so the returned objects can have methods, getters, and setters. For performance reasons, class constructors are not called: initializers do not run and private fields are not accessible. @example ## Custom class ```ts class User { rawBirthdate: string; get birthdate() { return new Date(this.rawBirthdate); } } const db = new Database(":memory:"); db.run("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rawBirthdate TEXT)"); db.run("INSERT INTO users …

title: Statement.native
text: readonly native: any; — Native object representing the underlying `sqlite3_stmt` This is left untyped because the ABI of the native bindings may change at any time. For stable, typed access to statement metadata, use the typed properties on the Statement class: - columnNames for column names - paramsCount for parameter count - columnTypes for actual data types from the first row - declaredTypes for schema-declared column types

text: Database.aggregate can return. `undefined` is stored as `NULL`.

title: Database.MAX_QUERY_CACHE_SIZE
text: static MAX_QUERY_CACHE_SIZE: number; — Maximum number of distinct SQL strings Database.query keeps cached per `Database`. Least-recently-used entries are evicted first. SQL text over 64 KB is never cached.

title: FunctionOptions.varargs
text: varargs?: boolean | undefined; — The SQL function takes any number of arguments, whatever the number of parameters of the JavaScript function.

title: FunctionOptions.deterministic
text: deterministic?: boolean | undefined; — Promise SQLite that the function returns the same result for the same arguments. SQLite then allows it in an index and in a generated column, and can call it fewer times. Equivalent to `SQLITE_DETERMINISTIC`

title: FunctionOptions.directOnly
text: directOnly?: boolean | undefined; — Only SQL that is passed to the `Database` can call the function. A view, a trigger or another part of the schema cannot. Use it for a function with side effects when the database file comes from somebody else. Equivalent to `SQLITE_DIRECTONLY`

title: FunctionOptions.safeIntegers
text: safeIntegers?: boolean | undefined; — An `INTEGER` argument is a `bigint` instead of a `number`, and a `bigint` result that does not fit in a signed 64-bit integer throws a `RangeError`.

title: AggregateOptions.start
text: start?: T | (() => T) | undefined; — The accumulator that each group of rows starts with. A function is called for each group and returns it: use one for an object or an array, so that groups do not share it.

title: Database.clearQueryCache()
text: clearQueryCache(): void; — Finalize the statements that Database.query has cached and empty the cache.

title: AggregateOptions.step
text: step: (accumulator: T, ...args: any[]) => T | void; — Called for each row of a group, with the accumulator and the arguments of the SQL function. What it returns is the new accumulator. When it returns `undefined`, the accumulator stays. The number of its parameters after the first one is the number of arguments the SQL function takes, unless `varargs` is set.

title: AggregateOptions.inverse
text: inverse?: ((accumulator: T, ...args: any[]) => T | void) | null | undefined; — Called for each row that leaves the window, with the arguments that `step` got for that row. It undoes `step`. Without it, the function cannot be used as a window function.

title: AggregateOptions.result
text: result?: ((accumulator: T) => SQLFunctionResult) | null | undefined; — Makes the result of the SQL function from the accumulator. Without it, the accumulator is the result. For a window function it is called once for each row, so it must leave the accumulator as it is.

title: SQLiteError.errno
text: errno: number; — The SQLite3 extended error code This corresponds to `sqlite3_extended_errcode`.

title: SQLiteError.code
text: code?: string; — The name of the SQLite3 error code @example ```ts "SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE" @since v1.0.21

title: SQLiteError.byteOffset
text: readonly byteOffset: number; — The UTF-8 byte offset of the token that the error refers to, counted from the start of the SQL string that was passed, also when a later statement of Database.run failed. `-1` if the error refers to no token. The offset comes from `sqlite3_error_offset`.

title: Changes.changes
text: changes: number; — The number of rows that the last `run` or `exec` call inserted, updated, or deleted itself. Rows that a trigger or a foreign key action such as `ON DELETE CASCADE` changes do not count. Database.run with several statements in one string reports their sum.

title: Changes.lastInsertRowid
text: lastInsertRowid: number | bigint; — The `rowid` of the most recently inserted row. If `safeIntegers` is `true`, this is a `bigint`. Otherwise, it is a `number`.

title: Database.run()
text: run (sql: string, ...bindings: ParamsType[]): Changes; — Execute a SQL query **without returning any results**. This does not cache the query. To run a query multiple times, use prepare instead. Internally, this calls `sqlite3_prepare_v3` followed by `sqlite3_step` and `sqlite3_finalize`. The string can hold several statements, separated by `;`. They run in order, and the first one gets the bindings. The first statement that fails throws, and the statements after it do not run. The following types can be used when binding parameters: | JavaScript type | SQLite type | | --------------- | …

title: Database.exec()
text: exec (sql: string, ...bindings: ParamsType[]): Changes; — This is an alias of Database.run

title: Database.query()
text: query ( — Compile a SQL query and return a Statement object. This is the same as prepare except that it caches the compiled query if possible. This **does not execute** the query; it prepares it for later execution. Internally, this calls `sqlite3_prepare_v3`, which compiles the first statement of the string and ignores the rest. run runs them all. @example ```ts // compile the query const stmt = db.query("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); // run the query stmt.all("baz"); // run the query again stmt.all(); @param sql The SQL query to compile @returns A {@link Statement} instance

title: Database.prepare()
text: prepare ( — Compile a SQL query and return a Statement object. This does not cache the compiled query and does not execute the query. Internally, this calls `sqlite3_prepare_v3`, which compiles the first statement of the string and ignores the rest. run runs them all. @example ```ts // compile the query const stmt = db.query("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); // run the query stmt.all("baz"); @param sql The SQL query to compile @param params Optional bindings for the query @returns A {@link Statement} instance

title: Database.close()
text: close( — Close the database connection. Statements created with Database.query are finalized immediately. With `throwOnError` unset or `false`, statements created with Database.prepare keep working until they are finalized or garbage collected, and the underlying connection is released after the last one (`sqlite3_close_v2`). With `throwOnError: true`, every outstanding statement is finalized, the connection is released immediately, and an error is thrown if SQLite fails to close it. It is safe to call this method multiple times. If the database is already closed, this is a no-op. Creating new …

title: Database.transaction()
text: transaction ( — Creates a function that always runs inside a transaction. When the function is invoked, it begins a new transaction. When the function returns, the transaction is committed. If an exception is thrown, the transaction is rolled back (and the exception propagates as usual). The function must be synchronous, because the transaction is committed when it returns. An `async` function returns at its first `await`: everything after that `await` runs outside the transaction, and an error thrown there does not roll anything back. Do the awaited work first and pass the results in. If the …

title: DatabaseOptions.create
text: create?: boolean | undefined; — Allow creating a new database Equivalent to constants.SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE When `false`, opening a file that does not exist throws an error with the code `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`.

title: Database.function()
text: function(name: string, fn: (...args: any[]) => SQLFunctionResult): this; — Define a SQL function that calls a JavaScript function. The number of parameters of `fn` (`fn.length`) is the number of arguments the SQL function takes, unless `varargs` is set. Functions with the same name and different numbers of arguments exist side by side. A function with the same name and number of arguments replaces the earlier one, also a function that is built into SQLite. An argument has the type that a column of a result row has: `INTEGER` is a `number` (a `bigint` with `safeIntegers`), `BLOB` is a …

title: Database.aggregate()
text: aggregate (name: string, options: AggregateOptions ): this; — Define a SQL aggregate function, such as `sum()` or `group_concat()`, that calls JavaScript functions. With `inverse` it is also a [window function](https://www.sqlite.org/windowfunctions.html). What is said about arguments, results, thrown values and the use of the `Database` in Database.function holds for each callback. @example ```ts db.aggregate("add_all", { start: 0, step: (total, value) => total + value, }); db.query("SELECT add_all(dollars) AS total FROM expenses").get(); // => { total: 92 }

title: Database.onInsert()
text: get onInsert(): UpdateHook | null; — Called after a row is inserted through this `Database`. `null` when not set. Set it to `null` to remove it. Internally, `onInsert`, onUpdate and onDelete are one [`sqlite3_update_hook`](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/update_hook.html). SQLite calls it while the statement runs, for each row, before a transaction commits. A change that is rolled back later has been reported. title: Database.onUpdate()
text: get onUpdate(): UpdateHook | null; — Called after a row is updated through this `Database`. `null` when not set. `rowid` is the rowid that the row has after the update. See onInsert.

title: Database.onDelete()
text: get onDelete(): UpdateHook | null; — Called after a row is deleted through this `Database`. `null` when not set. See onInsert.

title: DatabaseOptions.safeIntegers
text: safeIntegers?: boolean | undefined; — When `true`, integers are returned as `bigint`. When `false`, integers are returned as `number`, and integers beyond 53 bits are rounded to the nearest `number`. When `true`, a `bigint` parameter that does not fit in a signed 64-bit integer throws a `RangeError`. When `false`, it keeps its low 64 bits: `2n ** 64n - 1n` is stored as `-1`.

title: Database.fileControl()

SQLite reads the input of `op` from `arg` and writes its output there. - A `number` is passed as a 32-bit integer. What SQLite writes back is not returned. - A `TypedArray` or `DataView` of at least 8 bytes is passed as is. Use it to read what SQLite writes back. - `null` or no argument is for an `op` that takes none, such as `SQLITE_FCNTL_RESET_CACHE`. An `op` that reads its argument reads `-1`. @example ```ts // -1 asks for the flag. SQLite writes 0 or 1 to the first …

title: Statement
text: This is returned by Database.prepare and Database.query. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.all("baz"); // => [{bar: "baz"}] @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.get("baz"); // => {bar: "baz"} @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.run("baz");

title: Statement.constructor()
text: constructor(nativeHandle: any); — Creates a new prepared statement from native code. Used internally by the Database class. You don't need to call this yourself.

title: Statement.all()
text: all(...params: ParamsType): ReturnType[]; — Execute the prepared statement and return all results as objects. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.all(); // => [] (nothing is bound yet) stmt.all("baz"); // => [{bar: "baz"}] stmt.all(); // => [{bar: "baz"}] (the last bound value) stmt.all("foo"); // => [{bar: "foo"}]

title: Statement.get()
text: get(...params: ParamsType): ReturnType | null; — Execute the prepared statement and return **the first** result. If no result is returned, this returns `null`. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.get(); // => null (nothing is bound yet) stmt.get("baz"); // => {bar: "baz"} stmt.get(); // => {bar: "baz"} (the last bound value) stmt.get("foo"); // => {bar: "foo"} The following types can be used when binding parameters: | JavaScript type | SQLite type | | --------------- | ---------------------- | | `string` | `TEXT` | | `number` | `INTEGER` or `REAL` | …

title: Statement.iterate()
text: iterate(...params: ParamsType): IterableIterator ; — Execute the prepared statement and return an iterator over the results. A statement has one cursor, and its newest run owns it: after another call of `get`, `all`, `values`, `raw`, `run` or `iterate` on the same `Statement`, the next step of this iterator throws. Use Database.prepare to get a statement with a cursor of its own.

title: Statement.run()
text: run(...params: ParamsType): Changes; — Execute the prepared statement. @example ```ts const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)"); insert.run("Alice"); // => { changes: 1, lastInsertRowid: 1 } insert.run("Bob"); // => { changes: 1, lastInsertRowid: 2 } const update = db.prepare("UPDATE users SET name = ? WHERE id = ?"); update.run("Charlie", 1); // => { changes: 1, lastInsertRowid: 2 } The following types can be used when binding parameters: | JavaScript type | SQLite type | | --------------- | ---------------------- | | `string` | `TEXT` | | `number` | `INTEGER` or `REAL` …

title: DatabaseOptions.strict
text: strict?: boolean | undefined; — When set to `true`, a query with a missing bound parameter throws an error. When set to `false` or `undefined`, the parameter is `NULL`. In both modes, the key of a named parameter can include the `$`, `:`, or `@` prefix or leave it out. If an object has both keys, the key without the prefix wins in strict mode, and the key with the prefix otherwise. @example ```ts const db = new Database(":memory:", { strict: true }); db.run("INSERT INTO foo (name) VALUES ($name)", { name: "foo" }); db.run("INSERT INTO foo (name) VALUES ($name)", { nmae: "foo" }); // throws …

title: Statement.values()
text: values(...params: ParamsType): Array >; — Execute the prepared statement and return the results as an array of arrays. If there are no results, returns an empty array. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.values("baz"); // => [baz] stmt.values(); // => [baz] stmt.values("foo"); // => [foo] stmt.values("not-found"); // => [] The following types can be used when binding parameters: | JavaScript type | SQLite type | | --------------- | ---------------------- | | `string` | `TEXT` | | `number` | `INTEGER` or `REAL` | | `boolean` | `INTEGER` (1 or 0) | | …

title: Statement.raw()
text: raw(...params: ParamsType): Array >; — Execute the prepared statement and return all results as arrays of `Uint8Array`s. This is similar to values but returns every value as a `Uint8Array`, regardless of its original SQLite type. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); stmt.raw("baz"); // => [Uint8Array(24)] stmt.raw(); // => [Uint8Array(24)]

title: Statement.columnNames
text: readonly columnNames: string[]; — The names of the columns returned by the prepared statement. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT bar FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); console.log(stmt.columnNames); // => ["bar"]

title: Statement.paramsCount
text: readonly paramsCount: number; — The number of parameters expected in the prepared statement. @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ?"); console.log(stmt.paramsCount); // => 1 @example ```ts const stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = ? AND baz = ?"); console.log(stmt.paramsCount); // => 2

title: Statement.reader
text: readonly reader: boolean; — Whether the prepared statement returns rows: it has at least one column. `true` for `SELECT`, for `INSERT ... RETURNING` and for a `PRAGMA` that reports a value.

title: Statement.readonly
text: readonly readonly: boolean; — Whether the prepared statement makes no direct change to the database file, as reported by `sqlite3_stmt_readonly()`. `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and `SAVEPOINT` are read-only in this sense.

title: Statement.isFinalized
text: readonly isFinalized: boolean; — Whether finalize was called, or the Database finalized the statement when it closed.

title: Test
text: ```ts test("can check if using Bun", () => { expect(Bun).toBeDefined(); }); test("can make a fetch() request", async () => { const response = await fetch("https://example.com/"); expect(response.ok).toBe(true); }); test("can set a timeout", async () => { await Bun.sleep(100); }, 50); // or { timeout: 50 } @param label the label for the test @param fn the test function @param options the test timeout or options @category Testing

title: Test.options
text: options?: number | TestOptions, — - If a `number`, sets the timeout for the test in milliseconds. - If an `object`, sets the options for the test. - `timeout` sets the timeout for the test in milliseconds. - `retry` sets the number of times to retry the test if it fails. - `repeats` sets the number of times to repeat the test, regardless of whether it passed or failed.

title: Test.only
text: only: Test ; — Skips all other tests, except this test.

title: Test.skip
text: skip: ((label: string) => void) & Test ; — Skips this test.

title: Test.todo
text: todo: ((label: string) => void) & Test ; — Marks this test as to be written or to be fixed. These tests only run when the `--todo` flag is passed. With the flag, a `.todo` test that passes is marked as `fail` in the results: remove the `.todo` or check that the test is implemented correctly.

title: Test.failing

The value must be an object. @example expect({ a: hello, b: world }).toContainAnyKeys([a]); expect({ a: hello, b: world }).toContainAnyKeys([b]); expect({ a: hello, b: world }).toContainAnyKeys([b, c]); expect({ a: hello, b: world }).not.toContainAnyKeys([c]); @param expected the expected value

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainValue()
text: toContainValue(expected: unknown): R; — Asserts that an `object` contains the provided value. This check is deep: it looks through child properties to find the expected value. The input value must be an object. @example const shallow = { hello: "world" }; const deep = { message: shallow }; const deepArray = { message: [shallow] }; const o = { a: "foo", b: [1, "hello", true], c: "baz" }; expect(shallow).toContainValue("world"); expect({ foo: false }).toContainValue(false); expect(deep).toContainValue({ hello: "world" }); expect(deepArray).toContainValue([{ hello: "world" }]); …

title: jest.mock()
text: function mock(id: string, factory?: ModuleMockFactory): typeof jest; — Replace the module `id` with the return value of `factory`. The call is hoisted above the file's imports. Without a factory, the module is replaced with the file of the same name in a `__mocks__` directory. If there isn't one, it's replaced with a copy of the module where every function is a mock.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainValues()
text: toContainValues(expected: Array ): R; — Asserts that an `object` contains the provided values. This is the same as toContainValue, but accepts an array of values instead. The value must be an object. @example const o = { a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }; expect(o).toContainValues([foo]); expect(o).toContainValues([baz, bar]); expect(o).not.toContainValues([qux, foo]); @param expected the expected value

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainAllValues()
text: toContainAllValues(expected: Array ): R; — Asserts that an `object` contains all the provided values. The value must be an object. @example const o = { a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }; expect(o).toContainAllValues([foo, bar, baz]); expect(o).toContainAllValues([baz, bar, foo]); expect(o).not.toContainAllValues([bar, foo]); @param expected the expected value

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainAnyValues()
text: toContainAnyValues(expected: Array ): R; — Asserts that an `object` contains any of the provided values. The value must be an object. @example const o = { a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }; expect(o).toContainAnyValues([qux, foo]); expect(o).toContainAnyValues([qux, bar]); expect(o).toContainAnyValues([qux, baz]); expect(o).not.toContainAnyValues([qux]); @param expected the expected value

title: jest.doMock()
text: function doMock(id: string, factory?: ModuleMockFactory): typeof jest; — Like mock, but the call isn't hoisted.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainKeys()
text: toContainKeys(expected: Array<__internal.IfNeverThenElse >): R; — Asserts that an `object` contains all the provided keys. @example expect({ a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }).toContainKeys([a, b]); expect({ a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }).toContainKeys([a, b, c]); expect({ a: foo, b: bar, c: baz }).not.toContainKeys([a, b, e]); @param expected the expected value

title: MatchersBuiltin.toContainEqual()
text: toContainEqual(expected: T extends Iterable ? U : T): R; — Asserts that a value contains and equals what is expected. This matcher performs a deep equality check on array members, rather than checking for object identity. @example expect([{ a: 1 }]).toContainEqual({ a: 1 }); expect([{ a: 1 }]).not.toContainEqual({ a: 2 }); @param expected the expected value

title: MatchersBuiltin.toHaveLength()
text: toHaveLength(length: number): R; — Asserts that a value has a `.length` property that is equal to the expected length. @example expect([]).toHaveLength(0); expect("hello").toHaveLength(5); @param length the expected length

title: jest.unmock()
text: function unmock(id: string): typeof jest; — Stop mocking the module `id`. The call is hoisted above the file's imports.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toHaveProperty()
text: toHaveProperty(keyPath: string | number | Array , value?: unknown): R; — Asserts that a value has a property with the expected name, and value if provided. @example expect(new Set()).toHaveProperty("size"); expect(new Uint8Array()).toHaveProperty("byteLength", 0); expect({ kitchen: { area: 20 }}).toHaveProperty("kitchen.area", 20); expect({ kitchen: { area: 20 }}).toHaveProperty(["kitchen", "area"], 20); @param keyPath the expected property name or path, or an index @param value the expected property value, if provided

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeTruthy()
text: toBeTruthy(): R; — Asserts that a value is "truthy". To assert that a value equals `true`, use `toBe(true)` instead. @example expect(true).toBeTruthy(); expect(1).toBeTruthy(); expect({}).toBeTruthy();

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeFalsy()
text: toBeFalsy(): R; — Asserts that a value is "falsy". To assert that a value equals `false`, use `toBe(false)` instead. @example expect(false).toBeFalsy(); expect(0).toBeFalsy(); expect("").toBeFalsy();

title: jest.dontMock()
text: function dontMock(id: string): typeof jest; — Like unmock, but the call isn't hoisted.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeDefined()

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeInstanceOf()

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeNaN()

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeGreaterThan()

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeGreaterThanOrEqual()

title: MatchersBuiltin.toBeLessThanOrEqual()
text: toBeLessThanOrEqual(expected: number | bigint): R; — Asserts that a value is a `number` and is less than or equal to the expected value. @example expect(-1).toBeLessThanOrEqual(0); expect(3).toBeLessThanOrEqual(3.14); expect(9).toBeLessThanOrEqual(9); @param expected the expected number

title: MatchersBuiltin.toThrow()
text: toThrow(expected?: unknown): R; — Asserts that a function throws an error. - If expected is a `string` or `RegExp`, it checks the `message` property. - If expected is an `Error` object, it checks the `name` and `message` properties. - If expected is an `Error` constructor, it checks the class of the `Error`. - If expected is not provided, it checks that anything was thrown. @example function fail() { throw new Error("Oops!"); } expect(fail).toThrow("Oops!"); expect(fail).toThrow(/oops/i); expect(fail).toThrow(Error); expect(fail).toThrow(); @param expected the expected error, error message, or …

title: jest.createMockFromModule()
text: function createMockFromModule (id: string): Mocked ; — `require()` the real module `id` and return a copy where every function is a mock.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toThrowError()
text: toThrowError(expected?: unknown): R; — Asserts that a function throws an error. - If expected is a `string` or `RegExp`, it checks the `message` property. - If expected is an `Error` object, it checks the `name` and `message` properties. - If expected is an `Error` constructor, it checks the class of the `Error`. - If expected is not provided, it checks that anything was thrown. @example function fail() { throw new Error("Oops!"); } expect(fail).toThrowError("Oops!"); expect(fail).toThrowError(/oops/i); expect(fail).toThrowError(Error); expect(fail).toThrowError(); @param expected the expected …

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatch()
text: toMatch(expected: string | RegExp): R; — Asserts that a value matches a regular expression or includes a substring. @example expect("dog").toMatch(/dog/); expect("dog").toMatch("og"); @param expected the expected substring or pattern.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchSnapshot()
text: toMatchSnapshot(hint?: string): R; — Asserts that a value matches the most recent snapshot. @example expect([1, 2, 3]).toMatchSnapshot('hint message'); @param hint Hint used to identify the snapshot in the snapshot file.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchSnapshot()
text: toMatchSnapshot(propertyMatchers?: object, hint?: string): R; — Asserts that a value matches the most recent snapshot. @example expect([1, 2, 3]).toMatchSnapshot(); expect({ a: 1, b: 2 }).toMatchSnapshot({ a: 1 }); expect({ c: new Date() }).toMatchSnapshot({ c: expect.any(Date) }); @param propertyMatchers Object containing properties to match against the value. @param hint Hint used to identify the snapshot in the snapshot file.

title: jest.resetModules()
text: function resetModules(): typeof jest; — Re-evaluate each module on its next `import()` or `require()`. Mocked modules stay mocked, and their factories run again.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchInlineSnapshot()
text: toMatchInlineSnapshot(value?: string): R; — Asserts that a value matches the most recent inline snapshot. @example expect("Hello").toMatchInlineSnapshot(); expect("Hello").toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"Hello"`); @param value The latest automatically-updated snapshot value.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchInlineSnapshot()
text: toMatchInlineSnapshot(propertyMatchers?: object, value?: string): R; — Asserts that a value matches the most recent inline snapshot. @example expect({ c: new Date() }).toMatchInlineSnapshot({ c: expect.any(Date) }); expect({ c: new Date() }).toMatchInlineSnapshot({ c: expect.any(Date) }, ` { "v": Any , } `); @param propertyMatchers Object containing properties to match against the value. @param value The latest automatically-updated snapshot value.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchFileSnapshot()
text: toMatchFileSnapshot(path: string, hint?: string): Promise ; — Asserts that a value matches the contents of its own snapshot file. A string is compared as is. Any other value is first printed the way a snapshot prints it. If the file doesn't exist, it's created, except in CI. `--update-snapshots` rewrites a file that differs. @example await expect(render(page)).toMatchFileSnapshot("./snapshots/page.html"); @param path The file's path, relative to the test file. @param hint Hint used to number the snapshot among the test's other snapshots.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot()
text: toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot(hint?: string): R; — Asserts that a function throws an error matching the most recent snapshot. @example function fail() { throw new Error("Oops!"); } expect(fail).toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot(); expect(fail).toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot("This one should say Oops!"); @param hint Hint used to identify the snapshot in the snapshot file.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot()
text: toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot(value?: string): R; — Asserts that a function throws an error matching the most recent snapshot. @example function fail() { throw new Error("Oops!"); } expect(fail).toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot(); expect(fail).toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot(`"Oops!"`); @param value The latest automatically-updated snapshot value.

title: MatchersBuiltin.toMatchObject()
text: toMatchObject(subset: object): R; — Asserts that an object matches a subset of properties. @example expect({ a: 1, b: 2 }).toMatchObject({ b: 2 }); expect({ c: new Date(), d: 2 }).toMatchObject({ d: 2 }); @param subset Subset of properties to match with.

title: jest.useFakeTimers()
text: function useFakeTimers(options?: FakeTimersOptions | "modern" | "legacy"): typeof jest; — Replace the timer functions on `globalThis` with fakes that use a fake clock. The clock only moves when the test moves it. A reference saved before this call, such as `const savedSetTimeout = setTimeout`, stays real. The real timers are restored when the test file ends, unless a preload made this call at its top level.

title: jest.advanceTimersByTime()

title: Bun's new text-based lockfile › Not a breaking change (fork only)
text: We're planning to make `bun.lock` the default in Bun v1.2.0. In the meantime, we continue to support the binary `bun.lockb` format and will do so for awhile. Until Bun v1.2, the `bun install --save-text-lockfile` flag will be required to generate the text-based lockfile. When a `bun.lock` file exists, `bun install` will use the text-based lockfile and ignore the binary lockfile. Otherwise, it will generate the binary lockfile.

title: JavaScript Macros in Bun › Security considerations (fork only)
text: Macros must explicitly be imported with `{ type: "macro" }` in order to be executed at bundle-time. These imports have no effect if they are not called, unlike regular JavaScript imports which may have side effects. You can disable macros entirely by passing the `--no-macros` flag to Bun. It produces a build error like this: ```js error: Macros are disabled foo(); ^ ./hello.js:3:1 53

title: JavaScript Macros in Bun › When to use macros (fork only)
text: For small things where you would otherwise have a one-off build script, bundle-time code execution can be easier to maintain. It lives with the rest of your code, it runs with the rest of the build, it is automatically paralellized, and if it fails, the build fails too. If you find yourself running a lot of code at bundle-time though, consider running a server instead. Let's look at some scenarios where macros might be useful.

We wanted to avoid the possibility of sending any JavaScript/TypeScript source code, environment variables, or other sensitive information in the reports. This is why we only send the Zig/C++ stack trace and a few other details. Instead of sending everything by default, this approach sends only what we (probably) need to diagnose the issue. title: Bun v0.6.4 › bun test reads `.env.test` and `.env.test.local` (fork only)
text: - `NODE_ENV=test` is now properly set. - Environment variables can be read from `.env.test` and `.env.test.local` files. {% raw %} In the next version of Bun "bun test" sets NODE_ENV=test by default and loads .env.test & .env.test.local pic.twitter.com/VuxMUmppxR — Jarred Sumner (@jarredsumner) May 23, 2023 {% /raw %}

title: Bun v0.6.4 › bun test timeouts (fork only)
text: You can now set a timeout for your tests by passing `--timeout` or by passing a third optional `number` argument to `test()`. ```js test("i took too long", async () => { await Bun.sleep(100); // the last argument is a timeout in milliseconds }, 50);

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Bundler bugfixes (fork only)
text: Thanks to [@dylan-conway](https://github.com/dylan-conway) for fixing: - Bun was auto-importing JSX when using the "classic" JSX runtime, which is incorrect. - Bun was not importing `Fragment` from `jsxImportSource` when using the "automatic" JSX runtime. - Bun was incorrectly choosing the "production" JSX runtime when using `jsxImportSource` and `NODE_ENV=development` (or unset) in certain case.

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Change the timezone (fork only)
text: You can now change the [timezone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones#List) that Bun uses for `Date` and `Intl` by setting `TZ` environment variable or assigning `process.env.TZ` in your code. This is also used by Node.js. ```js process.env.TZ = "America/New_York"; When using `bun test`, instead of using your machine's timezone, the default timezone is set to `Etc/UTC` to help prevent flaky tests when running in your CI environment. [View on Twitter](https://twitter.com/jarredsumner/status/1660887638948335617)

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Implemented `require.cache` (fork only)
text: `require.cache` is a Node.js API that allows you to delete a module from the cache. This is useful for controlling hot reloading behavior, and is now supported in Bun. Unlike Node.js, `delete require.cache[id]` works with ESM too. {% raw %} In the next version of Bun `delete require.cache[id]` works on ESM pic.twitter.com/xVKYwkVhLy — Jarred Sumner (@jarredsumner) May 24, 2023 {% /raw %}

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Node.js compatiblity bugfixes (fork only)
text: - `node:https` now uses the correct port when using `node:https` and `port` is not set. Thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari) for the fix. - `node:http` now has the correct return type for `getHeader()`. Thanks to [@Jarred-Sumner](https://github.com/Jarred-Sumner) for the fix. - `node:https` now correctly uses `{ tls: true }` when using `createServer()`. Thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari) for the fix.

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Rewrote JavaScript builtins in TypeScript (fork only)
text: Bun's internal JavaScript builtins are now implemented in TypeScript and bundled + minified with `bun build`, which reduces Bun's binary size by about 900 KB and makes it easier for us to catch bugs. This is thanks to [@paperclover](https://github.com/paperclover). It also improves Bun's development velocity on these JavaScript builtins because the previous builtins generator script used by WebKit takes around 9s to run and this new builtins generator script takes around 0.9s.

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Transpiler bugfixes (fork only)
text: - A regression related to printing tagged template literals containing non-ascii characters when running in Bun's runtime has been fixed.

title: Bun v0.6.4 › Up to 80% faster `bun test` (fork only)
text: We've made `bun test` up to 80% faster, particularly when there are lots of small test files. {% raw %} bun:test just got 80% faster (in a benchmark rendering React components) pic.twitter.com/BJTW0VqakQ — Jarred Sumner (@jarredsumner) May 23, 2023 {% /raw %} Bun was over-scheduling the garbage collector to run on every file synchronously. It already schedules GC whenever the heap size changes, so this is unnecessary. This resulted in a 9% growth in memory usage, or so, which is fine given that comparing other test runners with the same code, Bun uses 2-4x less memory.

title: Bun v0.6.5 › Bugfix for Bun.serve() with streaming files (fork only)
text: Bun now globally ignores `SIGPIPE` signals, which fixes a bug where Bun could crash when using `new Response(Bun.file(path))` to stream files on Linux when the client disconnects early.

title: Bun v0.6.5 › Bugfix for `createConnection` in `node:net` (fork only)
text: This fixes an arguments parsing issue in `node:net` that caused `createConnection` to fail in some cases. Thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari) for this contribution!

title: Bun v0.6.5 › Native CommonJS runtime support (fork only)
text: We've reimplemented CommonJS support in Bun from being transpiler-only into natively supported in the runtime. This fixes many bugs that blocked npm packages from working in Bun, and improves compatibility with Node.js. Here are 3 packages this unblocks:

title: Bun v0.6.5 › $npm_lifecycle_event in bun run (fork only)
text: You can now access `$npm_lifecycle_event` in `bun run` scripts. The `$npm_lifecycle_event` environment variable is set to the name of the script that was run. This is useful for detecting which package.json script was run. {% codetabs %} ```sh#output $ bun run hey hey ```js#input.js console.log(process.env.npm_lifecycle_event); {% /codetabs %} Thanks to [@TiranexDev](https://github.com/TiranexDev) for this contribution!

title: Bun v0.6.5 › Transpiler & bundler bugfix (fork only)
text: Bun was incorrectly transpiling `Symbol["for"]` and a few dozen other global side-effect free getters accessed via statically-known computed property string literal to `undefined`. This has been fixed. This bug was introduced in Bun v0.6.0, and began impacting Bun's JavaScript runtime in v0.6.4. Thanks to [@zloirock](https://github.com/zloirock) for reporting this issue.

title: Bun v0.6.6 › Bug fixes (fork only)
text: We also made various bug fixes. Regressions in 0.6.5 from the CommonJS rewrite: - `--watch` and `--hot` were broken when importing CommonJS modules, this is now fixed. - Fixed a bug with `Object.defineProperty(module, "exports", { get })`, which fixes packages like `supports-color`. More bugfixes: - A bundler transform would incorrectly rewrite `module.exports` to `exports` when used in UMD modules, this is now fixed. - Fixed a bug with `path.parse()` that did not resolve certain paths properly, thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari). - Fixed a crash with …

title: Bun v0.6.6 › `bun test --only` (fork only)
text: You can now specify `--only` to only run tests that are marked with `test.only()` or `describe.only()`. This is useful when you want to debug a specific test in a file. ```js describe.only("describe #1", () => { test("test #1", () => { // runs }); test.skip("test #2", () => { // does not run }); }); test("test #3", () => { // does not run }); test.only("test #4", () => { // runs });

title: Bun v0.6.6 › `bun test --todo` (fork only)
text: In addition to `test.skip()`, you can also define a test using `test.todo()` or `describe.todo()`. By default, these tests are not run, _unless_ you specify `--todo`. This is useful for tests that are not yet implemented or are broken or flaky in some way. ```js test("test #1", () => { // runs }); test.todo("test #2"); // never runs test.todo("test #3", () => { // only runs if --todo is passed });

title: Bun v0.6.6 › `test.if()` and `describe.if()` (fork only)
text: You can now specify a conditional test, based on a boolean value. You can also use `test.skipIf()` if you want the inverse behaviour. So instead of doing this: ```js const macOS = process.arch === "darwin"; const test = macOS ? test : test.skip; You can just do this: ```js const macOS = process.arch === "darwin"; test.if(macOS)("test #1", () => { // runs if macOS }); test.skipIf(macOS)("test #2", () => { // skips if macOS }); describe.if(macOS)("describe #1", () => { test("test #3", () => { // runs if macOS }); });

title: Bun v0.6.6 › Timeouts in `test()` (fork only)
text: In Jest, you can specify a third argument to `test()` as a timeout value in milliseconds. In Vitest, you can also specify an object, with a `timeout` property. In Bun, you can now do both. ```js test("timeout #1", async () => { await sleep(10); }, 1); test( "timeout #2", async () => { await sleep(10); }, { timeout: 1 }, ); The default timeout is 5000, you can change the default by using `--timeout`. ```sh $ bun test --timeout 1000 # 1 second

title: Bun v0.8.1 › Reduced memory usage when there are lots of Headers & Blob objects (fork only)
text: Bun's `Headers` and `Blob` implementations were not reporting their size to the garbage collector. Since Bun implements many classes in native code, the garbage collector cannot always see how much memory is really being used by a class. When `Headers` or `Blob` are large enough, this can cause the garbage collector to not run as often as it should be. Now Bun reports the size of `Headers` and `Blob` to the garbage collector.

title: Bun v0.8.1 › Sourcemap bugfix in `bun --inspect` (fork only)
text: Since Bun transpiles every file, Bun must also keep a sourcemap for every file. This is used to make `Error.prototype.stack` produce sourcemapped stacktraces and `console.log` to report accurate line numbers. Sourcemaps unfortunately cost a lot of memory. Instead of storing the entire sourcemap in memory, we store a more compact version until it's first used. The first 24 bytes of the compact version contains extra metadata (such as, the number of lines the original input source code had). This 24 byte header was mistakenly being included in the inline sourcemaps used in `bun --inspect`, …

text: There was a bug where `AsyncLocalStorage` could not be disabled multiple times. This has been fixed. title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: bug when missing certain headers in HTTP client responses (fork only)
text: For HTTP/1.1, the `Content-Length` header and the `Transfer-Encoding` headers are both optional. When these headers are omitted, the HTTP client is supposed to wait until the connection is closed to determine the length of the response body (and implicitly, disable keep-alive). Previously, Bun was not handling this case and treating these HTTP responses as malformed. Now, Bun properly handles this scenario and disables keep-alive when the `Content-Length` & `Transfer-Encoding` headers are omitted. It is not recommended to omit these headers (keep-alive is an important optimization for HTTP/1.1 …

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: Bun does not forward arguments to lifecycle scripts (fork only)
text: We fixed a bug where Bun would pass arguments to lifecycle scripts. For example, if you ran `bun run build --production`, Bun would pass `--production` to the `prebuild` script, which could cause unexpected failures. ```json#package.json { "scripts": { "prebuild": "echo \"Building...\"", "build": "bun scripts/build.ts" } } Before: $ echo "Building..." --production Building... --production After: $ echo "Building..." Building... Thanks to [@nektro](https://github.com/nektro) for fixing this issue.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `bun init` would contain an invalid `.gitignore` (fork only)
text: Ther was a bug where `bun init` would contain an invalid `.gitignore` file. This has been fixed thanks to [@Pierre-Mike](https://github.com/Pierre-Mike).

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `bun install --yarn` would occasionally produce invalid YAML (fork only)
text: There was a bug in Bun's yarn.lock file printer that would not properly escape identifiers in certain cases. This would cause `bun install --yarn` to produce a yarn.lock file that Yarn v1 was unable to parse. Note that technically yarn.lock is not a YAML file, it is a bespoke Yarn v1 specific format (but saying "YAML" is easier since it is very close to YAML).

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `bun install` with a package that contains `~` (fork only)
text: We fixed a bug where `bun install` would fail if a package contained a `~` in the version. This has been fixed, thanks to [@Hanaasagi](https://github.com/Hanaasagi).

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: crash in debugger (fork only)
text: A crash could occur on start when using `bun --inspect` to debug an application, which has been fixed. The crash was due to assuming a debugger was started when it might not have been started yet.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `Dirent.name` setter must be a string (fork only)

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `ENOENT` when using `bun install` + `package-lock.json` (fork only)
text: We fixed an edge-case in `bun install` that would have caused a barrage of `ENOENT` errors. This would have occured when no `bun.lockb` existed, but a `package-lock.json` existed.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `fs.read()` returned incorrect value when promisified (fork only)
text: We fixed a bug where `fs.read()` would return an incorrect value when `util.promisify(fs.read)` was used. Before: ```js const read = promisify(fs.read); const fd = await fs.promises.open("hello.txt"); const buffer = new Uint8Array(16); const result = await read(fd, buffer, 0, 16, 0); console.log(result); // 16 After: ```js const read = promisify(fs.read); const fd = await fs.promises.open("hello.txt"); const buffer = new Uint8Array(16); const result = await read(fd, buffer, 0, 16, 0); console.log(result); // { bytesRead: 16, buffer } Thanks to [@nektro](https://github.com/nektro) for fixing …

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: Hang in `bun:sqlite`'s .get() method (fork only)
text: Previously, the following code would potentially hang after being called about 5,000 times in quick succession: ```js const db = new Database(":memory:"); const query = db.prepare("SELECT 1"); for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) { query.get(); } This has been fixed.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: potential crash in `require()` after exception is thrown (fork only)
text: A crash that sometimes happened when a CommonJS module that was loaded via `require()` and threw an exception during initialization while nested inside many other modules that were also incompletely initialized has been fixed. One way this crash manifested was a module requiring `sharp` when native addons were not installed and that module was nested inside many other modules that were also incompletely initialized.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: `Set-Cookie` header capitalization with `headers.raw()` (fork only)
text: We fixed an issue where `headers.raw()` from `node-fetch` would return the `Set-Cookie` header with the wrong capitalization. Before: ```js const headers = new Headers({ "User-Agent": "Bun", "Set-Cookie": "foo=bar", }); console.log(headers.raw()); // { "user-agent": "Bun", "Set-Cookie": ["foo=bar"] } After: ```js const headers = new Headers({ "Set-Cookie": "foo=bar", }); console.log(headers.raw()); // { "user-agent": "Bun", "set-cookie": ["foo=bar"] } Thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari) for fixing this issue.

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: sometimes bun install would binlink the wrong version (fork only)
text: In certain cases, bun install could have binlinked the wrong version of a package. We previously were not bin linking into `my-dependency/node_modules/.bin`, preferring the root `node_modules/.bin` instead. This has been fixed, thanks to [@dylan-conway](https://github.com/dylan-conway).

title: Bun v1.0.12 › Fixed: transpiler preserves custom directives (fork only)
text: Previously, if you had an unknown directive at the top of the file, Bun's transpiler would consider it dead code and remove it. This has been fixed. ```jsx "use client"; // <-- this line is preserved now

text: You can now access environment variables using `import.meta.env`, a pattern used by frameworks such as Vite. ```js console.log(import.meta.env.NODE_ENV); // "development" `import.meta.env` is an alias of `process.env` and `Bun.env`. title: Bun v1.0.12 › `mock.module(...)` now supports re-exports (fork only)

title: Bun v1.0.12 › `server.url` (fork only)
text: We added support for `server.url`, which returns a URL object that defines the location of the HTTP server. title: Bun v1.0.13 › Fixed: `new Server` in node:http (fork only)
text: The following error was fixed: ```js new Server({ key: "123" }); Previously, this would throw the following error: ```js TypeError: key argument must be an string, Buffer, TypedArray, BunFile or an array containing string, Buffer, TypedArray or BunFile This error was incorrect. It no longer errors. Thanks to [@HK-SHAO](https://github.com/HK-SHAO) for the fix.

title: Bun v1.0.13 › Fixed: `The Stats.atime getter can only be used on instances of Stats` (fork only)
text: The following error was fixed: ```js const { Stats } = require("node:fs"); const stat = Object.create(Stats.prototype); stat.atime; // previously: threw "The Stats.atime getter can only be used on instances of Stats" Some libraries create `Stats` objects using `Object.create(Stats.prototype)`. Previously, Bun would throw an error when you tried to access `atime` on a `Stats` object created this way (it is implemented as a class currently). Now, Bun will return `undefined` instead of throwing an error and allow the fields to be set. This unblocks certain libraires.

title: Bun v1.0.13 › http2 client support (fork only)
text: You can now use the `node:http2` module's client functions in Bun! ```js const client = connect("https://example.com"); const req = client.request({ ":path": "/" }); req.on("response", (headers, flags) => { for (const name in headers) { console.log(`${name}: ${headers[name]}`); } }); Thanks to [@cirospaciari](https://github.com/cirospaciari)

title: Bun v1.0.13 › Improved support for ES5 `with` statements (fork only)
text: Before the days of destructuring, the `with` statement was a popular way to avoid typing out long object names. For example, instead of writing ```js join(__dirname, "foo"); You could write ```js with (require("path")) { join(__dirname, "foo"); } Today, a lot of developers would get mad at you for using `with`. But it is a part of JavaScript, and Bun must support it. Importantly, there are popular libraries people depend on that use `with`, and those must work in Bun.

title: Bun v1.0.13 › Regression in `bun install` fixed (fork only)
text: A regression that caused `"FileNotFound"` errors to appear in `bun install` in certain cases has been fixed, thanks to [@dylan-conway](https://github.com/dylan-conway).

title: Bun v1.0.13 › Slightly fewer strings are allocated in CommonJS modules (fork only)
text: CommonJS modules have `require` and `require.resolve` functions. In Bun, these are implemented as the native code equivalent of a `.bind` call. Bound functions by default change the name, but code expects `require.name` to return `"require"` and `require.resolve.name` to return `"resolve"` - so we must manually set the name. It turns out, the way we were manually setting the name caused the name to be a new string created every time any CommonJS module was loaded. text: Yesterday in Bun v1.0.17, we enabled lifecycle scripts for the top 500 packages on npm. While we did plenty of testing ourselves, we missed a few cases that were reported by users. For example, what happens if `node-gyp` was not installed? ```sh $ bun install > node-gyp rebuild Command not found: node-gyp That's no good. We've fixed this. Or what if a lifecycle script you're using depends on `node`, but you're running in Docker and the container does not have …

title: Bun v1.0.18 › Fixed: Lifecycle scripts running in the wrong working directory (fork only)

text: A bug where wildcard `tsconfig.json` `paths` would fail to resolve due to the suffix not being added has been fixed ```js error: Cannot find module "@faasjs/bar" from ".../test/js/bun/resolve/resolve-test.js" Thanks to [@james-elicx](https://github.com/james-elicx) for fixing this.

title: Bun v1.0.18 › Reflinks on Linux (fork only)
text: Reflinks are copy-on-write copies of files. They make it faster to copy files. macOS has supported reflinks since APFS was released in 2017. Linux has supported reflinks with brtfs and more recently more filesystems have added support for reflinks. Bun already used `copy_file_range` on Linux to make copying files faster, but some hypervisors (like gVisor) disable this system call. Now Bun will try to use `ioctl_ficlone`, which is a lower-level system call that internally does something very similar to `copy_file_range`. `ioctl_ficlone` is overall less well-supported than `copy_file_range`, but …

title: Bun v1.0.18 › Symlinking `node` to `bun` works better (fork only)
text: Bun will automatically symlink `node` to `bun` when it is not available to ensure scripts that expect `node` to exist still work. However, Bun's CLI is very different from Node's, so when running a command like `node build` or `node install`, it is expected to find a file like `build.js`, not invoke a bundler or package manager. Previously: ```sh $ ln -s $(which bun) node && chmod +x node $ ./node build bun build v1.0.18 (a648ed9e) error: Missing entrypoints. What would you like to bundle? Usage: $ bun build <entrypoint> [...<entrypoints>] [...flags] To see full documentation: $ bun build …

title: Bun v1.0.19 › `bun install --verbose` now streams post-install script output (fork only)
text: When running `bun install --verbose`, post-install script output is now streamed to the terminal instead of buffered and printed at the end. This makes it easier to see what's happening. Thanks to [@dylan-conway](https://github.com/dylan-conway) for implementing this.

title: Bun v1.0.19 › `Bun.peek()` gets 90x faster (fork only)
text: `Bun.peek(promise)` lets you read a promise's value without waiting for it to resolve, if it's no longer pending. This is useful to avoid microtasks and improve performance. We've switched the implementation from relying on C++ SPI to using a JavaScriptCore bytecode intrinsic which makes it 90x faster. Thanks to [@paperclover](https://github.com/paperclover)
