text: To improve startup time, enable bytecode compilation: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --minify --sourcemap --bytecode ./path/to/my/app.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./path/to/my/app.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", }, minify: true, sourcemap: "linked", bytecode: true, }); Using bytecode compilation, `tsc` starts 2x faster: ![Bytecode performance comparison](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dc8913db-01d2-48f8-a8ef-ac4e984f9763) Bytecode compilation moves parsing overhead for large input files …

title: Single-file executable › Code signing on macOS
text: To codesign a standalone executable on macOS (which fixes Gatekeeper warnings), use the `codesign` command. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" codesign --deep --force -vvvv --sign "XXXXXXXXXX" ./myapp We recommend including an `entitlements.plist` file with JIT permissions. ```xml icon="xml" title="entitlements.plist" <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd"> <plist version="1.0"> <dict> <key>com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit</key> <true/> …

title: Single-file executable › Code splitting
text: Standalone executables support code splitting. Use `--compile` with `--splitting` to create an executable that loads code-split chunks at runtime. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile --splitting ./src/entry.ts --outfile ./build/entry ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./src/entry.ts"], compile: true, splitting: true, outdir: "./build", }); ```ts src/entry.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log("Entrypoint loaded"); const lazy = await import("./lazy.ts"); lazy.hello(); ```ts src/lazy.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" …

title: Single-file executable › Complete example
text: ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const myPlugin: BunPlugin = { name: "my-plugin", setup(build) { // Plugin implementation }, }; const result = await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./src/cli.ts"], compile: { target: "bun-linux-x64", outfile: "./dist/mycli", execArgv: ["--smol"], autoloadDotenv: false, autoloadBunfig: false, }, minify: true, sourcemap: "linked", bytecode: true, define: { "process.env.NODE_ENV": JSON.stringify("production"), VERSION: JSON.stringify("1.0.0"), }, plugins: [myPlugin], }); if (result.success) { console.log("Build successful:", result.outputs[0].path); }

title: Single-file executable › Content hash
text: By default, Bun appends a content hash to the name of each embedded file, which helps with cache invalidation when you serve the files from a URL or CDN. To keep the original name instead, configure asset naming: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile --asset-naming="[name].[ext]" ./index.ts ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", }, naming: { asset: "[name].[ext]", }, });

title: Single-file executable › Cross-compile to other platforms
text: Use the `--target` flag to compile your standalone executable for a different operating system, architecture, or version of Bun than the machine you're running `bun build` on. To build for Linux x64 (most servers): ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --target=bun-linux-x64 ./index.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts"], compile: { target: "bun-linux-x64", outfile: "./myapp", }, }); To build for Linux ARM64 (for example, Graviton or Raspberry Pi): ```bash icon="terminal" terminal # Note: the default …

title: Single-file executable › Deploying to production
text: Compiled executables reduce memory usage and improve Bun's start time. Normally, Bun reads and transpiles JavaScript and TypeScript files on `import` and `require`. This is part of what makes so much of Bun "just work", but it's not free: reading files from disk, resolving paths, parsing, transpiling, and printing source code costs time and memory. Compiled executables move that cost from runtime to build time. When deploying to production, we recommend the following: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --minify --sourcemap ./path/to/my/app.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts …

title: Single-file executable › Detecting standalone mode at runtime
text: Use `Bun.isStandaloneExecutable` to check whether the current process is running from a compiled binary: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" if (Bun.isStandaloneExecutable) { // Running from `bun build --compile` output } else { // Running via `bun <file>` or as a library } Unlike `Bun.embeddedFiles.length > 0`, this check does not allocate `Blob` objects for each embedded file, so it is safe to call at startup in binaries that embed large assets.

title: Single-file executable › Disabling config loading at runtime
text: To disable `.env` or `bunfig.toml` loading for deterministic execution: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal # Disable .env loading bun build --compile --no-compile-autoload-dotenv ./app.ts --outfile myapp # Disable bunfig.toml loading bun build --compile --no-compile-autoload-bunfig ./app.ts --outfile myapp # Disable all config loading bun build --compile --no-compile-autoload-dotenv --no-compile-autoload-bunfig ./app.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./app.ts"], compile: { // tsconfig.json and package.json are disabled by default …

title: Single-file executable › Embed assets & files
text: Standalone executables can embed files directly into the binary, so a single executable can ship images, JSON configs, templates, or any other assets your application needs.

title: Single-file executable › Embed directories
text: Use `--asset` (or `compile.assets` in the JavaScript API) to embed a file or directory tree into the executable under its original relative path. The embedded files live under `import.meta.dir` at runtime and are reachable via `node:fs` (`existsSync`, `statSync`, `readdirSync`, `readFileSync`) and `Bun.file()`. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile ./index.ts --asset ./public --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", assets: ["./public"], }, }); ```ts index.ts …

title: Single-file executable › Embed N-API Addons
text: You can embed `.node` files into executables. ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const addon = require("./addon.node"); console.log(addon.hello()); If you're using `@mapbox/node-pre-gyp` or similar tools, require the `.node` file directly, or it won't bundle correctly. Some addons load a shared library that ships beside them, like `sharp` and `libvips`. With `--aot`, embed the folder that holds both: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile --aot ./index.ts --asset node_modules/@img --outfile mycli

title: Single-file executable › Embed SQLite databases
text: To embed a SQLite database into the compiled executable, set `type: "sqlite"` in the import attribute and the `embed` attribute to `"true"`. The database file must already exist on disk. Then, import it in your code: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log(myEmbeddedDb.query("select * from users LIMIT 1").get()); Finally, compile it into a standalone executable: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile ./index.ts --outfile mycli The database file must exist on disk when you run `bun build --compile`. The `embed: "true"` attribute tells the bundler to include the …

title: Single-file executable › Embed text as a string
text: Use the `text` loader when you want the contents of a file as a string. `.txt` files use it by default. For other extensions, add `with { type: "text" }` or pass `--loader .md:text`. ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log(notes); // the contents of notes.txt In a compiled executable the text is stored once, in the form the JavaScript engine uses for strings (one byte per character for ASCII text, UTF-16 otherwise). The runtime hands the string back without a copy, so a large text import costs its size in the binary and no extra copy on the heap. A text import is a module, not …

title: Single-file executable › Embedding a JSON config file
text: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Load the embedded default configuration const defaultConfig = await file(configPath).json(); // Merge with user config if it exists const userConfig = await file("./user-config.json") .json() .catch(() => ({})); const config = { ...defaultConfig, ...userConfig };

title: Single-file executable › Embedding binary files
text: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Load a WebAssembly module const wasmBytes = await file(wasmPath).arrayBuffer(); const wasmModule = await WebAssembly.instantiate(wasmBytes); // Read binary font data const fontData = await file(fontPath).bytes();

title: Single-file executable › Embedding runtime arguments
text: **`--compile-exec-argv="args"`** - Embed runtime arguments, available at runtime in `process.execArgv`: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --compile-exec-argv="--smol --user-agent=MyBot" ./app.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./app.ts"], compile: { execArgv: ["--smol", "--user-agent=MyBot"], outfile: "./myapp", }, }); ```ts app.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // In the compiled app console.log(process.execArgv); // ["--smol", "--user-agent=MyBot"]

title: Single-file executable › Embedding templates
text: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" async function sendWelcomeEmail(user: { name: string; email: string }) { const template = await file(templatePath).text(); const html = template.replace("name", user.name).replace("email", user.email); // Send email with the rendered template... }

title: Single-file executable › Enabling config loading at runtime
text: If your executable needs to read `tsconfig.json` or `package.json` at runtime, opt in with these flags: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal # Enable runtime loading of tsconfig.json bun build --compile --compile-autoload-tsconfig ./app.ts --outfile myapp # Enable runtime loading of package.json bun build --compile --compile-autoload-package-json ./app.ts --outfile myapp # Enable both bun build --compile --compile-autoload-tsconfig --compile-autoload-package-json ./app.ts --outfile myapp

title: Single-file executable › Full-stack executables
text: New in Bun v1.2.17 The `--compile` flag can create a standalone executable that contains both server and client code, which suits full-stack applications. When you import an HTML file in your server code, Bun bundles the frontend assets (JavaScript, CSS, and so on) and embeds them into the executable. ```ts server.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const server = serve({ routes: { "/": index, "/api/hello": { GET: () => Response.json({ message: "Hello from API" }) }, }, }); console.log(`Server running at http://localhost:${server.port}`); ```html index.html icon="file-code" <!DOCTYPE html> <html> …

title: Single-file executable › How it works
text: Use the `with { type: "file" }` [import attribute](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-import-attributes) to embed a file: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log(icon); // During development: "./icon.png" // After compilation: "/$bunfs/root/icon-a1b2c3d4.png" (internal path) The import returns a **path string** that points to the embedded file. At build time, Bun: 1. Reads the file contents 2. Embeds the data into the executable 3. Replaces the import with an internal path (prefixed with `/$bunfs/`) You can then read this embedded file using `Bun.file()` or Node.js `fs` APIs.

title: Single-file executable › JIT policy
text: Code that only runs during startup rarely pays back the time the JIT spends compiling it. `--compile-jit-policy <n>` (`compile: { jitPolicy: n }` in `Bun.build`) starts the executable with JavaScriptCore's tier-up thresholds multiplied by `n`, so startup code stays in the interpreter longer. The default, `1`, is the normal JIT policy. The scale stays in effect until the program calls `Bun.unsafe.setJITPolicy(1)`, which it should do once it is interactive: ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./app.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", jitPolicy: 8 }, …

title: Single-file executable › Listing embedded files
text: `Bun.embeddedFiles` exposes all embedded files as `Blob` objects: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // List all embedded files for (const blob of embeddedFiles) { console.log(`${blob.name} - ${blob.size} bytes`); } // Output: // icon-a1b2c3d4.png - 4096 bytes // data-e5f6g7h8.json - 256 bytes // template-i9j0k1l2.html - 1024 bytes Each item in `Bun.embeddedFiles` is a `Blob` with a `name` property: ```ts embeddedFiles: ReadonlyArray<Blob>; Use it to serve every embedded asset through static routes: ```ts server.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Build static routes from all embedded …

title: Single-file executable › Minification
text: To trim down the size of the executable, enable minification: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile --minify ./index.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", }, minify: true, // Enable all minification }); // Or granular control: await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", }, minify: { whitespace: true, syntax: true, identifiers: true, }, }); This uses Bun's minifier to reduce the code size. Overall though, Bun's binary is still way too big and we …

title: Single-file executable › Profile-guided bytecode layout
text: `--bytecode-order` is profile-guided optimization (PGO) for `--bytecode`. Run your executable once to record which functions it uses, then build again with that profile. Bun places the bytecode the run used together at the front of the file, so the executable reads and decodes less of itself: it starts faster and uses less memory. In one large CLI application, cold start went from 1.0s to 0.53s and memory at startup dropped by 40 MB. ```sh # 1. Build bun build --compile --bytecode ./cli.ts --outfile myapp # 2. Run it the way your users do. The profile is written on exit. …

title: Single-file executable › Reading embedded files with Bun.file()
text: `Bun.file()` is the recommended way to read embedded files: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Get file contents as different types const bytes = await file(icon).arrayBuffer(); // ArrayBuffer const text = await file(icon).text(); // string (for text files) const blob = file(icon); // Blob // Stream the file in a response fetch(req) { return new Response(file(icon), { headers: { "Content-Type": "image/png" }, }); }, };

title: Single-file executable › Reading embedded files with Node.js fs
text: Embedded files work with the Node.js file system APIs: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Synchronous read const iconBuffer = readFileSync(icon); // Async read const configData = await fs.readFile(config, "utf-8"); const parsed = JSON.parse(configData); // Check file stats const stats = await fs.stat(icon); console.log(`Icon size: ${stats.size} bytes`);

title: Single-file executable › Runtime arguments via `BUN_OPTIONS`
text: Standalone executables read the `BUN_OPTIONS` environment variable, so you can pass runtime flags without recompiling: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Enable CPU profiling on a compiled executable BUN_OPTIONS="--cpu-prof" ./myapp # Enable heap profiling with markdown output BUN_OPTIONS="--heap-prof-md" ./myapp # Combine multiple flags BUN_OPTIONS="--smol --cpu-prof-md" ./myapp An executable built with `bun compile` only takes `--inspect` if you built it with [`--compile-inspector`](/compiler/debugging).

title: Single-file executable › Serving static assets in an HTTP server
text: Use static routes in `Bun.serve()` for efficient static file serving: ```ts server.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" serve({ // Inside the compiled executable, file() on an embedded path returns an // in-memory Blob, which routes only accepts wrapped in a Response. routes: { "/favicon.ico": new Response(file(favicon)), "/logo.png": new Response(file(logo)), "/styles.css": new Response(file(styles)), }, fetch(req) { return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 }); }, }); Bun automatically handles Content-Type headers and caching for static routes.

title: Single-file executable › Smaller executables
text: `--trim` is experimental. ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --trim ./app.ts --outfile myapp A standalone executable is a copy of `bun` with your program attached, so it also contains the package manager, the test runner and the type checker. `--trim` removes them. With [`bun compile`](/compiler/aot), it also removes the Bun and Node.js APIs your code never calls. See [Smaller executables](/compiler/size).

title: Single-file executable › SQLite
text: You can use `bun:sqlite` imports with `bun build --compile`. By default, Bun resolves the database relative to the current working directory of the process. ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log(db.query("select * from users LIMIT 1").get()); That means if the executable is at `/usr/bin/hello` and the user's terminal is in `/home/me/Desktop`, Bun looks for `/home/me/Desktop/my.db`. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" cd /home/me/Desktop ./hello

text: The segments of the `--target` value can appear in any order, as long as they're delimited by `-`. | --target | Operating System | Architecture | Libc | | -------------------- | ---------------- | ------------ | ----- | | bun-linux-x64 | Linux | x64 | glibc | | bun-linux-arm64 | Linux | arm64 | glibc | | bun-windows-x64 | Windows | x64 | - | | bun-windows-arm64 | Windows | arm64 | - | | bun-darwin-x64 | macOS | x64 | - | | bun-darwin-arm64 | macOS | arm64 | - | | bun-linux-x64-musl | Linux | x64 | musl | | bun-linux-arm64-musl | Linux | arm64 | musl | On x64, Bun ships a single binary that …

title: Single-file executable › Turn off `eval` and `new Function`
text: ```bash icon="terminal" terminal bun build --compile --disallow-code-generation-from-strings ./app.ts --outfile myapp In this executable, `eval()` and `new Function()` throw an `EvalError`. It's Bun's [runtime flag](/runtime/code-generation-from-strings) of the same name, embedded in the executable. In `Bun.build`, the option is `compile: { disallowCodeGenerationFromStrings: true }`.

title: Single-file executable › Unsupported CLI arguments
text: The `--compile` flag does not support the following flags: - `--outdir` — use `outfile` instead. - `--public-path` - `--target=node` - `--target=browser` (without HTML entrypoints — see [Standalone HTML](/bundler/standalone-html) for `--compile --target=browser` with `.html` files) - `--no-bundle` - Bun always bundles everything into the executable.

title: Single-file executable › Using plugins
text: Plugins work with standalone executables; use them to transform files during the build: ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const envPlugin: BunPlugin = { name: "env-loader", setup(build) { build.onLoad({ filter: /\.env\.json$/ }, async args => { // Transform .env.json files into validated config objects const env = await Bun.file(args.path).json(); return { contents: `export default ${JSON.stringify(env)};`, loader: "js", }; }); }, }; await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./cli.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./mycli", }, plugins: [envPlugin], }); Example use case - embedding environment config …

title: Single-file executable › What do these flags do?
text: The `--minify` argument reduces the size of the transpiled output code. For a large application, this can save megabytes of space. For smaller applications, it might still improve start time a little. The `--sourcemap` argument embeds a sourcemap compressed with zstd, so that errors & stacktraces point to their original locations instead of the transpiled location. Bun decompresses & resolves the sourcemap automatically when an error occurs. The `--bytecode` argument enables bytecode compilation. Every time you run JavaScript code in Bun, JavaScriptCore (the engine) compiles your source code …

title: Single-file executable › Windows-specific flags
text: When compiling a standalone executable on Windows, platform-specific options customize metadata on the generated `.exe` file: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Custom icon bun build --compile --windows-icon=path/to/icon.ico ./app.ts --outfile myapp # Hide console window (for GUI apps) bun build --compile --windows-hide-console ./app.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./app.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", windows: { icon: "./path/to/icon.ico", hideConsole: true, // Additional Windows metadata: title: "My Application", publisher: …

title: Single-file executable › Worker
text: To use workers in a standalone executable, add the worker's entrypoint to the build: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun build --compile ./index.ts ./my-worker.ts --outfile myapp ```ts build.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await Bun.build({ entrypoints: ["./index.ts", "./my-worker.ts"], compile: { outfile: "./myapp", }, }); Then, reference the worker in your code: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" console.log("Hello from Bun!"); // Any of these will work: new Worker("./my-worker.ts"); new Worker(new URL("./my-worker.ts", import.meta.url)); new Worker(new URL("./my-worker.ts", …

title: Get more of your program typed › Causes
text: The first line of an entry has one of these codes.

title: Get more of your program typed › lost-track
text: An operator such as `+`, `<` or `===` runs on a value whose type the compiler doesn't know. The entry goes away when the type of the value is known, for example with typeof.

title: Get more of your program typed › Other reports
text: | Flag | Lists | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | `--explain=json` | Every entry, one JSON object per line | | `--explain=guards` | [Type guards that can fail at run time](/compiler/debugging) | | `--explain=guards-json` | The same guards, one JSON object per line | | `--explain=trim` | [What `--trim` kept, and why](/compiler/size) | | `--explain=allocations` | Where objects are allocated | You can pass `--explain` more than once. In `Bun.build`, `compile: { aotExplain: ["guards"] }` adds the lines to `result.logs`.

title: Get more of your program typed › Read an entry
text: ```ts main.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" interface Item { sku: string; price: number; } const items: Item[] = [{ sku: "A-1", price: 2.5 }]; const saved: any = JSON.parse('{ "sku": "B-2", "price": 10 }'); items.push(saved); let total = 0; for (const item of items) total += item.price; console.log(total); ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun compile ./main.ts --explain ```txt 7 | const saved: any = JSON.parse('{ "sku": "B-2", "price": 10 }'); ^ note: 1. unknown-object: The compiler doesn't know the shape of what JSON.parse() returns. at main.ts:7:25 note: 1 of 1 untyped access note: 1 of these …

title: Get more of your program typed › unknown
text: The compiler recorded no reason. That's a bug in Bun. [Report it](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues) with the entry.

title: Get more of your program typed › unknown-callee
text: The compiler can't tell which function a call reaches, as in `handlers[name](request)` or a method of an [unknown object](#unknown-object). The call is indirect and its result has no type. Call the function directly. If you can't, narrow the result so that the code after it is typed.

title: Get more of your program typed › unknown-object
text: The compiler doesn't know the shape of an object, so accesses to it are lookups or need a check. Without a reason of its own, the entry has the location of the access. | The object | What to do | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Comes from `JSON.parse`, `response.json()`, `eval` or a module loaded at run time | Check its fields and build a new object from them | | Comes from Bun or Node.js, like `process.env` or `fs.statSync()` | Read what …

text: The report ends with the share of your property accesses that are typed. Code in `node_modules` gets a line of its own. ```txt Dependencies: 3.1% of property accesses are one load: 210 free, 1,320 tested, 5,244 by name (6,774) 92.4% of property accesses are one load: 1,204 free, 61 tested, 38 by name (1,303) | Word | The compiled code | | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `free` | One load or store at a fixed offset | | `tested` | A check each time, such as of the shape, then the load or store | | `by name` | A lookup at run time | Only the code …

text: Next.js and Angular put the paths of your pages together while the server runs, so the build doesn't find them. Pass the pages as entry points, and what the server reads from disk with [`--asset`](/compiler/executables#embed-directories). The other frameworks only need the assets. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Next.js with output: "standalone", in .next/standalone bun compile ./server.js ".next/server/**/*.js" --asset .next --asset public # Nuxt bun compile ./.output/server/index.mjs --asset .output/public # Astro bun compile ./dist/server/entry.mjs --asset dist/client # SvelteKit bun …

text: Most packages ship JavaScript and `.d.ts` files, so the types inside their functions are gone. `bun compile --library` also writes your TypeScript, and a `package.json` whose `exports` point `bun compile` at it. ```ts src/index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" return "hello " + name; } ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "greeter", "version": "1.0.0" } ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun compile --library ```txt index.js 87 bytes (entry point) index.d.ts 53 bytes (declaration) index.aot.ts 103 bytes (aot source) package.json 430 bytes (asset) ```json title="dist/package.json" …

title: Smaller executables › Feature names
text: `allow` and `remove` take these names. Your editor completes them from the type `Bun.Build.TrimFeature`, and `--explain=trim` prints them in parentheses. Each size is roughly what the feature adds to a trimmed executable. No size means less than 0.1 MB. | Name | What it covers | Linux x64 | macOS arm64 | | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | …

title: Smaller executables › Make it smaller
text: - `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` removes the parser and the interpreter. `eval` and `new Function` then throw. - `--trim-locales en,de` removes the `Intl` data for every other locale. Using another locale exits the process. - `--no-compile-function-source` removes the source text of functions. `fn.toString()` then returns `[native code]`, and an error message [quotes less](/compiler/compatibility) of the code that failed. Without `--trim-locales`, Bun keeps the locales that your code passes as constants, as in `toLocaleString("de")`. One call with a computed locale, or with none, …

title: Smaller executables › See what the compiler found
text: `--trim` only removes what the compiler can prove you don't use. `--explain=trim` lists what it keeps and why. With `bun check --aot`, it builds nothing. ```ts server.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" Bun.serve({ port: 3000, routes: { "/": () => new Response("hello") }, }); console.log("listening"); ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun check --aot --explain=trim ./server.ts ```txt aot: trim: the compiler can see every API this program uses aot: trim: kept Bun.serve (serve): used (Bun.serve) at server.ts:1:1 aot: trim: removed bun:sqlite and node:sqlite (sqlite): unused

title: Smaller executables › Turn off code from strings
text: A dependency that calls `new Function` is the most common reason `--trim` is blocked. With [`--disallow-code-generation-from-strings`](/runtime/code-generation-from-strings), those calls throw an `EvalError`, so they block nothing. A library that tries `new Function` in a `try` block falls back to plain code, and one that needs generated code throws at startup. `bun` takes the flag too, so you can find out which before you build. `node:vm` and `module._compile` still run code from strings with that flag, as in Node.js. With `=strict` they throw the `EvalError` too, and block nothing.

title: Smaller executables › Using a removed feature
text: Bun removes code, not names. `typeof HTMLRewriter` gives the same result as before. A call throws an `Error` with the code `ERR_FEATURE_REMOVED` and a message that says how to keep the feature. Your program runs into this through a name that isn't known until run time, as in `Bun[name]()` or `globalThis[name]()`, and in code that the compiler never sees, like a string passed to `eval`. That code finds the APIs that the rest of your program uses. For `Bun[name]()`, the parts of `Bun` that are written in JavaScript, like `Bun.$` and `Bun.sql`, are always kept, and others may be. title: Troubleshooting › The executable is slower than `bun run`
text: Look for these causes, in this order. 1. Your hot code is untyped. [`bun compile --explain`](/compiler/explain) lists the code that compiled to a slow path, worst first, with a fix for each. 2. A library generates code at run time, and [Bun interprets it](/compiler/compatibility#code-from-strings). 4. The program runs [WebAssembly that it downloads or assembles at run time](/compiler/compatibility#webassembly). 5. Code is …

title: Troubleshooting › The executable is too large
text: [`--trim`](/compiler/size) removes the Bun and Node.js APIs that your code never calls. If that changes little, something in your program could reach any API, usually `eval` or a dynamic `require()`. `--explain=trim` says what. `--no-compile-function-source` leaves out the source text of your functions.

title: How bun compile uses your types › 32-bit integers
text: To TypeScript, and under `bun run`, `int32` is a `number`. In an executable it takes four bytes instead of eight, and arithmetic on it skips the checks for fractions. It pays off in the fields of objects that you create by the million. ```ts cursor.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" class Cursor { column: int32 = 0; advance(by: int32) { this.column = this.column + by; // [!code --] this.column = (this.column + by) | 0; // [!code ++] } } The build has to prove that every value you store in an `int32` is a whole number in range. Where it can't, it stops (`TS100031`), and the error says what to …

title: How bun compile uses your types › Build your own objects from what you parse
text: ```ts const user: User = JSON.parse(text); // [!code --] const { id, name } = JSON.parse(text); // [!code ++] const user: User = { id, name }; // [!code ++] `JSON.parse`, `response.json()` and `request.json()` return ordinary objects, whatever type you declare for the result. They don't have the fixed layout of `User`, so every read looks the property up. An object that [your own code creates](/compiler/explain#unknown-object) has the layout.

title: How bun compile uses your types › Convert, don't cast
text: ```ts const query: any = { page: "2" }; const page = query.page as number; // [!code --] const page = Number(query.page); // [!code ++] console.log(page + 1); `as`, `any` and `!` do nothing at run time. With the cast, `page` is still a string and this prints `21`, compiled or not. With the conversion, the compiler knows that `page` is a number, so there's no guard to fail.

title: How bun compile uses your types › Keep computed keys in a `Map`
text: ```ts class Counter { count = 0; labels = new Map<string, string>(); // [!code ++] } (counter as any)[key] = "visits"; // [!code --] counter.labels.set(key, "visits"); // [!code ++] A store with a computed key can change the object's shape. So can `Object.defineProperty` and `Object.setPrototypeOf`. Any `Counter` could be the one that changed, so every access to a `Counter` gets slower.

title: How bun compile uses your types › What types get you
text: ```ts account.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" class Account { balance = 0; } function total(accounts: Account[]): number { let sum = 0; for (const account of accounts) sum += account.balance; return sum; } Every `Account` has the same fields in the same places, like a struct in Go or Rust, so `account.balance` is one load from a fixed offset. A call to `total` is a direct call that the compiler can inline. You don't have to annotate everything. The compiler follows each object from where it's created to where it's used, in `.js` files too. Annotations matter where it can't do that, such as the …

title: How bun compile uses your types › When a value doesn't match its type
text: ```ts visits.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" function double(n: number): number { return n * 2; } const body: any = JSON.parse('{"visits":"3"}'); console.log(double(body.visits)); ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun compile ./visits.ts && ./visits ```txt 6 `bun run` prints `6` too. TypeScript lets you call a value a `number` when it isn't one, through `any`, `as`, `!`, `JSON.parse` and `.d.ts` files. So where compiled code relies on a declared type, it checks the value first. title: Formatter › Git hooks
text: `--staged` formats only the files you're about to commit and stages them again, so you don't need `lint-staged`. ```sh .git/hooks/pre-commit icon="terminal" #!/bin/sh bun fmt --staged If a file has both staged and unstaged changes, Bun looks at the staged version, which is what the commit gets. title: Formatter › Ignore code
text: `bun fmt` uses Prettier's comment, so existing ones keep working. It applies to the next statement, element, or rule. ```ts // prettier-ignore const matrix = [ 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, ]; In JSX it's `{/* prettier-ignore */}`, in CSS `/* prettier-ignore */`, in HTML and Markdown `<!-- prettier-ignore -->`, and in YAML and GraphQL `# prettier-ignore`.

title: Formatter › Ignore files
text: Every `.gitignore` in the repository counts, whichever directory you run `bun fmt` from. Outside a repository, those in the current directory and below it count. With a Prettier config, only the `.gitignore` in the current directory does, because that's the only one Prettier reads. To skip more than `.gitignore` does, list the files in `bunfig.toml`. A `.prettierignore` file works too. ```toml bunfig.toml icon="settings" [fmt] ignorePatterns = ["vendor/", "**/*.gen.ts"]

text: ```toml bunfig.toml icon="settings" [fmt] sortImports = true ```ts title="Before" ```ts title="After" - Imports are grouped: built-in modules, packages, aliases like `@/`, relative paths, styles. - Each group is sorted by path, and the names in `{ }` are sorted too. - Two imports from the same module become one. - Side-effect imports like `import "./setup"` never move, and nothing moves past one. - A comment directly above an import moves with it. text: Pipe text through `bun fmt`. It prints the result and writes nothing. The path picks the language and the options. title: Formatter › Svelte

title: Build-time constants with --define › Why use build-time constants?
text: Bun embeds build-time constants directly into your compiled code, making them: - **Zero runtime overhead** - No environment variable lookups or file reads - **Immutable** - Values are baked into the binary at compile time - **Optimizable** - Dead code elimination can remove unused branches - **Secure** - No external dependencies or configuration files to manage Build-time constants are similar to `gcc -D` or `#define` in C/C++, but for JavaScript/TypeScript.

title: Define and replace static globals & constants › How is this different than find-and-replace or string replacement?
text: The `--define` flag operates on the AST (Abstract Syntax Tree), not on text. The replacement happens during transpilation, so it participates in optimizations like dead code elimination. String replacement tools tend to have escaping issues and replace unintended parts of the code.

title: Define and replace static globals & constants › How is this different than setting a variable?
text: You can also set `process.env.NODE_ENV` to `"production"` in your code, but that doesn't help with dead code elimination. In JavaScript, property accesses can have side effects. Getters & setters can be functions, and even dynamically defined (due to prototype chains and Proxy). Even if you set `process.env.NODE_ENV` to `"production"`, static analysis tools can't assume it is still `"production"` on the next line.

title: Define and replace static globals & constants › Replace global identifiers

For example, to replace all usages of `global` with `globalThis`: ```sh bun --define global="globalThis" src/index.ts `global` is a global object in Node.js, but not in web browsers, so this replacement fixes code …

title: Define and replace static globals & constants › Replace values with JSON
text: `--define` can also replace values with JSON objects and arrays. To replace all usages of `AWS` with the JSON object `{"ACCESS_KEY":"abc","SECRET_KEY":"def"}`: ```sh # JSON bun --define AWS='{"ACCESS_KEY":"abc","SECRET_KEY":"def"}' src/index.ts Bun transforms these into the equivalent JavaScript code. From: ```ts console.log(AWS.ACCESS_KEY); // => "abc" To: ```ts console.log({ ACCESS_KEY: "abc", SECRET_KEY: "def" }.ACCESS_KEY);

title: Selectively run tests concurrently with glob patterns › Migration Strategy
text: To migrate existing tests to concurrent execution: 1. **Start with independent integration tests** - these typically don't share state 2. **Rename files to match the glob pattern**: `mv api.test.ts concurrent-api.test.ts` 3. **Run `bun test`** - check for race conditions and flaky or unexpected failures 4. **Continue migrating stable tests** file by file

title: Catalogs › 1. Define Catalogs in Root package.json
text: In your root-level `package.json`, add a `catalog` or `catalogs` field within the `workspaces` object: ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "my-monorepo", "workspaces": { "packages": ["packages/*"], "catalog": { "react": "^19.0.0", "react-dom": "^19.0.0" }, "catalogs": { "testing": { "jest": "30.0.0", "testing-library": "14.0.0" } } } } `catalog` and `catalogs` also work at the top level of `package.json`.

title: Catalogs › 2. Reference Catalog Versions in Workspace Packages
text: In your workspace packages, use the `catalog:` protocol to reference versions: ```json packages/app/package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "catalog:", "react-dom": "catalog:", "jest": "catalog:testing" } } ```json packages/ui/package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "ui", "dependencies": { "react": "catalog:", "react-dom": "catalog:" }, "devDependencies": { "jest": "catalog:testing", "testing-library": "catalog:testing" }, "peerDependencies": { "react": "catalog:" } } `catalog:` references work in `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, …

title: Catalogs › 3. Run Bun Install
text: Run `bun install` to install all dependencies according to the catalog versions.

title: Catalogs › Adding to the catalog with `bun add`
text: `bun add --catalog` adds the entry to the root catalog and writes `"catalog:"` to the current package; `--catalog=<name>` adds it to `catalogs.<name>` and writes `"catalog:<name>"`. Bun reuses an existing catalog entry unless you pass an explicit version. See [`bun add --catalog`](/pm/cli/add#--catalog). ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add react --catalog Even without the flag, `bun add react` (no version) writes `"catalog:"` when the default catalog already lists `react`. Pass a version to write a concrete range instead.

title: Catalogs › Benefits of Using Catalogs
text: - **Consistency**: All packages use the same version of critical dependencies - **Maintenance**: Update a dependency version in one place instead of across multiple `package.json` files - **Clarity**: Makes it obvious which dependencies are standardized across your monorepo - **Simplicity**: No extra version resolution strategies or external tools

title: Catalogs › Catalog vs Catalogs
text: Bun supports two ways to define catalogs: 1. **`catalog`** (singular): A single default catalog for commonly used dependencies ```json package.json icon="file-json" "catalog": { "react": "^19.0.0", "react-dom": "^19.0.0" } Reference with `catalog:`: ```json packages/app/package.json icon="file-json" "dependencies": { "react": "catalog:" } 2. **`catalogs`** (plural): Multiple named catalogs for grouping dependencies ```json package.json icon="file-json" "catalogs": { "testing": { "jest": "30.0.0" }, "ui": { "tailwind": "4.0.0" } } Reference with `catalog:<name>`: ```json …

title: Catalogs › Limitations and Edge Cases
text: - Catalog references must match a dependency defined in either `catalog` or one of the named `catalogs` - Bun ignores empty strings and whitespace in catalog names and treats them as the default catalog - `catalog:default` is the same as `catalog:`. You can define the default catalog as either `catalog` or `catalogs.default`, but a package listed in both is an error - Invalid dependency versions in catalogs fail to resolve during `bun install` - `catalog:` only works in the root and workspace `package.json` files. Inside a published package it fails to resolve. Publish with `bun publish` or …

title: Catalogs › Lockfile Integration
text: Bun's lockfile tracks catalog versions, so installs are consistent across environments. The lockfile includes: - The catalog definitions from your package.json - The resolution of each cataloged dependency ```json bun.lock(excerpt) icon="file-json" { "lockfileVersion": 2, "workspaces": { "": { "name": "react-monorepo", }, "packages/app": { "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "catalog:", "react-dom": "catalog:", ... }, }, ... }, "catalog": { "react": "^19.0.0", "react-dom": "^19.0.0", ... }, "catalogs": { "build": { "webpack": "5.88.2", ... }, ... }, "packages": { ... } }

title: Catalogs › Overview
text: Instead of each workspace package specifying its own versions, you: 1. Define version catalogs in the root `package.json` 2. Reference those versions with the `catalog:` protocol 3. Update every package at once by changing the version in one place Catalogs matter most in large monorepos where dozens of packages depend on the same versions of key dependencies.

title: Catalogs › Publishing
text: When you run `bun publish` or `bun pm pack`, Bun replaces `catalog:` references in your `package.json` with the resolved version numbers. The published package includes regular semver strings and no longer depends on your catalog definitions.

text: Unlike other npm clients, Bun does not execute arbitrary lifecycle scripts for installed dependencies, such as `postinstall`. These scripts represent a potential security risk, as they can execute arbitrary code on your machine. To tell Bun to allow lifecycle scripts for a particular package, add the package to `trustedDependencies` in your package.json. ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "my-app", "version": "1.0.0", "trustedDependencies": ["my-trusted-package"] // [!code ++] } Bun reads this field and runs lifecycle scripts for `my-trusted-package`.

title: bun audit › `bun audit fix`
text: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun audit fix Runs the audit, then upgrades each vulnerable package to the lowest non-vulnerable version that every dependent's range allows, and installs. Only `bun.lock` and `node_modules` change, with one exception: Bun treats an exact version pin in your own `package.json` (a dependency, a catalog entry, or an [`overrides`](/pm/overrides) rule) as `^version`. If Bun finds a fix, it rewrites the pin. fixing: ms@0.7.0 → 0.7.1 lodash@4.17.20 → 4.17.21 package.json: 4.17.20 → 4.17.21 tar@6.1.11 → 6.1.12 package.json (overrides): 6.1.11 → 6.1.12 blocked by a …

title: bun audit › `bun audit fix --latest`
text: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun audit fix --latest Same as `bun audit fix`, but ranges in your own `package.json` files, catalogs, and `overrides` no longer block a fix. Bun rewrites them to accept the new version, keeping their style (`^5.0.0` → `^6.3.1`, `~5.7.1` → `~6.3.1`, exact stays exact). Ranges declared by third-party packages still block; use `overrides` for those.

title: bun audit › Exit code
text: `0` if no vulnerabilities remain after Bun applies `--audit-level` and `--ignore`, `1` otherwise. For `bun audit fix`, this is based on the re-audit after installing (or the plan, with `--dry-run`). If the registry request fails, both commands print an error to stderr and exit `1`. The same goes for a response that is not an advisory report (for example, a registry or proxy that answers the audit request with an HTML page, an error object or an empty body): a response Bun cannot read never counts as a clean audit.

text: **`--audit-level=<lowmoderatehigh|critical>`** - Only report vulnerabilities at this severity or higher: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun audit --audit-level=high **`--prod`** (`-p`, `-P`, `--production`) - Only audit packages reachable through `dependencies`, `optionalDependencies`, or `peerDependencies`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun audit --prod **`--omit=<devoptionalpeer>`** - Skip packages only reachable through the given dependency type. Repeatable. `--omit=dev` is the same as `--prod`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun audit --omit=optional --omit=peer **`--ignore <id>`** …

title: bun dedupe › `--check` and `--dry-run`
text: `--check` reports what Bun would remove without changing anything, and exits `1` if there are duplicates. Use it in CI: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun dedupe --check bun dedupe v1.4.0 (abc12345) ↳ esbuild 0.15.10 → 0.15.11 ↳ react 18.2.0 → 18.3.1 2 duplicate versions can be removed (checked 5 packages in bun.lock) [9.00ms] bun dedupe `--dry-run` prints the same output but always exits `0`. `--lockfile-only` rewrites `bun.lock` without installing.

title: bun install › Default strategy
text: The default linker strategy depends on whether you're starting fresh or have an existing project: - **New workspaces/monorepos**: `isolated` (prevents phantom dependencies) - **New single-package projects**: `hoisted` (traditional npm behavior) - **Existing projects (made pre-v1.3.2)**: `hoisted` (preserves backward compatibility) A `configVersion` field in your lockfile controls the default. For a detailed explanation, see [isolated installs](/pm/isolated-installs).

title: bun install › Dry run
text: To perform a dry run, without installing anything: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --dry-run Bun resolves the dependency tree and lists every package in it, installed already or not. During a dry run, Bun does not: - install packages into `node_modules` - change an existing `package.json` - write `bun.lock` or `yarn.lock` - run your project's lifecycle scripts To write `yarn.lock`, run `bun install --yarn` without `--dry-run`.

text: To install a package globally, use the `-g`/`--global` flag. Use it to install command-line tools. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --global cowsay # or `bun install -g cowsay` cowsay "Bun!" ```txt ______ < Bun! > \ ^__^ \ (oo)\_______ (__)\ )\/\ ||----w | || ||

text: The traditional npm/Yarn approach that flattens dependencies into a shared `node_modules` directory: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --linker hoisted

title: bun install › Installation strategies
text: Bun supports two package installation strategies that determine how dependencies are organized in `node_modules`:

title: bun install › Installing dependencies for specific packages
text: In a monorepo, you can install the dependencies for a subset of packages using the `--filter` flag. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Install dependencies for all workspaces except `pkg-c` bun install --filter '!pkg-c' # Install dependencies for only `pkg-a` in `./packages/pkg-a` bun install --filter './packages/pkg-a' See [filtering](/pm/filter#bun-install-and-bun-outdated).

title: bun install › Isolated installs
text: A pnpm-like approach that creates strict dependency isolation to prevent [phantom dependencies](/pm/isolated-installs), packages you can import without declaring them in `package.json`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --linker isolated Isolated installs create a central package store in `node_modules/.bun/` with symlinks in the top-level `node_modules`. This ensures packages can only access their declared dependencies.

title: bun install › Lifecycle scripts
text: Unlike other npm clients, Bun does not execute arbitrary lifecycle scripts like `postinstall` for installed dependencies. Executing arbitrary scripts represents a potential security risk. To tell Bun to allow lifecycle scripts for a particular package, add the package to `trustedDependencies` in your package.json. ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "my-app", "version": "1.0.0", "trustedDependencies": ["my-trusted-package"] // [!code ++] } Then re-install the package. Bun reads this field and runs lifecycle scripts for `my-trusted-package`. Lifecycle scripts run in parallel during …

title: bun install › Lockfile
text: `bun.lock` is Bun’s lockfile format. See [our blog post about the text lockfile](https://bun.com/blog/bun-lock-text-lockfile). Before Bun 1.2, the lockfile was binary and called `bun.lockb`. To upgrade an old lockfile to the new format, run `bun install --save-text-lockfile --frozen-lockfile --lockfile-only`, then delete `bun.lockb`.

title: bun install › Lockfile Migration
text: - Converts `pnpm-lock.yaml` (lockfile versions 7–9, including pnpm 11's multi-document files) to `bun.lock` - Preserves resolved versions and integrity hashes - Preserves peer dependency ranges and `peerDependenciesMeta`, so the next `bun install` leaves the migrated lockfile unchanged - Writes every catalog entry declared in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` to `bun.lock`, including entries no workspace uses yet (`pnpm-lock.yaml` lists only the entries in use), so the next `bun install` leaves the catalog unchanged - Keeps `catalog:` and `workspace:` specifiers as written and records each workspace …

title: bun install › Logging
text: To modify logging verbosity: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --verbose # debug logging bun install --silent # no logging

title: bun install › Minimum release age
text: To protect against supply chain attacks where malicious packages are quickly published, you can configure a minimum age requirement for npm packages. Bun filters out package versions published more recently than the specified threshold (in seconds) during installation. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Only install package versions published at least 3 days ago bun add @types/bun --minimum-release-age 259200 # seconds # Exempt packages from the age gate (comma-separated, or repeat the flag) bun install --minimum-release-age 259200 --minimum-release-age-excludes @types/node,typescript@5.4.5 A …

title: bun install › Non-npm dependencies
text: Bun supports installing dependencies from Git, GitHub, and local or remotely-hosted tarballs. See [`bun add`](/pm/cli/add). ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "dependencies": { "dayjs": "git+https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs.git", "lodash": "git+ssh://github.com/lodash/lodash.git#4.17.21", "moment": "git@github.com:moment/moment.git", "zod": "github:colinhacks/zod", "react": "https://registry.npmjs.org/react/-/react-18.2.0.tgz", "bun-types": "npm:@types/bun" } }

title: bun install › npm registry metadata
text: Bun uses a binary format for caching npm registry responses. This loads much faster than JSON and tends to be smaller on disk. These files live in `~/.bun/install/cache/*.npm`. The filename pattern is `${hash(packageName)}.npm`. It’s a hash so that Bun doesn’t need to create extra directories for scoped packages. Bun's usage of `Cache-Control` ignores `Age`. This improves performance, but means Bun may be about 5 minutes behind the latest package version metadata from npm.

title: bun install › Offline installs
text: With a warm cache, `bun install` can run without the network: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Use cached package metadata regardless of age; only fetch what is missing from the cache bun install --prefer-offline # Never touch the network (registry, tarball URLs, git); a required dependency that is not cached is an error bun install --offline `--prefer-offline` is also what `install.prefer = "offline"` in `bunfig.toml` selects; `install.offline = true` is the config form of `--offline`. With a complete restored cache, `--offline --frozen-lockfile` makes a CI install fully deterministic and …

title: bun install › Omitting dependencies
text: To omit dev, peer, or optional dependencies, use the `--omit` flag. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Exclude "devDependencies" from the installation. This will apply to the # root package and workspaces if they exist. Transitive dependencies will # not have "devDependencies". bun install --omit dev # Install only dependencies from "dependencies" bun install --omit=dev --omit=peer --omit=optional A package listed under both `devDependencies` and optional `peerDependencies` is left out by `--omit dev` and `--production`, unless an installed package still depends on it.

title: bun install › Overrides and resolutions
text: Bun supports npm's `"overrides"` and Yarn's `"resolutions"` in `package.json`. Both specify a version range for _metadependencies_, the dependencies of your dependencies. See [overrides and resolutions](/pm/overrides). {/* prettier-ignore */} ```json package.json icon="file-json" { "name": "my-app", "dependencies": { "foo": "^2.0.0" }, "overrides": { // [!code ++] "bar": "~4.4.0" // [!code ++] } // [!code ++] } To add a dependency or peer dependency that a third-party package forgot to declare, use pnpm's and Yarn's `"packageExtensions"`. See [package extensions](/pm/package-extensions).

title: bun install › Peer dependencies?
text: `bun install` installs peer dependencies automatically, and picks versions much like pnpm does: 1. If a package above the one with the peer dependency depends on that name, the peer uses that version. "Above" means its parent, its parent's parent, and so on up to your workspace and the root `package.json`. This applies even if the version is out of range: if your app depends on `react@17`, every library that it uses gets `react@17`. 2. Otherwise, Bun picks one version that satisfies every package with a peer dependency on that name. It prefers a version that's already installed, then the …

text: For performance, `bun install` uses different system calls to install dependencies depending on the platform. You can force a specific backend with the `--backend` flag. **`hardlink`** is the default backend on Linux and Windows. Benchmarking showed it to be the fastest on Linux. ```bash rm -rf node_modules bun install --backend hardlink **`clonefile`** is the default backend on macOS. Benchmarking showed it to be the fastest on macOS. It is only available on macOS. ```bash rm -rf node_modules bun install --backend clonefile **`clonefile_each_dir`** is similar to `clonefile`, except it clones …

title: bun install › Platform-specific dependencies?
text: Bun stores normalized `cpu`, `os` and `libc` values from npm in the lockfile, along with the resolved packages. It skips downloading, extracting, and installing packages disabled for the current target at runtime. This means the lockfile doesn't change between platforms/architectures even if the packages ultimately installed do change. The `libc` field (`"glibc"` or `"musl"`) is how native packages such as `@rollup/rollup-linux-x64-gnu` and `@rollup/rollup-linux-x64-musl` tell the two Linux variants apart. npm only includes it in the full package metadata, so Bun requests the full metadata for …

title: bun install › pnpm migration

The original `pnpm-lock.yaml` file remains unmodified. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install Migration only runs when `bun.lock` is absent. There is currently no opt-out flag for pnpm migration. Bun writes the migrated `bun.lock` and the `package.json` edits described below together, and only when the command saves a lockfile. `bun install`, `bun add`, `bun remove`, `bun update`, `bun pm migrate`, and `bun pm …

title: bun install › Production mode
text: To install in production mode (without `devDependencies`): ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install --production `--production` implies `--frozen-lockfile`. It only controls what gets installed. `devDependencies` already in `node_modules` from an earlier install stay there. Use [`bun prune --production`](/pm/cli/prune) to remove them. For reproducible installs, use `--frozen-lockfile`. Bun installs the exact versions specified in the lockfile and does not update it. If your `package.json` disagrees with `bun.lock`, Bun exits with an error. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun install …

title: bun install › Yarn migration
text: Bun migrates a `yarn.lock` the same way when no `bun.lock` exists. Yarn v1 lockfiles and Yarn 2+ ("Berry") lockfiles, the YAML format with a `__metadata` header, are converted to `bun.lock` during `bun install` or `bun pm migrate`, and every locked version is kept. The original `yarn.lock` is left in place. A Yarn v1 lockfile that is older than `package.json` is still migrated: Bun resolves the dependencies it has no entry for and prints a warning that names them. A Yarn Berry lockfile is migrated only when Bun can keep everything it pins. If one package, patch, workspace or dependency cannot …

title: bun patch › A missing patch file
text: `bun install` and `bun patch <pkg>` fail when a file in `"patchedDependencies"` does not exist, and leave `node_modules` alone. While the patched package is still in `node_modules`, `bun patch --commit <pkg>` writes the file again. To start over, delete the entry from `"patchedDependencies"` and run `bun install`.

title: bun patch › Removing a patch
text: Undo your changes and commit again: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun patch react # restore the files you changed in node_modules/react bun patch --commit react When the package has no changes left, Bun removes it from `"patchedDependencies"` in `package.json` and the lockfile, deletes its patch file unless another entry uses it, and reinstalls the original package. You can also delete the entry from `"patchedDependencies"` and the patch file yourself, then run `bun install`.

title: bun patch › Step 1. Prepare the package for patching
text: Use `bun patch <pkg>` to prepare the package for patching: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # you can supply the package name bun patch react # ...and a precise version in case multiple versions are installed bun patch react@17.0.2 # or the path to the package bun patch node_modules/react Always run `bun patch <pkg>` first. It ensures the package folder in `node_modules/` contains a fresh copy of the package with no symlinks or hardlinks to Bun's cache. If you skip it, you might end up editing the package globally in the cache.

title: bun patch › Step 2. Test your changes locally
text: `bun patch <pkg>` makes it safe to edit `<pkg>` in `node_modules/` directly, while preserving the integrity of Bun's [Global Cache](/pm/global-cache). It works by re-creating an unlinked clone of the package in `node_modules/`. `bun patch --commit <pkg>` then diffs that clone against the original package in the Global Cache.

title: bun patch › Step 3. Commit your changes
text: Once you're happy with your changes, run `bun patch --commit <path or pkg>`. Bun generates a patch file in `patches/`, updates your `package.json` and lockfile, and starts using the patched package: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # you can supply the path to the patched package bun patch --commit node_modules/react # ... or the package name and optionally the version bun patch --commit react@17.0.2 # choose the directory to store the patch files bun patch --commit react --patches-dir=mypatches # `patch-commit` is available for compatibility with pnpm bun patch-commit react If `bun install` …

title: bun prune › `--filter`
text: Prune only the selected workspaces' `node_modules` folders (same patterns as [`bun install --filter`](/pm/filter)). Bun also cleans shared locations: the root `node_modules`, or `node_modules/.bun` with the isolated linker. title: bun prune › `--production`
text: Also remove everything `bun install --production` would not install (i.e. `devDependencies`). This lets you build with dev dependencies and ship without them: ```dockerfile COPY package.json bun.lock ./ RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile COPY . . RUN bun run build RUN bun prune --production `--omit=dev`, `--omit=optional`, and `--omit=peer` work the same way they do for `bun install`.

title: bun prune › Notes
text: - Always runs from the workspace root and covers every workspace's `node_modules`, even when invoked inside a workspace package. - Requires `bun.lock` to match `package.json`. If you edited dependencies since the last install, run `bun install` first. - Detects whether `node_modules` was laid out by the hoisted or the isolated linker and prunes it as it is. If the folders hold both layouts (for example a tree left by a switch of linkers under Bun 1.4 or older), Bun uses the linker `bun install` would use. Pass `--linker` to choose. - Matches packages by name. If a package is at the wrong …

title: bun publish › `--access`
text: `--access` sets the access level of the package being published, either `public` or `restricted`. title: bun --filter › Dependency Order
text: Bun respects package dependency order when running scripts. Say you have a package `foo` that depends on another package `bar` in your workspace, and both have a `build` script. When you run `bun --filter '*' build`, `foo` only starts once `bar` is done.

title: bun --filter › Directory `--filter '{<dir>}'`
text: A directory in braces selects every workspace in that directory or anywhere below it, resolved from the current directory. `--filter '{packages}'` selects everything under `packages/`; `--filter '{.}'` selects the current directory's workspace and everything below it.

title: bun --filter › Package Name `--filter <pattern>`
text: Name patterns select packages by the `name` field in `package.json`. For example, if you have packages `pkg-a`, `pkg-b` and `other`, you can match all of them with `*`, only `pkg-a` and `pkg-b` with `pkg*`, and a specific package with its full name.

title: bun --filter › Package Path `--filter ./<glob>`
text: Path patterns start with `./` and select all packages in directories matching the pattern. For example, to match all packages in subdirectories of `packages`, use `--filter './packages/**'`. To match the package in `packages/foo`, use `--filter ./packages/foo`. Name patterns match the full package name (`core` does not match `@acme/core`; use `@acme/*`), and `*` does not cross `/`. Path patterns must match the workspace directory itself: `./packages` selects nothing, `./packages/*` selects every workspace directly inside it.

title: Global cache › Fast copying
text: Once a package is downloaded into the cache, Bun still needs to copy those files into `node_modules`. It uses the fastest syscalls available for this: hardlinks on Linux and Windows, `clonefile` on macOS.

title: Global cache › Minimizing re-downloads
text: When installing a package, if the cache already contains a version in the range specified by `package.json`, Bun uses the cached copy instead of downloading it again. If the semver version has a pre-release suffix (`1.0.0-beta.0`) or a build suffix (`1.0.0+20220101`), Bun replaces the suffix with a hash of that value instead, to reduce the chance of errors from long file paths. When the `node_modules` folder exists, before installing, Bun checks that `node_modules` contains all expected packages with appropriate versions. If so, `bun install` completes. The hoisted linker reads `"name"` and …

title: Global cache › Saving disk space
text: On Linux and Windows, Bun uses hardlinks to "copy" a module into a project's `node_modules` directory, so the contents of the package only exist in a single location on disk. This greatly reduces the disk space used by `node_modules`. The same applies on macOS, with a caveat. There Bun uses `clonefile`, which is copy-on-write: the clone occupies no extra disk space, but it counts towards the drive's limit. Because the copy only happens on write, patching `node_modules/*` in one project can't affect other installations. Configure this with the `--backend` flag, which all of Bun's package …

title: Global virtual store › Concurrency
text: Multiple `bun install` processes (parallel CI jobs, concurrent workspace builds) may race to populate the same global entry. Each process builds the entire entry (package files, dependency symlinks, bin links) under a private `<entry>.tmp-<random>/` staging directory. As the final step, it renames that directory into place. The loser of the rename sees `EEXIST` and discards its identical staging tree. A writer that crashes mid-build leaves only an unreferenced staging directory that the next install ignores. A published entry is therefore always complete; there is no separate completeness …

title: Global virtual store › Disk usage
text: Each unique `(package, version, resolved-dependency-set)` triple gets one directory in `<cache>/links/`. Across many projects that's a large net win: one copy on disk instead of one per checkout. But the store does grow over time as new versions and new peer-dependency combinations land. Run `bun pm cache rm` to clear the cache including the global store; the next install repopulates only what that project needs. [`bun pm cache prune`](/pm/cli/pm#cache) removes old downloaded packages but leaves the global store alone. `bun pm cache rm` deletes `<cache>/links/`. Every project that uses the …

title: Global virtual store › Enabling
text: The global virtual store is **off by default**. It only applies to the [isolated linker](/pm/isolated-installs); the hoisted linker does not use it. To enable it for a project: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] linker = "isolated" globalStore = true Or per invocation, through the environment: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_STORE=1 bun install --linker isolated To explicitly opt out (the default), set `globalStore = false` or `BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_STORE=0`.

title: Global virtual store › `node_modules` is mostly symlinks
text: Tools that scan `node_modules` without following symlinks, or that compare file paths by string equality, may behave differently. This is the same caveat as any pnpm-style layout.

title: Global virtual store › Peer dependencies
text: Bun folds resolved peer dependencies (required and optional) into each global entry as dep symlinks. These peer dependencies contribute to the entry's hash. Bun synthesizes an implicit `"*"` optional peer for packages that list a name only in `peerDependenciesMeta` without a matching `peerDependencies` entry (matching pnpm and yarn). As a result, a package like `webpack` that declares `webpack-cli` only in `peerDependenciesMeta` still gets a `webpack-cli` symlink in its global entry when one is installed in the project.

title: Global virtual store › Phantom-dependency fallback
text: When packages live under the project's `node_modules/.bun/`, Node's module resolution walks up through `node_modules/.bun/node_modules/` — the hidden hoisted layer — before reaching the project root. With the global store, packages realpath into `<cache>/links/`, so that layer is no longer on the resolution path from inside a package. In practice this only affects **true phantom dependencies**: a package doing `require(helper)` for something it never declared in `dependencies`, `peerDependencies`, or `peerDependenciesMeta`. If you hit this, add the helper to the consuming package's …

title: Isolated installs › Backend strategies
