title: Binary Data › `File`
text: [`File`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/File) is a subclass of `Blob` that adds a `name` and `lastModified` property. It's commonly used in the browser to represent files uploaded with an `<input type="file">` element. Node.js and Bun implement `File`. ```ts // on browser! // <input type="file" id="file" /> const files = document.getElementById("file").files; // => File[] ```ts const file = new File(["<html>Hello</html>"], "index.html", { type: "text/html", }); See the [MDN documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Blob).

title: Binary Data › From `ArrayBuffer`
text: Since `ArrayBuffer` stores the data that underlies other binary structures like `TypedArray`, the following snippets are not _converting_ from `ArrayBuffer` to another format. Instead, they _create_ a new instance using the underlying data.

title: Binary Data › From `ReadableStream`
text: [`Response`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Response) is a common intermediate for converting a `ReadableStream` to other formats. ```ts stream; // ReadableStream const buffer = await new Response(stream).arrayBuffer(); But this approach is verbose and adds unnecessary overhead. Bun implements optimized convenience functions for converting a `ReadableStream` to various binary formats.

title: Binary Data › Streams
text: Streams let you work with binary data without loading it all into memory at once. They're commonly used for reading and writing files, sending and receiving network requests, and processing large amounts of data. Bun implements the Web APIs [`ReadableStream`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ReadableStream) and [`WritableStream`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WritableStream). Bun also implements the `node:stream` module, including [`Readable`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#stream_readable_streams), …

title: Binary Data › To `ArrayBuffer`
text: The `buffer` property is the underlying `ArrayBuffer`. A `TypedArray` can be a view of a _slice_ of that buffer, so the sizes may differ. ```ts arr.buffer;

title: Binary Data › To `Blob`
text: ```ts new Blob([buf], { type: "text/plain" });

title: Binary Data › To `Buffer`
text: ```ts // create Buffer over entire ArrayBuffer Buffer.from(buf); // create Buffer over a slice of the ArrayBuffer Buffer.from(buf, 0, 10);

title: Binary Data › To `DataView`
text: ```ts new DataView(buf);

title: Binary Data › To `number[]`
text: ```ts Array.from(new Uint8Array(buf));

title: Binary Data › To `ReadableStream`
text: The following snippet creates a `ReadableStream` and enqueues the entire `ArrayBuffer` as a single chunk. ```ts new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { controller.enqueue(buf); controller.close(); }, }); To stream the `ArrayBuffer` in chunks, use a `Uint8Array` view and enqueue each chunk. ```ts const view = new Uint8Array(buf); const chunkSize = 1024; new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { for (let i = 0; i < view.length; i += chunkSize) { controller.enqueue(view.slice(i, i + chunkSize)); } controller.close(); }, });

title: Binary Data › To `string`
text: As UTF-8: ```ts new TextDecoder().decode(buf);

title: Binary Data › To `TypedArray`
text: ```ts new Uint8Array(buf);

title: Binary Data › To `Uint8Array`
text: ```ts // with Response new Response(stream).bytes(); // with Bun function Bun.readableStreamToBytes(stream);

title: Binary Data › `TypedArray`
text: Typed arrays are a family of classes that provide an `Array`-like interface for interacting with data in an `ArrayBuffer`. Whereas a `DataView` lets you write numbers of varying size at a particular offset, a `TypedArray` interprets the underlying bytes as an array of numbers, each of a fixed size. It's common to refer to this family of classes collectively by their shared superclass `TypedArray`. This class is _internal_ to JavaScript; you can't directly create instances of it, and `TypedArray` is not defined in the global scope. Think of it as an `interface` or an abstract class. ```ts const …

title: Binary Data › `Uint8Array`
text: `Uint8Array` is the most common typed array in JavaScript. It represents a classic "byte array": a sequence of 8-bit unsigned integers between 0 and 255. In Bun, it has methods for converting between byte arrays and their base64 or hex string representations. ```ts new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).toBase64(); // "AQIDBAU=" Uint8Array.fromBase64("AQIDBAU="); // Uint8Array(5) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] new Uint8Array([255, 254, 253, 252, 251]).toHex(); // "fffefdfcfb" Uint8Array.fromHex("fffefdfcfb"); // Uint8Array(5) [255, 254, 253, 252, 251] It is the return value of …

title: bunfig.toml › All keys
text: Every flag that makes sense as a default is also a key, in camelCase: `--max-warnings 0` is `maxWarnings = 0`, and `--no-inline-config` is `inlineConfig = false`. The command line wins over `bunfig.toml`. | Key | Value | Flag | | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | `rules` | table | `--rule` | | `plugins` | array | `--plugin` | | `categories` | table | `-A`, `-W`, `-D` | | `overrides` | array of tables | | | `globals` | table | `--global` | | `settings` | table | | | `ignorePatterns` | array | …

title: bunfig.toml › `bun run`
text: The `[run]` section configures the `bun run` command. These settings also apply to the `bun` command when running a file, script, or executable. For `bun run`, Bun only loads the local project's `bunfig.toml` automatically (it doesn't check for a global `.bunfig.toml`).

title: bunfig.toml › `console`
text: Configure console output behavior.

title: bunfig.toml › `console.depth`
text: Set the default depth for `console.log()` object inspection. Default `2`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [console] depth = 3 Higher values show more nested properties but may produce verbose output for complex objects. The `--console-depth` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `define`
text: The `define` field replaces global identifiers with constant expressions wherever they appear. The expression should be a JSON string. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [define] # Replace any usage of "process.env.bagel" with the string `lox`. # The values are parsed as JSON, except single-quoted strings are supported and `undefined` becomes `undefined` in JS. # This will probably change in a future release to be just regular TOML instead. It is a holdover from the CLI argument parsing. "process.env.bagel" = "lox"

title: bunfig.toml › `env`
text: Configure automatic `.env` file loading. Bun loads `.env` files by default. To disable this behavior: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" # Disable automatic .env file loading env = false You can also use object syntax with the `file` property: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [env] file = false Use this in production or CI/CD pipelines where you want to rely solely on system environment variables. Bun still loads files passed explicitly with `--env-file` even when default loading is disabled.

title: bunfig.toml › Every other flag
text: Any flag that makes sense as a default has a key: its name in camelCase. `bun fmt --help --all` lists the flags. The command line wins over `bunfig.toml`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] editorconfig = false # --no-editorconfig ignorePath = [".gitignore", ".formatignore"] # --ignore-path .gitignore --ignore-path .formatignore insertFinalNewline = false # --no-insert-final-newline logLevel = "warn" # --log-level warn threads = 4 # --threads 4 `[fmt]` also applies in a project with a `.prettierrc` or an `.oxfmtrc.json`, where a key overrides the config file as its flag does. …

title: bunfig.toml › `format.ignorePatterns`
text: Skip the files that match. `bun fmt` already skips `node_modules` and everything in `.gitignore`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] ignorePatterns = ["vendor/", "**/*.gen.ts"]

title: bunfig.toml › `format.jsdoc`
text: [Format JSDoc comments](/format#format-jsdoc-comments). Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] jsdoc = true | Key | Default | What it does | | ----------------------------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `capitalizeDescriptions` | `true` | Start descriptions with a capital letter | | `descriptionWithDot` | `false` | End descriptions with a period | | `descriptionTag` | `false` | Put `@description` before the description | | `addDefaultToDescription` | `true` | Add ``Default is `1` `` to the …

title: bunfig.toml › `format.overrides`
text: Different options for some files. Later entries win over earlier ones, and a flag wins over all of them. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt.overrides] files = ["*.test.ts", "scripts/**"] excludeFiles = ["scripts/vendor/**"] options = { printWidth = 120, sortImports = false } - `files` and `excludeFiles` take a glob or an array of globs, relative to `bunfig.toml`. They use the same syntax as [`Bun.Glob`](/runtime/glob). A glob without a slash matches the file name in any directory. - `options` takes the style options, `sortImports`, `sortTailwindcss`, `sortPackageJson`, `jsdoc`, …

title: bunfig.toml › `format.sortImports`
text: [Sort, group, and merge imports](/format#sort-imports). Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] sortImports = true To change the groups, use a table. These are the defaults: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt.sortImports] groups = ["builtin", "external", ["internal", "subpath"], ["parent", "sibling", "index"], "style", "unknown"] internalPattern = ["~/", "@/", "#"] newlinesBetween = true | Key | Default | What it does | | -------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `groups` | above | …

title: bunfig.toml › `format.sortPackageJson`
text: [Sort the keys of `package.json`](/format#sort-package-json). Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] sortPackageJson = true `sortPackageJson = { sortScripts = true }` sorts `scripts` by name too. If a `.prettierrc` lists `prettier-plugin-packagejson`, the keys are sorted in that plugin's order. Setting `sortPackageJson` overrides that: `true` sorts in Bun's order, and `false` doesn't sort.

title: bunfig.toml › `format.sortTailwindcss`
text: [Sort Tailwind CSS classes](/format#sort-tailwind-css-classes). Default `false`. Classes are sorted with your project's `tailwindcss`, version 3 or 4, and are left as they are if it isn't installed. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt.sortTailwindcss] stylesheet = "./src/app.css" functions = ["clsx", "tw"] | Key | What it does | | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `stylesheet` | Tailwind 4: the CSS file that imports Tailwind | | `config` | Tailwind 3: the path of `tailwind.config.js` | | `functions` | Sort the strings …

title: bunfig.toml › `format.svelte`
text: [Format Svelte components](/format#svelte). Default `true`. `svelte = false` leaves `.svelte` files alone, and the Svelte code blocks in Markdown. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt.svelte] sortOrder = "scripts-markup-styles-options" | Key | Default | What it does | | ---------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `sortOrder` | `"options-scripts-markup-styles"` | The order of `<svelte:options>`, the scripts, the markup, and the styles. `"none"` keeps it | | …

title: bunfig.toml › Formatter
text: The `[fmt]` section configures [`bun fmt`](/format). Run `bun fmt --init` to add it. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [fmt] printWidth = 100 semi = false sortImports = true ignorePatterns = ["vendor/", "**/*.gen.ts"] `bun fmt` uses the nearest `bunfig.toml` that has a `[fmt]` section, from the working directory up, so it prints the same from any directory of the project. Paths and patterns in the section are relative to the file. With `bun --config=<path> fmt` they are relative to the working directory. A typo doesn't go unnoticed. An unknown key or a bad value is an error, and `bun …

title: bunfig.toml › Global vs. local
text: Put `bunfig.toml` in your project root, alongside your `package.json`. To configure Bun's package manager globally, you can also create a `.bunfig.toml` file at one of the following paths: - `$HOME/.bunfig.toml` - `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/.bunfig.toml` When `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set to an absolute path, Bun reads the file there and not the one in `$HOME`. Only package manager commands (`bun install`, `bun add`, `bun remove`, `bun update`, `bun pm`, `bunx`, and so on) read the global file. If Bun finds both a global and a local `bunfig`, it loads both; keys set in the local file override the same keys …

title: bunfig.toml › `install.auto`
text: Configure Bun's [auto-install](/runtime/auto-install) behavior. Default `"auto"` — when no `node_modules` folder is found, Bun installs dependencies on the fly during execution. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] auto = "auto" Valid values are: | Value | Description | | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `"auto"` | Resolve modules from local `node_modules` if it exists. Otherwise, auto-install dependencies on the fly. | | `"force"` | Always auto-install …

title: bunfig.toml › `install.ca` and `install.cafile`
text: To configure a CA certificate, set `install.ca` to the certificate string or `install.cafile` to the path of a certificate file. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # The CA certificate as a string ca = "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n...\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----" # A path to a CA certificate file. The file can contain multiple certificates. cafile = "path/to/cafile" Set one of the two. If both are set, only `cafile` is used. `--ca` or `--cafile` on the command line replaces both.

title: bunfig.toml › `install.cache`
text: To configure the cache behavior: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install.cache] # the directory to use for the cache dir = "~/.bun/install/cache" # when true, don't use the global cache or cached registry metadata (same as `cache = false`). # Bun extracts packages to node_modules/.cache instead disable = false # when true, always resolve the latest versions from the registry disableManifest = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.concurrentScripts`
text: The maximum number of concurrent lifecycle scripts to run at once. Defaults to two times the number of CPU cores. Equivalent to the `--concurrent-scripts` flag. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] concurrentScripts = 5

title: bunfig.toml › `install.dev`
text: Whether to install development dependencies. Default `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] dev = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.dryRun`
text: Whether `bun install` resolves dependencies without installing them. Default `false`. When `true`, it's equivalent to passing `--dry-run` to every package manager command, including `bun publish`, `bun pm pack`, `bun prune`, `bun dedupe` and `bun audit fix`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] dryRun = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.exact`
text: Whether to set an exact version in `package.json`. Default `false`. By default Bun uses caret ranges. If the `latest` version of a package is `2.4.1`, Bun writes `^2.4.1` to your `package.json`. That range accepts any version from `2.4.1` up to (but not including) `3.0.0`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] exact = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.frozenLockfile`
text: When `true`, `bun install` does not update `bun.lock`. Default `false`. If `package.json` and the existing `bun.lock` disagree, the install errors. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] frozenLockfile = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.globalBinDir`
text: The directory where Bun links the binaries of globally installed packages. Like `globalDir`, Bun ignores it in a project's `bunfig.toml`. Environment variable: `BUN_INSTALL_BIN` ```toml title="~/.bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # where globally-installed package bins are linked globalBinDir = "~/.bun/bin"

title: bunfig.toml › `install.globalDir`
text: The directory where Bun puts globally installed packages. Set it in the global `.bunfig.toml` (see [Global vs. local](#global-vs-local)) or in a file passed with `--config`. Bun ignores it in a project's `bunfig.toml`. Environment variable: `BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_DIR` ```toml title="~/.bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # where `bun install --global` installs packages globalDir = "~/.bun/install/global"

title: bunfig.toml › `install.globalStore`
text: When using the `"isolated"` linker, share package installations across projects in a global virtual store at `<cache>/links/`. Bun links `node_modules/.bun/<pkg>@<ver>` into the store instead of materializing each package into the project. Makes warm installs after `rm -rf node_modules` an order of magnitude faster. Default `false`. You can also set it with the `BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_STORE` environment variable. See [Global virtual store](/pm/global-store). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] globalStore = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.hoist`
text: When using the `"isolated"` linker, Bun creates `node_modules/.bun/node_modules`. This fallback directory contains a symlink for every dependency name, or only for the names matching `install.hoistPattern` when one is set. The directory sits on the upward resolution path of every package in the store, so a package can still resolve dependencies it never declared ("phantom dependencies"). Set `hoist = false` to skip creating this directory entirely. An undeclared import from a store package then fails unless the imported package is linked at the project root `node_modules` (a direct dependency, …

title: bunfig.toml › `install.hoistPattern`
text: When using the `"isolated"` linker, Bun hoists packages matching these glob patterns to a fallback directory inside the virtual store (`node_modules/.bun/node_modules`) so other packages in the virtual store can resolve them. By default Bun hoists every package there, equivalent to `["*"]`. A pattern is matched against the dependency name, which for an `npm:` alias is the alias, and the link in the fallback directory has that name. Similar to pnpm's `hoist-pattern`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] hoistPattern = ["*"]

title: bunfig.toml › `install.ignoreScripts`
text: Whether to skip lifecycle scripts during install. Default `false`. Equivalent to the `--ignore-scripts` flag and to `NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=true` in the environment. When `true`, Bun does not run any `preinstall` / `install` / `postinstall` / `prepare` scripts, both for your project and for packages in `trustedDependencies`. See [Lifecycle scripts](/pm/lifecycle). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] ignoreScripts = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.linker`
text: Configure the linker strategy: how `bun install` lays out dependencies in `node_modules`. Defaults to `"isolated"` for new workspaces, `"hoisted"` for new single-package projects and existing projects (made pre-v1.3.2). See [Isolated installs](/pm/isolated-installs). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] linker = "hoisted" Valid values are: | Value | Description | | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `"hoisted"` | Link dependencies in a shared `node_modules` directory. | | `"isolated"` | Link dependencies inside each package installation. …

title: bunfig.toml › `install.linkWorkspacePackages`
text: Whether to link workspace packages from the monorepo root to their respective `node_modules` directories. Default `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] linkWorkspacePackages = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.lockfile`
text: Whether to generate a lockfile on `bun install`. Default `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install.lockfile] save = true Whether to generate a non-Bun lockfile alongside `bun.lock`. (Bun always creates a `bun.lock`.) `"yarn"` is the only supported value. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install.lockfile] print = "yarn"

title: bunfig.toml › `install.logLevel`
text: Set the log level for `bun install`. This can be one of `"debug"`, `"warn"`, or `"error"`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] logLevel = "warn"

title: bunfig.toml › `install.minimumReleaseAge`
text: Configure a minimum age (in seconds) for npm package versions. During installation, Bun filters out package versions published more recently than this threshold. Default `null` (disabled). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # Only install package versions published at least 3 days ago minimumReleaseAge = 259200 See [Minimum release age](/pm/cli/install#minimum-release-age).

title: bunfig.toml › `install.minimumReleaseAgeExcludes`
text: An array of packages that are exempt from the `minimumReleaseAge` check. A package name exempts every version of the package; `name@version` (or `name@1.0.0 || 1.0.1`) exempts only the listed exact versions. Default `[]`. The `--minimum-release-age-excludes` flag replaces this list. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] minimumReleaseAge = 259200 # Every version of @types/bun, and only typescript 5.4.5, bypass the 3-day minimum age requirement minimumReleaseAgeExcludes = ["@types/bun", "typescript@5.4.5"] See [Minimum release age](/pm/cli/install#minimum-release-age).

title: bunfig.toml › `install.offline`
text: When `true`, `bun install` never touches the network: package metadata and tarballs must already be in the cache, and anything missing is an error. Default `false`. Equivalent to `bun install --offline`. For the softer "use the cache when possible" behaviour see `install.prefer = "offline"` / `--prefer-offline`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] offline = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.optional`
text: Whether to install optional dependencies. Default `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] optional = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.peer`
text: Whether to install peer dependencies. Default `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] peer = true

title: bunfig.toml › `install.prefer`
text: Configure how Bun resolves package versions against the npm registry when running scripts. Default `"online"`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] prefer = "online" Valid values are: | Value | Description | | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `"online"` | Default. Check the registry for stale packages as needed. | | `"offline"` | Skip staleness checks and resolve packages from the local cache. Equivalent to `--prefer-offline` (also honoured by `bun install`). | …

title: bunfig.toml › `install.production`
text: Whether `bun install` runs in "production mode". Default `false`. In production mode, Bun does not install `"devDependencies"` and freezes the lockfile (same as [`install.frozenLockfile`](#install-frozenlockfile)). Use the `--production` CLI flag to enable it for a single install. Since production mode freezes the lockfile, `bun add`, `bun remove`, and `bun update` fail while it is set. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] production = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.publicHoistPattern`
text: When using the `"isolated"` linker, Bun hoists packages matching these glob patterns to the root `node_modules` directory so any package in the project can resolve them. Default `[]`. Similar to pnpm's `public-hoist-pattern`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] publicHoistPattern = ["*eslint*", "*prettier*"]

title: bunfig.toml › `install.registry`
text: The default registry is `https://registry.npmjs.org/`. To change it: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # set default registry as a string registry = "https://registry.npmjs.org" # set a token registry = { url = "https://registry.npmjs.org", token = "123456" } # set a username/password registry = "https://username:password@registry.npmjs.org"

title: bunfig.toml › `install.saveTextLockfile`
text: If `false`, `bun install` generates a binary `bun.lockb` instead of a text-based `bun.lock` file when no lockfile is present. Default `true` (since Bun v1.2). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] saveTextLockfile = false

title: bunfig.toml › `install.scopes`
text: To configure a registry for a particular scope (for example, `@myorg/<package>`), use `install.scopes`. You can reference environment variables with `$variable` notation. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install.scopes] # registry as string myorg = "https://username:password@registry.myorg.com/" # registry with username/password # you can reference environment variables myorg = { username = "myusername", password = "$npm_password", url = "https://registry.myorg.com/" } # registry with token myorg = { token = "$npm_token", url = "https://registry.myorg.com/" }

title: bunfig.toml › `install.security.scanner`
text: Configure a security scanner to scan packages for vulnerabilities before installation. First, install a security scanner from npm: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add -d @oven/bun-security-scanner `@oven/bun-security-scanner` is an example package name, not a real package. Replace it with the scanner you want to use, and consult that scanner's documentation for the exact package name and installation instructions. Most scanners are installed with `bun add`. Then configure it in your `bunfig.toml`: ```toml bunfig.toml icon="settings" [install.security] scanner = …

title: bunfig.toml › `jsx`
text: Configure how Bun handles JSX. You can also set these fields in the `compilerOptions` of your `tsconfig.json`, but `bunfig.toml` supports them for non-TypeScript projects. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" jsx = "react" jsxFactory = "h" jsxFragment = "Fragment" jsxImportSource = "react" Refer to the tsconfig docs for more information on these fields. - [`jsx`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#jsx) - [`jsxFactory`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#jsxFactory) - [`jsxFragment`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#jsxFragment) - …

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.categories`
text: Set a whole category of rules at once. `[lint.rules]` wins over a category. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.categories] suspicious = "warn" perf = "warn" | Category | What its rules report | | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | | `correctness` | Code that is wrong or useless | | `suspicious` | Code that is probably wrong or useless | | `pedantic` | Strict checks, with some false positives | | `perf` | Code that could run faster | | `style` | Code that could be more idiomatic | | `restriction` | Language features and patterns you want to ban | | …

title: bunfig.toml › Linter
text: The `[lint]` section configures [`bun lint`](/lint). Run `bun lint --init` to add it. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] typeAware = true ignorePatterns = ["vendor/", "**/*.gen.ts"] [lint.rules] "no-console" = "warn" eqeqeq = ["error", "smart"] [lint.overrides] files = ["scripts/**"] rules = { "no-console" = "off" } `bun lint` uses the nearest `bunfig.toml` that has a `[lint]` section, from the working directory up, so it finds the same problems from any directory of the project. Next to an ESLint or oxlint config, what those tools read from the working directory is still read …

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.globals`
text: Declare global variables, so that `no-undef` accepts them. A global is `"readonly"`, `"writable"`, or `"off"`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.globals] MY_GLOBAL = "readonly"

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.ignorePatterns`
text: Skip the files that match. `bun lint` already skips `node_modules` and everything in `.gitignore`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] ignorePatterns = ["vendor/", "**/*.gen.ts"] Each pattern is a line of a `.gitignore` next to `bunfig.toml`, like [`format.ignorePatterns`](#format-ignorepatterns): `vendor/` skips every directory with that name, `/vendor/` only the one next to `bunfig.toml`, and `!` keeps what an earlier pattern skips. The exception is a project with an `eslint.config.*` file, where they're added to its …

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.maxWarnings`
text: Exit with code `1` if there are more warnings than this. By default, warnings never fail a run. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] maxWarnings = 0

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.overrides`
text: Use different rules for some files. `files` is required. `excludeFiles`, `rules`, `globals`, and `settings` are optional. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.overrides] files = ["*.test.ts", "scripts/**"] excludeFiles = ["scripts/vendor/**"] rules = { "no-console" = "off" } Patterns use the same syntax as [`Bun.Glob`](/runtime/glob) and are relative to `bunfig.toml`. A pattern without a slash matches the file name in any directory. Later overrides win over earlier ones, and all of them win over `[lint.rules]`.

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.plugins`
text: Load [ESLint plugins](/lint/plugins): paths, relative to `bunfig.toml`, or package names. Their rules are added to the built-in ones. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] plugins = ["./lint/plugin.js", "eslint-plugin-perfectionist"] [lint.rules] "local/no-todo" = "warn" "perfectionist/sort-imports" = "error"

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.rules`
text: Set a rule to `"off"`, `"warn"`, or `"error"`. To pass options, use an array. Every rule in `bun lint --rules` works, with nothing to install. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.rules] "no-console" = "warn" "@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any" = "off" "unicorn/prefer-node-protocol" = "error" "no-restricted-imports" = ["error", { paths = ["lodash"] }] Use `*` as the rule name to turn off every rule of a plugin. In the same table, a setting for a single rule overrides the wildcard, in either order. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.rules] "jsx-a11y/*" = "off" …

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.settings`
text: Settings that rules share, such as the React version. The same as `settings` in an ESLint or oxlint config. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint.settings.react] version = "18.2" [lint.settings."jsx-a11y".components] Picture = "img"

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.typeAware`
text: Turn on typescript-eslint's recommended [type-aware rules](/lint#type-aware-rules), such as `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises`. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] typeAware = true tsconfig = "./tsconfig.lint.json" # default: the nearest tsconfig.json You don't need it for a single rule. A type-aware rule runs as soon as you turn it on in `[lint.rules]`. `typeAware = false` skips every type-aware rule.

title: bunfig.toml › `lint.typeCheck`
text: Also report type errors, like [`bun check`](/runtime/check). It turns on no rules. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [lint] typeCheck = true

title: bunfig.toml › `loader`
text: Configure how Bun maps file extensions to [loaders](/bundler/loaders). Use this to load file types Bun doesn't support natively. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [loader] # when a .bagel file is imported, treat it like a tsx file ".bagel" = "tsx" Bun supports the following loaders: - `jsx` - `js` - `ts` - `tsx` - `css` - `file` - `json` - `toml` - `wasm` - `napi` - `base64` - `dataurl` - `text`

title: bunfig.toml › `logLevel`
text: Set the log level: `"debug"`, `"warn"`, or `"error"`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" logLevel = "debug" # "debug" | "warn" | "error"

title: bunfig.toml › Package manager
text: The `[install]` section configures the behavior of `bun install`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # configuration here A relative path in `cafile`, `cache`, `globalDir` or `globalBinDir` is relative to the file it is written in. A relative path in a flag (`--config`, `--cafile`, `--cache-dir`) is relative to the directory you run `bun` in. A relative `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR` is relative to the project's root. In all of these, a leading `~/` is your home directory.

title: bunfig.toml › `preload`
text: An array of scripts/plugins to execute before running a file or script. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" # scripts to run before `bun run`-ing a file or script # register plugins by adding them to this list preload = ["./preload.ts"]

title: bunfig.toml › `run.bun` - auto alias `node` to `bun`
text: When `true`, Bun prepends `$PATH` with a `node` symlink that points to the `bun` binary for all scripts or executables invoked by `bun run` or `bun`. A script that runs `node` runs `bun` instead, with no changes to the script. This works recursively, so a script that runs another script that runs `node` also runs `bun`. The alias also applies to shebangs that point to `node`. By default, this is enabled if `node` is not already in your `$PATH`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [run] # equivalent to `bun --bun` for all `bun run` commands bun = true You can test this by running: ```sh …

title: bunfig.toml › `run.elide-lines` - truncate filtered output
text: Truncate each script's output to its last N lines when using `--filter` in a terminal. Default `0` (show all lines). Equivalent to the `--elide-lines` flag. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [run] elide-lines = 10

title: bunfig.toml › `run.noOrphans` - don't leave orphan processes behind
text: When `true`, Bun watches the process that spawned it and exits as soon as that parent goes away, even if the parent was force-killed and never got a chance to forward a signal. On its own exit, Bun also terminates every descendant process so nothing it spawned outlives it. Useful when Bun is launched by a supervisor (Electron, a CI runner, a thin shim) that may be force-killed. On Linux, Bun uses `prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG)` and a `/proc` descendant walk. On macOS, it uses `EVFILT_PROC`/`NOTE_EXIT` on the event loop's kqueue and a libproc descendant walk. On Windows, it uses a thread-pool wait on …

title: bunfig.toml › `run.shell` - use the system shell or Bun's shell
text: The shell used to run `package.json` scripts with `bun run` or `bun`. Defaults to `"bun"` on Windows and `"system"` on other platforms. To always use the system shell instead of Bun's shell (the default everywhere except Windows): ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [run] # default outside of Windows shell = "system" To always use Bun's shell instead of the system shell: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [run] # default on Windows shell = "bun"

title: bunfig.toml › `run.silent` - suppress reporting the command being run
text: When `true`, `bun run` and `bun` don't print the command being run. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [run] silent = true Without this option, Bun prints the command being run to the console: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun run dev echo "Running \"dev\"..." ```txt Running "dev"... With this option, Bun does not print the command being run: ```sh bun run dev ```txt Running "dev"... This is equivalent to passing `--silent` to all `bun run` commands: ```sh bun --silent run dev bun --silent dev bun run --silent dev

title: bunfig.toml › Runtime
text: Top-level fields in `bunfig.toml` configure Bun's runtime behavior.

title: bunfig.toml › Serve
text: The `[serve]` section configures `Bun.serve` and `bun run` when serving HTTP.

title: bunfig.toml › `serve.port`
text: The default port for `Bun.serve` to listen on. Default `3000`. You can also set it with the `BUN_PORT` or `PORT` environment variables, or the `--port` flag. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [serve] port = 3000

title: bunfig.toml › `smol`
text: Enable `smol` mode. This reduces memory usage at the cost of performance. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" # Reduce memory usage at the cost of performance smol = true

title: bunfig.toml › Style options
text: Same names, defaults, and meaning as [Prettier's options](https://prettier.io/docs/options). Each one is also a flag, like `--print-width 100` or `--no-semi`, and the flag wins. | Key | Default | What it does | | ------------------------------ | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `printWidth` | `80` | Wrap lines at this column | | `tabWidth` | `2` | Spaces per indentation level | | `useTabs` | `false` | Indent with tabs | | `semi` | `true` | Print semicolons | | `singleQuote` | `false` | Use single quotes | | `jsxSingleQuote` | `false` | …

title: bunfig.toml › `telemetry`
text: The `telemetry` field enables or disables analytics. By default, telemetry is enabled. This setting is equivalent to the `DO_NOT_TRACK` environment variable. We do not currently collect telemetry; this setting only controls anonymous crash reports. We plan to collect information like which Bun APIs are used most or how long `bun build` takes. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" telemetry = false

title: bunfig.toml › Test runner
text: The `[test]` section of `bunfig.toml` configures the test runner. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # configuration goes here

title: bunfig.toml › `test.clearMocks`
text: Clear every mock function's calls and results before each test. Default `false`, or `true` for tests that use `test` from `"vitest"`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] clearMocks = true `mockReset`, `restoreMocks`, `unstubEnvs` and `unstubGlobals` work the same way. They call `vi.resetAllMocks()`, `vi.restoreAllMocks()`, `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` and `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` before each test. Default `false`.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.concurrentTestGlob`
text: Test files matching this glob pattern run all of their tests concurrently, as if you passed the `--concurrent` flag. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] concurrentTestGlob = "**/concurrent-*.test.ts" Use this to migrate a test suite to concurrent execution gradually, or to run integration tests concurrently while keeping unit tests sequential. The `--concurrent` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverage`
text: Enables coverage reporting. Default `false`. Use `--coverage` to override. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverage = false

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverageDir`
text: Set the path where coverage reports are saved. This only applies to persistent reporters like `lcov`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageDir = "path/to/somewhere" # default "coverage"

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverageIgnoreSourcemaps`
text: Whether to report coverage against transpiled output instead of remapping line numbers through sourcemaps back to the original source. Default `false`. Primarily useful for debugging. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageIgnoreSourcemaps = false

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coveragePathIgnorePatterns`
text: Exclude files from coverage reports using glob patterns. Accepts a single pattern or an array of patterns. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Single pattern coveragePathIgnorePatterns = "**/*.spec.ts" # Multiple patterns coveragePathIgnorePatterns = [ "**/*.spec.ts", "**/*.test.ts", "src/utils/**", "*.config.js" ]

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverageReporter`
text: By default, the test runner prints coverage reports to the console. For persistent reports that CI and other tools can read, use `lcov`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageReporter = ["text", "lcov"] # default ["text"]

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverageSkipTestFiles`
text: Whether to skip test files when computing coverage statistics. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageSkipTestFiles = false

title: bunfig.toml › `test.coverageThreshold`
text: The coverage threshold. By default, no threshold is set. If your test suite does not meet it, `bun test` exits with a non-zero exit code. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # to require 90% line-level and function-level coverage coverageThreshold = 0.9 You can set separate thresholds for line and function coverage. Bun accepts a `statements` key but does not currently enforce it. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageThreshold = { lines = 0.7, functions = 0.8 }

title: bunfig.toml › `test.environment`
text: The DOM that test files run with. One of `"happy-dom"`, `"jsdom"`, or `"node"` for no DOM. Default `"node"`. A `// @vitest-environment <name>` comment in a test file overrides it. See [DOM testing](/test/dom#test-environments). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] environment = "happy-dom" Equivalent CLI flag: `--environment`. It overrides the `bunfig.toml` value.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.globals`
text: Which module `test`, `expect` and the other globals come from. Default `"bun"`. - `"bun"`: a file that imports anything from `"vitest"` gets them from `"vitest"`. Any other file gets them from `"bun:test"`. - `"vitest"`: every file gets them from `"vitest"`, like `globals: true` in a Vitest project. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] globals = "vitest" Equivalent CLI flag: `--globals`. It overrides the `bunfig.toml` value.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.onlyFailures`
text: When enabled, the output shows only failed tests, which reduces noise in large test suites. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] onlyFailures = true Equivalent to the `--only-failures` flag.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.pathIgnorePatterns`
text: Exclude files and directories from test discovery using glob patterns. The test runner prunes matched directories during scanning, so it never traverses their contents. Use this when your project contains submodules or vendored code with `*.test.ts` files that you don't want `bun test` to pick up. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] pathIgnorePatterns = ["vendor/**", "submodules/**", "fixtures/**"] Equivalent CLI flag: `--path-ignore-patterns`. CLI flags override the `bunfig.toml` value entirely.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.preload`
text: Same as the top-level `preload` field, but only applies to `bun test`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] preload = ["./setup.ts"]

title: bunfig.toml › `test.randomize`
text: Run tests in random order. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] randomize = true Running tests in a different order each time helps catch bugs related to test interdependencies. When combined with `seed`, the random order becomes reproducible. The `--randomize` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.reactCompiler`
text: Compile components and hooks with Bun's built-in React Compiler. Default `false`. Experimental. - `true`: every JavaScript and TypeScript file, except test files, preload scripts and `node_modules`. - An array of folders or glob patterns: only the files in them. - A table with `include` and `exclude`: the files that `include` matches and `exclude` doesn't. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reactCompiler] include = ["src", "packages/ui"] exclude = ["**/*.stories.*"] Equivalent CLI flag: `--react-compiler`. See [React Compiler](/test/configuration#react-compiler).

title: bunfig.toml › `test.reporter`
text: Configure the test reporter settings.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.reporter.dots`
text: Enable the dots reporter, which prints one dot per test. Default `false`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reporter] dots = true

title: bunfig.toml › `test.reporter.junit`
text: Enable JUnit XML reporting and specify the output file path. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reporter] junit = "test-results.xml" CI systems and other tools can consume the report.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.reporter.junitSuites`
text: How the JUnit report represents `describe` blocks. Default `"nested"`. - `"nested"`: each block gets its own `<testsuite>` inside its file's `<testsuite>`. - `"flat"`: each file gets one `<testsuite>`, and each test's name is prefixed with the names of its blocks. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reporter] junit = "test-results.xml" junitSuites = "flat" Equivalent to the `--reporter-junit-suites` flag.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.rerunEach`
text: Re-run each test file a specified number of times. Default `0` (run once). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] rerunEach = 3 Use this to catch flaky tests or non-deterministic behavior. The `--rerun-each` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.retry`
text: Default retry count for all tests. The test runner retries failed tests up to this many times. Per-test `{ retry: N }` overrides this value. Default `0` (no retries). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] retry = 3 The `--retry` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.root`
text: The root directory to run tests from. Default `.`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] root = "./__tests__"

title: bunfig.toml › `test.seed`
text: Set the random seed for test randomization. This option requires `randomize` to be `true`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] randomize = true seed = 2444615283 A seed makes the randomized test order reproducible across runs, which helps when debugging flaky tests. The `--seed` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: bunfig.toml › `test.smol`
text: Same as the top-level `smol` field, but only applies to `bun test`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] smol = true

title: C Compiler › `define: Record<string, string>`
text: `define` is an optional object of preprocessor definitions passed to the TinyCC compiler. ```ts type Defines = Record<string, string>; cc({ source: "hello.c", define: { NDEBUG: "1", }, });

title: C Compiler › Disabling `cc`
text: Pass `--no-ffi-cc` to disable the C compiler for a process. Any call to `cc()` then throws an error with the code `ERR_FFI_CC_DISABLED`. The `--no-addons` flag also disables `cc()`, in addition to `process.dlopen`. ```sh bun --no-ffi-cc ./app.ts Workers inherit the setting from their parent. A Worker can also set it for itself with `execArgv: ["--no-ffi-cc"]`. Standalone executables can bake it in with `bun build --compile --compile-exec-argv="--no-ffi-cc"`.

title: C Compiler › `flags: string | string[]`
text: `flags` is an optional string or array of strings passed to the TinyCC compiler. ```ts type Flags = string | string[]; These are flags like `-I` for include directories and `-D` for preprocessor definitions.

title: C Compiler › `library: string | string[]`
text: Use `library` to specify the libraries to link with the C code. ```ts type Library = string | string[]; cc({ source: "hello.c", library: ["sqlite3"], });

title: C Compiler › Primitive types
text: `cc` supports the same `FFIType` values as [`dlopen`](/runtime/ffi), except `buffer_length`. Only `cc` supports `napi_env` and `napi_value`. | `FFIType` | C Type | Aliases | | ---------- | -------------- | --------------------------- | | buffer | `char*` | | | cstring | `char*` | | | function | `(void*)(*)()` | `fn`, `callback` | | ptr | `void*` | `pointer`, `void*`, `char*` | | i8 | `int8_t` | `int8_t` | | i16 | `int16_t` | `int16_t` | | i32 | `int32_t` | `int32_t`, `int` | | i64 | `int64_t` | `int64_t`, `isize` | | i64_fast | `int64_t` | | | u8 | `uint8_t` | `uint8_t` | | u16 | `uint16_t` | …

title: C Compiler › Returning a C string to JavaScript
text: For example, to return a string from C to JavaScript: ```ts hello.ts const { symbols: { hello }, } = cc({ source, symbols: { hello: { args: ["napi_env"], returns: "napi_value", }, }, }); const result = hello(); And in C: ```c hello.c #include <node/node_api.h> napi_value hello(napi_env env) { napi_value result; napi_create_string_utf8(env, "Hello, Napi!", NAPI_AUTO_LENGTH, &result); return result; } The same approach returns other types like objects and arrays: ```c hello.c #include <node/node_api.h> napi_value hello(napi_env env) { napi_value result; napi_create_object(env, &result); return …

title: C Compiler › `source`
text: `source` is the path to the C code to compile and link with the JavaScript runtime. ```ts type Source = string | URL | BunFile; cc({ source: "hello.c", symbols: { hello: { args: [], returns: "int", }, }, });

title: C Compiler › Strings, objects, and non-primitive types
text: For strings, objects, and other non-primitive types that don't map 1:1 to C types, `cc` supports N-API. Use `napi_value` to pass or receive JavaScript values from a C function without any type conversions. You can also pass a `napi_env` to receive the N-API environment used to call the JavaScript function.

title: C Compiler › `symbols`
text: Use the `symbols` object to specify the functions and variables to expose to JavaScript. ```ts type Symbols = { [key: string]: { args: FFIType[]; returns: FFIType; }; };

title: C Compiler › Usage (cc in `bun:ffi`)
text: See the [introduction blog post](https://bun.com/blog/compile-and-run-c-in-js) for background. JavaScript: ```ts hello.ts icon="file-code" const { symbols: { hello }, } = cc({ source, symbols: { hello: { args: [], returns: "int", }, }, }); console.log("What is the answer to the universe?", hello()); C source: ```c hello.c int hello() { return 42; } Running `hello.ts` prints: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun hello.ts What is the answer to the universe? 42 `cc` uses [TinyCC](https://bellard.org/tcc/) to compile the C code, then links it with the JavaScript runtime, converting types in-place.

title: Type checking › A `tsconfig.json` with nothing but `references`
text: The `tsconfig.json` from `create vite` has `"files": []` and `references`. `tsc` without `-b` checks nothing there and succeeds. `bun check` follows the references, and says so: ```txt note: tsconfig.json has no files of its own. Checked the projects it references, like tsc -b.

title: Type checking › AI agents
text: When `AGENT=1`, `CLAUDECODE=1`, or `REPL_ID=1` is set, `bun check` prints each error as a tagged block with the source lines and no colors. ```txt <error file="src/index.ts" line="3" column="25" code="TS2322"> Type string is not assignable to type number. <source> 1 | import { greet } from "./user"; 2 | 3 | const message = greet({ id: "1", name: "Ada" }); ^^ 4 | export default message; </source> <related file="src/user.ts" line="2" column="3">The expected type comes from property id which is declared here on type 'User'</related> </error>

title: Type checking › Another project
text: Use `-p` with a `tsconfig.json` or the directory that contains one. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun check -p packages/server bun check -p tsconfig.test.json

title: Type checking › `bun build`
text: `bun build --check` runs the check after the bundler has read every file and before it writes any output. The type checker gets the files from the bundler, so Bun reads each file from disk once. Bun prints a type error like any other build error: ```txt 3 | console.log(greet({ age: "36" })); ^ error: TS2322: Type string is not assignable to type number. at /app/src/index.ts:3:21 1 | export function greet(user: { name?: string; age: number }) { ^ note: TS6500: The expected type comes from property age which is declared here on type '{ name?: string | undefined; age: number; }' at …

title: Type checking › `bun check` and my editor disagree
text: Your editor runs its own copy of TypeScript: the `typescript` package in your project, or a version that ships with the editor. `bun check` matches one exact version of TypeScript and uses that version's `lib.*.d.ts` files, whichever version you have installed. `process.versions.typescript` is that version. Install the same version so that both follow the same rules: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add -d typescript@$(bun -p process.versions.typescript) Then tell your editor to use the version in your project. In VS Code, run **TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version** from the Command …

title: Type checking › `bun check` runs a script instead of the type checker
text: Your `package.json` has a `check` script. Use `bun check --no-script`. See [If `package.json` has a `check` script](#if-packagejson-has-a-check-script).

title: Type checking › `bun compile`
text: [`bun compile`](/compiler/aot) always type checks, because it uses your types to generate machine code. `bun check --aot ./server.ts` reports every error that the build would report, and builds nothing. Like the build, it takes entry points. It also reports the type errors in code that the executable leaves out, such as a function that nothing calls. `bun compile --check` stops at those too. The build doesn't stop for a type error in a package. If the TypeScript of a package that gets compiled has type errors, `bun check --aot` prints one warning that names the package, and still exits with 0. …

title: Type checking › `Bun.build`
text: Pass `check: true` to [`Bun.build`](/bundler). A type error fails the build like any other build error. Each one is a `BuildMessage` whose message starts with the TypeScript error code. title: Type checking › Cannot find module './logo.svg' or './index.css'
text: Bun can import these files, but TypeScript needs a declaration for each file type. Add a `.d.ts` file to your project. The React templates of `bun init` include this one: ```ts bun-env.d.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" declare module "*.svg" { const path: `${string}.svg`; } declare module "*.css" {} declare module "*.module.css" { const classes: { readonly [key: string]: string }; } `@types/bun` already declares `.txt`, `.toml`, and `.html` imports.

text: Every compiler option works as a flag, as it does for `tsc`. A flag overrides `tsconfig.json`. title: Type checking › Monorepos
text: `bun check` checks the project that `tsc` checks in the same directory: the one with the nearest `tsconfig.json`.

title: Type checking › Watch mode
text: With [`--watch`](/runtime/watch-mode), Bun checks again before every restart. After a type error, Bun waits for the next change to any file in the program, including files that contain only types. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun --watch --check src/index.ts bun test --watch --check `--hot --check` restarts the process like `--watch`, so that Bun checks the code again before it runs. If you save a file while a check is running, Bun stops that check and starts again with the new contents.

title: Spawn › Blocking API (`Bun.spawnSync()`)
text: `Bun.spawnSync` is the blocking equivalent of `Bun.spawn`. It supports the same inputs and parameters and returns a `SyncSubprocess` object, which differs from `Subprocess` in a few ways. 1. The returned object contains a `success` property that indicates whether the process exited with a zero exit code. 2. The `stdout` and `stderr` properties are instances of `Buffer` instead of `ReadableStream`. 3. There is no `stdin` property. Use `Bun.spawn` to incrementally write to the subprocess's input stream. ```ts const proc = Bun.spawnSync(["echo", "hello"]); console.log(proc.stdout.toString()); // …

title: Spawn › Platform differences
text: `Bun.Terminal` uses `openpty()` on Linux and macOS, and ConPTY (`CreatePseudoConsole`) on Windows. The core behavior is the same on every platform: the child sees a TTY, `write()` reaches the child's stdin, child output reaches the `data` callback, and `resize()` updates the child's view. A few details differ: - **No termios on Windows.** `inputFlags`, `outputFlags`, `localFlags`, and `controlFlags` always read as `0` and setting them is a no-op. `setRawMode()` records the flag but has no effect on the child; the child controls its own console mode. - **No echo without a child process on …

title: Spawn › Resource limits with cgroups (Linux)
text: On Linux, pass `cgroup` to start the subprocess inside a [control group](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html). The child joins the cgroup before it begins executing, so limits configured on the cgroup (memory, pids, CPU) apply from the first instruction. They also apply to every process the child spawns in turn. When a memory limit is exceeded the kernel OOM-kills a process _inside_ the cgroup instead of reclaiming memory from the parent. A cgroup is a directory under `/sys/fs/cgroup`; create and configure it with ordinary file operations, then pass its path (or an open …

text: You can abort a subprocess using an `AbortSignal`: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const controller = new AbortController(); const { signal } = controller; const proc = Bun.spawn({ cmd: ["sleep", "100"], signal, }); // Later, to abort the process: controller.abort();

title: Spawn › Using maxBuffer
text: For `Bun.spawnSync`, `maxBuffer` limits how many bytes of output the process can emit before Bun kills it: ```ts index.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Kill yes after it emits over 100 bytes of output const result = Bun.spawnSync({ cmd: ["yes"], // or ["bun", "exec", "yes"] on Windows maxBuffer: 100, }); // process exits Bun stops reading as soon as the limit is passed. The returned output can therefore exceed `maxBuffer` only by the single read that passed it, never by whatever the process manages to write before the kill lands. This matches Node.js.
