text: To check if a file exists in S3, call `exists` on the `S3Client` instance. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={7} const client = new Bun.S3Client({ accessKeyId: "your-access-key", secretAccessKey: "your-secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", }); const exists = await client.exists("my-file.txt"); // equivalent to // const exists = await client.file("my-file.txt").exists();

title: S3 › `S3File`
text: Calling `file()` on an `S3Client` instance, or `s3.file()`, returns an `S3File`. Like `Bun.file()`, `S3File` instances are lazy: they don't refer to something that necessarily exists at the time of creation. That's why all the methods that don't involve network requests are fully synchronous. ```ts Type Reference icon="/icons/typescript.svg" expandable interface S3File extends Blob { slice(start: number, end?: number): S3File; exists(): Promise<boolean>; unlink(): Promise<void>; presign(options: S3Options): string; text(): Promise<string>; json(): Promise<any>; bytes(): Promise<Uint8Array>; …

title: S3 › Support for S3-Compatible Services
text: Bun's S3 implementation works with any S3-compatible storage service. Specify the appropriate endpoint:

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with AWS S3
text: AWS S3 is the default. With AWS S3, you can pass a `region` option instead of an `endpoint` option. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // AWS S3 const s3 = new S3Client({ accessKeyId: "access-key", secretAccessKey: "secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", // endpoint: "https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com", // region: "us-east-1", });

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with Cloudflare R2
text: To use Bun's S3 client with [Cloudflare R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/), set `endpoint` to the R2 endpoint in the `S3Client` constructor. The R2 endpoint includes your account ID. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={8} // CloudFlare R2 const r2 = new S3Client({ accessKeyId: "access-key", secretAccessKey: "secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", endpoint: "https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com", });

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with DigitalOcean Spaces
text: To use Bun's S3 client with [DigitalOcean Spaces](https://www.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/), set `endpoint` to the DigitalOcean Spaces endpoint in the `S3Client` constructor. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={8} const spaces = new S3Client({ accessKeyId: "access-key", secretAccessKey: "secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", // region: "nyc3", endpoint: "https://<region>.digitaloceanspaces.com", });

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with Google Cloud Storage

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with MinIO

title: S3 › Using Bun's S3Client with S3 Virtual Hosted-Style endpoints
text: When using a virtual hosted-style endpoint, set the `virtualHostedStyle` option to `true`. - If you don't specify an endpoint, Bun determines the AWS S3 endpoint from the provided region and bucket. - If you don't specify a region, Bun defaults to `us-east-1`. - If you explicitly provide an endpoint, you don't need to specify a bucket name. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={17, 25} // AWS S3 endpoint inferred from region and bucket const s3 = new S3Client({ accessKeyId: "access-key", secretAccessKey: "secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", virtualHostedStyle: true, // [!code ++] …

text: To use Bun's S3 client with [Supabase](https://supabase.com/), set `endpoint` to the Supabase endpoint in the `S3Client` constructor. The Supabase endpoint includes your account ID and the `/storage/v1/s3` path. In the Supabase dashboard at `https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/<account-id>/settings/storage`, turn on **Enable connection via S3 protocol** and use the region shown in that section. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3-10} const supabase = new S3Client({ accessKeyId: "access-key", secretAccessKey: "secret-key", bucket: "my-bucket", region: "us-west-1", endpoint: …

title: S3 › UTF-8, UTF-16, and BOM (byte order mark)
text: Like `Response` and `Blob`, `S3File` assumes UTF-8 encoding by default. When calling `text()` or `json()` on an `S3File`: - When Bun detects a UTF-16 byte order mark (BOM), it treats the data as UTF-16. JavaScriptCore natively supports UTF-16, so Bun skips the UTF-8 transcoding step (and strips the BOM). One consequence: invalid surrogate pairs in your UTF-16 string pass through to JavaScriptCore (same as source code). - When Bun detects a UTF-8 BOM, it strips the BOM and replaces invalid UTF-8 codepoints with the Unicode replacement character (`\uFFFD`) before passing the string to …

title: S3 › Working with large files (streams)
text: Bun automatically handles multipart uploads for large files and supports streaming. The same API that works for local files also works for S3 files. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Write a large file const bigFile = Buffer.alloc(10 * 1024 * 1024); // 10MB const writer = s3file.writer({ // Automatically retry on network errors up to 3 times retry: 3, // Queue up to 10 requests at a time queueSize: 10, // Upload in 5 MB chunks partSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024, }); for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { writer.write(bigFile); await writer.flush(); } await writer.end();

title: S3 › Working with S3 Files
text: The **`file`** method in `S3Client` returns a **lazy reference to a file on S3**. ```ts s3.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // A lazy reference to a file on S3 const s3file: S3File = client.file("123.json"); Like `Bun.file(path)`, the `S3Client`'s `file` method is synchronous. It makes no network requests until you call a method that needs one.

title: S3 › Writing & uploading files to S3

title: Secrets › Best Practices
text: 1. **Use descriptive service names**: Match the tool or application name If you're building a CLI for external use, use a UTI (Uniform Type Identifier) for the service name. ```javascript // Good - matches the actual tool { service: "com.docker.hub", name: "username" } { service: "com.vercel.cli", name: "team-name" } // Avoid - too generic { service: "api", name: "key" } 2. **Credentials-only**: Don't store application configuration in this API This API is slow; keep non-secret settings in a config file. 3. **Use for local development tools**: - ✅ CLI tools (gh, npm, docker, kubectl) - ✅ Local …

title: Secrets › `Bun.secrets.delete(options)`
text: Delete a stored credential. ```typescript const deleted = await Bun.secrets.delete({ service: "my-app", name: "alice@example.com", }); // Returns: boolean **Parameters:** - `options.service` (string, required) - The service or application name - `options.name` (string, required) - The username or account identifier **Returns:** - `Promise<boolean>` - `true` if a credential was deleted, `false` if not found

title: Secrets › `Bun.secrets.get(options)`
text: Retrieve a stored credential. ```typescript const password = await Bun.secrets.get({ service: "my-app", name: "alice@example.com", }); // Returns: string | null // Or if you prefer without an object const password = await Bun.secrets.get("my-app", "alice@example.com"); **Parameters:** - `options.service` (string, required) - The service or application name - `options.name` (string, required) - The username or account identifier **Returns:** - `Promise<string | null>` - The stored password, or `null` if not found

title: Secrets › `Bun.secrets.set(options)`
text: Store or update a credential. ```typescript await secrets.set({ service: "my-app", name: "alice@example.com", value: "super-secret-password", }); **Parameters:** - `options.service` (string, required) - The service or application name - `options.name` (string, required) - The username or account identifier - `options.value` (string, required) - The password or secret to store - `options.persist` (`"local"` or `"enterprise"`, optional) - Windows only. Which computers can see the credential. Defaults to `"enterprise"`. See [Windows (Credential Manager)](#windows-credential-manager) **Notes:** - …

title: Secrets › Comparison with Environment Variables
text: Unlike environment variables, `Bun.secrets`: - ✅ Encrypts credentials at rest (thanks to the operating system) - ✅ Avoids exposing secrets in process memory dumps (Bun zeros the memory after it's no longer needed) - ✅ Survives application restarts - ✅ Can be updated without restarting the application - ✅ Provides user-level access control - ❌ Requires OS credential service - ❌ Not very useful for deployment secrets (use environment variables in production)

title: Secrets › Error Handling
text: ```javascript try { await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "my-app", name: "alice", value: "password123", }); } catch (error) { console.error("Failed to store credential:", error.message); } // Check if a credential exists const password = await Bun.secrets.get({ service: "my-app", name: "alice", }); if (password === null) { console.log("No credential found"); }

title: Secrets › Limitations
text: - Maximum password length varies by platform (typically 2048-4096 bytes) - Keep `service` and `name` reasonably short (under 256 characters) - Some special characters may need escaping depending on the platform - Requires appropriate system services: - Linux: Secret service daemon must be running - macOS: Keychain Access must be available - Windows: Credential Manager service must be enabled

title: Secrets › Linux (libsecret)
text: - Requires a secret service daemon such as GNOME Keyring or KWallet - Bun stores credentials in the default collection - May prompt for unlock if the keyring is locked - The secret service must be running

title: Secrets › macOS (Keychain)
text: - Bun stores credentials in the user's login keychain - The keychain may prompt for access permission on first use - Credentials persist across system restarts - Accessible by the user who stored them

title: Secrets › Migrating from Plaintext Config Files
text: ```javascript // Instead of storing in ~/.aws/credentials await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "aws-cli", name: "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", value: process.env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, }); // Instead of .env files with sensitive data await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "my-app", name: "api-key", value: "sk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", }); // Load at runtime const apiKey = (await Bun.secrets.get({ service: "my-app", name: "api-key", })) || process.env.API_KEY; // Fallback for CI/production

title: Secrets › Overview
text: `Bun.secrets` provides a cross-platform API for managing sensitive credentials that CLI tools and development applications typically store in plaintext files like `~/.npmrc`, `~/.aws/credentials`, or `.env`. It uses: - **macOS**: Keychain Services - **Linux**: libsecret (GNOME Keyring, KWallet, and other secret service daemons) - **Windows**: Windows Credential Manager All operations are asynchronous and non-blocking, running on Bun's threadpool. This API is mostly useful for local development tools. We may later add a `provider` option for production deployment secrets.

title: Secrets › Security Considerations
text: 1. **Encryption**: The operating system's credential manager encrypts credentials 2. **Access Control**: Only the user who stored the credential can retrieve it 3. **No Plain Text**: Passwords are never stored in plain text 4. **Memory Safety**: Bun zeros out password memory after use 5. **Process Isolation**: Credentials are isolated per user account

title: Secrets › Storing CLI Tool Credentials
text: ```javascript // Store GitHub CLI token (instead of ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml) await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "my-app.com", name: "github-token", value: "ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", }); // Or if you prefer without an object await Bun.secrets.set("my-app.com", "github-token", "ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"); // Store npm registry token (instead of ~/.npmrc) await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "npm-registry", name: "https://registry.npmjs.org", value: "npm_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", }); // Retrieve for API calls const token = await Bun.secrets.get({ service: "my-app.com", name: "github-token", }); if (token) …

text: ```typescript namespace Bun { interface SecretsOptions { service: string; name: string; } interface Secrets { get(options: SecretsOptions): Promise<string | null>; set(options: SecretsOptions & { value: string; persist?: "local" | "enterprise" }): Promise<void>; delete(options: SecretsOptions): Promise<boolean>; } const secrets: Secrets; }

title: Secrets › Updating Credentials
text: ```javascript // Initial password await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "email-server", name: "admin@example.com", value: "old-password", }); // Update to new password await Bun.secrets.set({ service: "email-server", name: "admin@example.com", value: "new-password", }); // The old password is replaced

title: Secrets › Windows (Credential Manager)
text: - Bun stores credentials in Windows Credential Manager - Visible in Control Panel → Credential Manager → Windows Credentials - Persisted with the `CRED_PERSIST_ENTERPRISE` flag by default, so they're scoped per user - Encrypted using Windows Data Protection API With `CRED_PERSIST_ENTERPRISE`, a user account that has roaming state, such as a roaming profile on a domain, also sees the credential on other computers. To keep a secret on the current computer, for example a refresh token that belongs to one device, pass `persist: "local"`. Bun then stores the credential with …

title: Semver › `Bun.semver.order(versionA: string, versionB: string): 0 | 1 | -1`
text: Returns `0` if `versionA` and `versionB` are equal, `1` if `versionA` is greater than `versionB`, and `-1` if `versionA` is less than `versionB`. Example: ```typescript semver.order("1.0.0", "1.0.0"); // 0 semver.order("1.0.0", "1.0.1"); // -1 semver.order("1.0.1", "1.0.0"); // 1 const unsorted = ["1.0.0", "1.0.1", "1.0.0-alpha", "1.0.0-beta", "1.0.0-rc"]; unsorted.sort(semver.order); // ["1.0.0-alpha", "1.0.0-beta", "1.0.0-rc", "1.0.0", "1.0.1"] console.log(unsorted); If you need other semver functions, open an issue or pull request.

title: Semver › `Bun.semver.satisfies(version: string, range: string): boolean`
text: Returns `true` if `version` satisfies `range`, otherwise `false`. Example: ```typescript semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "^1.0.0"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "^1.0.1"); // false semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "~1.0.0"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "~1.0.1"); // false semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "1.0.0"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "1.0.1"); // false semver.satisfies("1.0.1", "1.0.0"); // false semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "1.0.x"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "1.x.x"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "x.x.x"); // true semver.satisfies("1.0.0", "1.0.0 - 2.0.0"); // true …

title: Shell › Argument injection
text: Bun Shell cannot know how an external command interprets its own command-line arguments. An attacker can supply input that the target program recognizes as one of its own options or flags, leading to unintended behavior. ```js // Malicious input formatted as a Git command-line flag const branch = "--upload-pack=echo pwned"; // UNSAFE: While Bun safely passes the string as a single argument, // the `git` program itself sees and acts upon the malicious flag. await $`git ls-remote origin ${branch}`; **Recommendation**: Always sanitize user-provided input before passing it as an argument to an …

title: Shell › `$.braces` (brace expansion)
text: `$.braces` implements [brace expansion](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Brace-Expansion.html) for shell commands: ```js await $.braces(`echo {1,2,3}`); // => ["echo 1", "echo 2", "echo 3"]

title: Shell › Builtin Commands
text: For cross-platform compatibility, Bun Shell implements a set of builtin commands, in addition to reading commands from the `PATH` environment variable. - `cd`: change the working directory - `ls`: list files in a directory (supports `-l` for long listing format) - `rm`: remove files and directories - `echo`: print text - `pwd`: print the working directory - `bun`: run bun in bun - `cat` - `touch` - `mkdir` - `which` - `mv` - `exit` - `true` - `false` - `yes` - `seq` - `dirname` - `basename` **Not** implemented yet, but planned: - See [Issue #9716](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/9716) …

title: Shell › Changing the environment variables
text: By default, all commands use `process.env` as their environment variables. To change the environment variables for a single command, call `.env()`: ```js await $`echo $FOO`.env({ ...process.env, FOO: "bar" }); // bar To change the default environment variables for all commands, call `$.env`: ```js $.env({ FOO: "bar" }); // the globally-set $FOO await $`echo $FOO`; // bar // the locally-set $FOO await $`echo $FOO`.env({ FOO: "baz" }); // baz To reset the environment variables to the default, call `$.env()` with no arguments: ```js $.env({ FOO: "bar" }); // the globally-set $FOO await $`echo …

title: Shell › Changing the working directory
text: To change the working directory of a command, pass a string to `.cwd()`: ```js await $`pwd`.cwd("/tmp"); // /tmp To change the default working directory for all commands, call `$.cwd`: ```js $.cwd("/tmp"); // the globally-set working directory await $`pwd`; // /tmp // the locally-set working directory await $`pwd`.cwd("/"); // /

title: Shell › Command substitution (`$(...)`)
text: Command substitution inserts the output of another command into the current script: ```js // Prints out the hash of the current commit await $`echo Hash of current commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD)`; Bun Shell inserts the output as text, so you can use it to declare a shell variable: ```js await $` REV=$(git rev-parse HEAD) docker build -t myapp:$REV . echo Done building docker image "myapp:$REV" `; Because Bun internally uses the special [`raw`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals#raw_strings) property on the input template literal, using the …

title: Shell › Credits
text: Large parts of this API were inspired by [zx](https://github.com/google/zx), [dax](https://github.com/dsherret/dax), and [bnx](https://github.com/wobsoriano/bnx). Thank you to the authors of those projects.

title: Shell › Environment variables
text:
Set environment variables like in bash: ```js await $`FOO=foo bun -e 'console.log(process.env.FOO)'`; // foo
 Use string interpolation to set the value: ```js const foo = "bar123"; await $`FOO=${foo + "456"} bun -e 'console.log(process.env.FOO)'`; // bar123456
 Bun Shell escapes input by default, preventing shell injection attacks: ```js const foo = "bar123; rm -rf /tmp"; await $`FOO=${foo} bun -e 'console.log(process.env.FOO)'`; // bar123; rm -rf /tmp

title: Shell › Error handling
text: By default, a non-zero exit code throws an error. The `ShellError` contains information about the command that ran. ```js try { const output = await $`something-that-may-fail`.text(); console.log(output); } catch (err) { console.log(`Failed with code ${err.exitCode}`); console.log(err.stdout.toString()); console.log(err.stderr.toString()); } `.nothrow()` disables throwing. Check the result's `exitCode` yourself. ```js const { stdout, stderr, exitCode } = await $`something-that-may-fail`.nothrow().quiet(); if (exitCode !== 0) { console.log(`Non-zero exit code ${exitCode}`); } …

title: Shell › `$.escape` (escape strings)
text: Exposes Bun Shell's escaping logic as a function: ```js console.log($.escape('$(foo) `bar` "baz"')); // => "\$(foo) \`bar\` \"baz\"" To skip escaping, wrap the string in a `{ raw: str }` object: ```js await $`echo $ raw: '$(foo) `bar` "baz"' `; // => bun: command not found: foo // => bun: command not found: bar // => baz

title: Shell › Example: Redirect input from JavaScript objects (`<`)
text: To use a JavaScript object as stdin, use the `<` operator: ```js const response = new Response("hello i am a response body"); const result = await $`cat < ${response}`.text(); console.log(result); // hello i am a response body You can redirect from these JavaScript objects: - `Buffer`, `Uint8Array`, `Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array`, `Int8Array`, `Int16Array`, `Int32Array`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer` (reads from the underlying buffer) - `Bun.file(path)`, `Bun.file(fd)` (reads from the file) - `Response` (reads from the body)

title: Shell › Example: Redirect output to JavaScript objects (`>`)
text: To redirect stdout to a JavaScript object, use the `>` operator: ```js const buffer = Buffer.alloc(100); await $`echo "Hello World!" > ${buffer}`; console.log(buffer.toString()); // Hello World!\n You can redirect output to these JavaScript objects: - `Buffer`, `Uint8Array`, `Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array`, `Int8Array`, `Int16Array`, `Int32Array`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer` (writes to the underlying buffer) - `Bun.file(path)`, `Bun.file(fd)` (writes to the file)

title: Shell › Example: Redirect stderr -> file
text: ```js await $`bun run index.ts 2> errors.txt`;

title: Shell › Example: Redirect stderr -> stdout
text: ```js // redirects stderr to stdout, so all output // will be available on stdout await $`bun run ./index.ts 2>&1`;

title: Shell › Example: Redirect stdin -> file
text: ```js await $`cat < myfile.txt`;

title: Shell › Example: Redirect stdout -> file
text: ```js await $`echo bun! > greeting.txt`;

title: Shell › Example: Redirect stdout -> stderr
text: ```js // redirects stdout to stderr, so all output // will be available on stderr await $`bun run ./index.ts 1>&2`;

title: Shell › Features
text: - **Cross-platform**: works on Windows, Linux & macOS. Instead of installing `rimraf` or `cross-env`, you can use Bun Shell. It implements common shell commands like `ls`, `cd`, and `rm` natively. - **Familiar**: Bun Shell is a bash-like shell that supports redirection, pipes, and environment variables. - **Globs**: Bun Shell supports glob patterns natively, including `**`, `*`, and `{expansion}`. - **Template literals**: Template literals execute shell commands and interpolate variables and expressions. - **Safety**: Bun Shell escapes all strings by default, preventing shell injection …

title: Shell › Getting started
text: Start with `echo`. To run it, use the `$` template literal tag: ```js await $`echo "Hello World!"`; // Hello World! By default, shell commands print to stdout. To quiet the output, call `.quiet()`: ```js await $`echo "Hello World!"`.quiet(); // No output To read the output of the command as text, use `.text()`: ```js // .text() automatically calls .quiet() for you const welcome = await $`echo "Hello World!"`.text(); console.log(welcome); // Hello World!\n By default, `await`ing returns stdout and stderr as `Buffer`s. ```js const { stdout, stderr } = await $`echo "Hello!"`.quiet(); …

title: Shell › Implementation notes
text: Bun Shell is a small programming language implemented in Rust, with a handwritten lexer, parser, and interpreter. Unlike bash, zsh, and other shells, Bun Shell runs operations concurrently.

title: Shell › Piping (`|`)
text: Like in bash, you can pipe the output of one command to another: ```js const result = await $`echo "Hello World!" | wc -w`.text(); console.log(result); // 2\n You can also pipe with JavaScript objects: ```js const response = new Response("hello i am a response body"); const result = await $`cat < ${response} | wc -w`.text(); console.log(result); // 6\n

title: Shell › Reading output
text: To read the output of a command as a string, use `.text()`: ```js const result = await $`echo "Hello World!"`.text(); console.log(result); // Hello World!\n

title: Shell › Reading output as a Blob
text: To read the output of a command as a Blob, use `.blob()`: ```js const result = await $`echo "Hello World!"`.blob(); console.log(result); // Blob(13) { size: 13, type: "text/plain" }

title: Shell › Reading output as JSON
text: To read the output of a command as JSON, use `.json()`: ```js const result = await $`echo '{"foo": "bar"}'`.json(); console.log(result); // { foo: "bar" }

title: Shell › Reading output line-by-line
text: To read the output of a command line-by-line, use `.lines()`: ```js for await (let line of $`echo "Hello World!"`.lines()) { console.log(line); // Hello World! } You can also use `.lines()` on a piped command: ```js const search = "bun"; for await (let line of $`cat list.txt | grep ${search}`.lines()) { console.log(line); }

title: Shell › Redirection
text: Redirect a command's _input_ or _output_ with the typical Bash operators: - `<` redirect stdin - `>` or `1>` redirect stdout - `2>` redirect stderr - `&>` redirect both stdout and stderr - `>>` or `1>>` redirect stdout, _appending_ to the destination, instead of overwriting - `2>>` redirect stderr, _appending_ to the destination, instead of overwriting - `&>>` redirect both stdout and stderr, _appending_ to the destination, instead of overwriting - `1>&2` redirect stdout to stderr (writes to stdout go to stderr instead) - `2>&1` redirect stderr to stdout (writes to stderr go to stdout instead) …

title: Shell › Security considerations
text: While Bun Shell prevents command injection by default, you are still responsible for security in certain scenarios. Similar to the `Bun.spawn` or `node:child_process.exec()` APIs, you can intentionally execute a command which spawns a new shell (for example, `bash -c`) with arguments. When you do this, you hand off control, and Bun's built-in protections no longer apply to the string interpreted by that new shell. ```js const userInput = "world; touch /tmp/pwned"; // UNSAFE: You have explicitly started a new shell process with `bash -c`. // This new shell will execute the `touch` command. Any …

title: Shell › Security in the Bun shell
text: By design, Bun Shell _does not invoke a system shell_ like `/bin/sh`. It's a re-implementation of bash that runs in the same Bun process. When parsing command arguments, Bun Shell treats all _interpolated variables_ as single, literal strings. This protects against **command injection**: ```js const userInput = "my-file.txt; rm -rf /"; // SAFE: `userInput` is treated as a single quoted string await $`ls ${userInput}`; Here, Bun Shell treats `userInput` as a single string, so `ls` tries to read the contents of a single directory named `my-file.txt; rm -rf /`.

title: Shell › `.sh` file loader
text: For simple shell scripts, you can use Bun Shell instead of `/bin/sh`. Pass a file with the `.sh` extension to `bun`: ```sh script.sh icon="file-code" echo "Hello World! pwd=$(pwd)" ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun ./script.sh ```txt Hello World! pwd=/home/demo Bun Shell scripts are cross-platform, so they work on Windows: ```powershell powershell icon="windows" bun .\script.sh ```txt Hello World! pwd=C:\Users\Demo

title: Shell › Utilities
text: Bun Shell also implements a set of utilities for working with shells.

title: SQL › After `release()`
text: `release()` closes the `reserved` client immediately. A query on it that has not started rejects with `ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_CLOSED` or `ERR_MYSQL_CONNECTION_CLOSED`, because the connection can already belong to another caller. Queries are lazy, so await each query before the release: ```ts async function countUsers() { using reserved = await sql.reserve(); return await reserved`SELECT count(*) FROM users`; // without `await`, the query starts after the release and rejects } - A transaction that you start with `reserved.begin()` keeps the connection until it ends, even if you call …

title: SQL › After the transaction ends
text: The `tx` client belongs to its transaction. Once Bun has sent `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, a query on `tx` never reaches the database. It rejects with `ERR_POSTGRES_INVALID_TRANSACTION_STATE`, or the same code with `MYSQL` or `SQLITE`. Queries are lazy, so this includes a query that you create inside the callback and first await later. Await every query inside the callback, or return the queries in an array. `sql.begin` resolves once the database has answered `COMMIT`. If the connection is lost while `COMMIT` is unanswered, `sql.begin` rejects and nobody can know whether the transaction was …

title: SQL › Authentication
text: Bun supports SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS (SASL), MD5, and Clear Text authentication. We recommend SASL for better security. See [Postgres SASL Authentication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sasl-authentication.html). A non-ASCII password logs in whichever Unicode form you type it in. Bun first logs in with the password as you typed it. If the server refuses it, Bun tries once more with its SASLprep form, the form that `psql` uses. A wrong non-ASCII password can therefore count as two failed logins.

title: SQL › Authentication Methods
text: MySQL supports multiple authentication plugins, which the client negotiates automatically: - **`mysql_native_password`** - Traditional MySQL authentication, widely compatible - **`caching_sha2_password`** - Default in MySQL 8.0+, more secure with RSA key exchange - **`sha256_password`** - SHA-256 based authentication The client automatically handles authentication plugin switching when the server requests it. For the two SHA-256 plugins, use TLS or `allowPublicKeyRetrieval: true`. `caching_sha2_password` also works over a unix socket.

text: On PostgreSQL and MySQL, `result.columns` describes each column of the result, as the server reported it. Use `type` to tell apart columns that give the same JavaScript value, such as `jsonb` and `text[]`. ```ts const result = await sql`SELECT id, tags, data FROM posts WHERE id = ${1}`; result.columns; // [ // { name: "id", type: 23, table: 16388, number: 1 }, // int4 // { name: "tags", type: 1009, table: 16388, number: 2 }, // text[] // { name: "data", type: 3802, table: 16388, number: 3 }, // jsonb // ] result.statement.string; // the text that Bun sent, with $1 for the parameter …

text: The `transform` option renames columns between the style of the database and the style of your code. `SQL.camel`, `SQL.pascal` and `SQL.kebab` are presets for a database that uses `snake_case`. They work on every adapter. ```ts const sql = new SQL({ transform: SQL.camel }); await sql`INSERT INTO users ${sql({ firstName: "Alice", createdAt: new Date() })}`; // INSERT INTO users ("first_name", "created_at") VALUES ($1, $2) const [user] = await sql`SELECT first_name, created_at FROM users`; console.log(user.firstName, user.createdAt); | Preset | `user_id` in your code | Results only | Helpers …

title: SQL › Conditional Queries

title: SQL › Connection callbacks
text: `onconnect(err)` and `onclose(err)` get one argument. Neither gets the connection. - `onconnect` runs once for each connection that opens, with `null`. Only SQLite passes an error here, when it cannot open the file. - `onclose` runs once for each connection that closes, and always gets an `Error`. After `sql.close()` its code is `ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_CLOSED` or `ERR_MYSQL_CONNECTION_CLOSED`. - On PostgreSQL and MySQL, Bun reports a failed connection attempt to `onclose`, not to `onconnect`. - The callbacks also run for the connection that `sql.listen()` opens.

title: SQL › Custom CA Certificates
text: To verify the server against a CA that is not in the default trust store (for example an Amazon RDS or Google Cloud SQL bundle), pass the CA certificate as `tls.ca`, or pass the `BunFile` directly as `tls`. Both forms verify the certificate chain and the hostname (`verify-full`). ```ts const sql = new SQL("postgres://user:password@db.example.com/mydb", { tls: { ca: Bun.file("./rds-ca-bundle.pem") }, }); // Shorthand for the same configuration const sql = new SQL("postgres://user:password@db.example.com/mydb", { tls: Bun.file("./rds-ca-bundle.pem"), });

title: SQL › Data Type Differences
text: SQLite has a more flexible type system than PostgreSQL: ```ts // SQLite stores data in 5 storage classes: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB const sqlite = new SQL("sqlite://app.db"); // SQLite is more lenient with types await sqlite` CREATE TABLE flexible ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, data TEXT, -- Can store numbers as strings value NUMERIC, -- Can store integers, reals, or text blob BLOB -- Binary data ) `; // JavaScript values are automatically converted await sqlite`INSERT INTO flexible VALUES (${1}, ${"text"}, ${123.45}, ${Buffer.from("binary")})`;

title: SQL › Database Environment Variables
text: `Bun.sql` and `new SQL()` read connection settings from environment variables.

title: SQL › Database Support
text: `Bun.SQL` provides a unified API for multiple database systems:

title: SQL › Dates and time zones
text: PostgreSQL `timestamp` and MySQL `DATETIME` / `TIMESTAMP` values have no offset on the wire. Bun reads them as **UTC**, whatever the machine's time zone, and reads `date` / `DATE` as UTC midnight. Bun stores a `Date` parameter as its UTC wall clock, so it reads back as the same instant. ```ts // created_at timestamp = 2024-01-15 12:00:00 const [row] = await sql`SELECT created_at FROM events`; row.created_at.toISOString(); // "2024-01-15T12:00:00.000Z" on every host `pg`, `postgres.js`, `mysql2` and `mariadb` read `timestamp` / `DATETIME` as **local time**. If you migrate from one of them on a …

title: SQL › Differences from PostgreSQL
text: The API is unified, but behavior differs: 1. **Parameter placeholders**: a tagged template writes the placeholders for you. A string that you pass to `sql.unsafe` or `sql.file` must use `?`, because MySQL rejects `$1` 2. **RETURNING clause**: MySQL doesn't support RETURNING; use `result.lastInsertRowid` or a separate SELECT. MariaDB supports `INSERT ... RETURNING` 3. **Array types**: MySQL doesn't have native array types like PostgreSQL. Bun sends a JavaScript array as JSON 4. **DDL in transactions**: `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` commit the open transaction (see [Transactions](#transactions)) …

title: SQL › Distributed Transactions
text: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) is a distributed transaction protocol. In phase 1, the coordinator prepares each node, making sure its data is written and ready to commit. In phase 2, the nodes commit or roll back based on the coordinator's decision. In PostgreSQL and MySQL, distributed transactions persist beyond their original session, so privileged users or coordinators can commit or roll them back later. PostgreSQL implements them as prepared transactions; MySQL uses XA Transactions. An uncaught exception during the distributed transaction rolls back all changes. Otherwise, you can commit or roll …

title: SQL › Dynamic columns in updates
text: Use `sql(object, ...string)` to pick which columns to update. If you don't list any columns, Bun uses all keys on the object. Bun skips a column whose value is `undefined`, unless [`transform.undefined`](#column-name-transforms) is set. ```ts await sql`UPDATE users SET ${sql(user, "name", "email")} WHERE id = ${user.id}`; // uses all keys from the object to update the row await sql`UPDATE users SET ${sql(user)} WHERE id = ${user.id}`;

title: SQL › Dynamic passwords
text: For alternative authentication schemes such as access tokens, or databases with rotating passwords, set `password` to a synchronous or asynchronous function. Bun calls it at connection time to resolve the password. ```ts const sql = new SQL(url, { // Other connection config ... // Password function for the database user password: async () => await signer.getAuthToken(), });

title: SQL › Dynamic Table Names
text: To reference tables, schemas or columns dynamically, use the `sql()` helper, which quotes the name as an identifier: ```ts // Safely reference tables dynamically await sql`SELECT * FROM ${sql("users")}`; // With schema qualification await sql`SELECT * FROM ${sql("public.users")}`; A dot separates schema, table and column, and Bun quotes each part: `sql("public.users")` becomes `"public"."users"`, or `` `public`.`users` `` on MySQL. Quoting prevents SQL injection, but it does not limit which table or column the name reaches. Check a name that comes from a user against a list of allowed names.

title: SQL › Dynamic values and `where in`
text: Value lists can also be created dynamically, for `WHERE IN` queries. You can also pass an array of objects and name the key to build the list from. ```ts await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN ${sql([1, 2, 3])}`; const users = [ { id: 1, name: "Alice" }, { id: 2, name: "Bob" }, { id: 3, name: "Charlie" }, ]; await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN ${sql(users, "id")}`; An empty list matches no row. On PostgreSQL and MySQL it becomes `IN (NULL)`, so `NOT IN` with an empty list matches no row either. On SQLite it becomes `IN ()`, and `NOT IN ()` matches every row.

title: SQL › Execute and Cancelling Queries
text: Queries are lazy: they only start executing when awaited or run with `.execute()`. A query starts in the call to `.then()`, `.catch()`, `.finally()` or `.execute()`. `await query` calls `.then()`. A query that you never await or execute never runs. `query.active` is `true` while a connection runs the query. To cancel a query, call `cancel()` on the query object. ```ts const query = sql`SELECT pg_sleep(30)`.execute(); setTimeout(() => query.cancel(), 100); await query; // rejects: canceling statement due to user request What `cancel()` does depends on how far the query got: | The query | …

title: SQL › Hot reloading
text: With `bun --hot`, a `new SQL()` with the same connection settings takes over the open connections of the previous load. A reload opens no new connection, and the database sees the same sessions. - `onconnect` runs again for each connection that the new client takes over. - Session state, such as `SET` and temporary tables, stays on the connection. - When you edit the settings, the old connections stay open for one more reload. At the first query of a load, Bun closes the connections of clients from earlier loads that ran no query during the whole previous load: idle ones at once, busy ones …

title: SQL › How it works
text: - All subscriptions on a client share one dedicated connection. The first `listen()` opens it, and removing the last subscription closes it. As a result, a client that never listens never pays for the connection, and unlistening everything lets the process exit without `sql.close()`. - While anything is subscribed, that connection keeps the process alive, like a listening server. - If the connection drops, Bun re-establishes it with exponential backoff (250ms doubling to 32s, with jitter) and re-subscribes every channel. title: SQL › Inserting data
text: Pass JavaScript values directly to the SQL template literal; Bun handles the escaping. ```ts // Basic insert with direct values const [user] = await sql` INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (${name}, ${email}) RETURNING * `; // Using object helper for cleaner syntax const userData = { name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", }; const [newUser] = await sql` INSERT INTO users ${sql(userData)} RETURNING * `; // Expands to: INSERT INTO users ("name", "email") VALUES ($1, $2)

title: SQL › LISTEN / NOTIFY (PostgreSQL)
text: `sql.listen()` subscribes to a PostgreSQL notification channel and `sql.notify()` publishes to one. Processes sharing a database can use this as a lightweight message bus: cache invalidation, waking workers when rows are inserted (typically from a trigger calling `pg_notify`), fan-out of small events. ```ts const subscription = await sql.listen("orders", payload => { console.log("new order", JSON.parse(payload)); }); await sql.notify("orders", JSON.stringify({ id: 42 })); await subscription.unlisten(); `listen()` resolves once PostgreSQL has acknowledged the `LISTEN`, so a `notify()` issued …

title: SQL › `notify()`
text: `notify()` is an ordinary query (`SELECT pg_notify($1, $2)`) on whichever handle you call it through. On `sql` it uses the pool. Inside `sql.begin()` it runs in the transaction, so PostgreSQL delivers it on `COMMIT` and drops it on `ROLLBACK`. Calling `notify()` inside a transaction is how to announce a change only once it is visible: ```ts await sql.begin(async tx => { const [order] = await tx`INSERT INTO orders ${sql(data)} RETURNING id`; await tx.notify("orders", String(order.id)); // delivered when the transaction commits }); The payload is optional: `sql.notify("cache-invalidated")` is …

title: SQL › Numbers and BigInt
text: Bun returns PostgreSQL `bigint` (`int8`) values, and MySQL `BIGINT` values outside the 32-bit range, as strings: ```ts const [{ x, y }] = await sql`SELECT 9223372036854777 as x, 12345 as y`; console.log(typeof x, x); // "string" "9223372036854777" console.log(typeof y, y); // "number" 12345 A `number` parameter is an integer (`int4` or `int8` on PostgreSQL, `INT` or `BIGINT` on MySQL) when `Number.isSafeInteger()` is true for it. Every other number is a double. The parameter's type carries over to a result that derives from it: on PostgreSQL, `` sql`SELECT ${2 ** 40} AS x` `` returns `x` as a …

On PostgreSQL the type that the server expects for the parameter also counts. | JavaScript value | PostgreSQL | MySQL / MariaDB | SQLite | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | `Date` | The instant for `timestamp` and `timestamptz`. ISO 8601 text for `date`, `time`, `text` | `DATETIME` in UTC | …

title: SQL › Performance Tips for MySQL
text: 1. **Use connection pooling**: Set appropriate `max` pool size based on your workload 2. **Enable prepared statements**: They're enabled by default and improve performance 3. **Use transactions for bulk operations**: Group related queries in transactions 4. **Index properly**: MySQL relies heavily on indexes for query performance 5. **Use `utf8mb4` charset**: It's set by default and handles all Unicode characters

The default The database name is the exception: `PGDATABASE`, `MYSQL_DATABASE` and `MARIADB_DATABASE` take priority over the database in a URL. title: SQL › Prepared Statements
text: By default, Bun's SQL client creates named prepared statements for queries it can infer are static, which is faster. Each connection keeps the statements it used last: 1,024 on PostgreSQL, 256 on MySQL and MariaDB, where all connections share the server's `max_prepared_stmt_count`. When it prepares another one, it closes the least recently used statement on the server. On PostgreSQL, a prepared statement can stop working: `ALTER TABLE` changes its result (`cached plan must not change result type`), and `DEALLOCATE ALL` or `DISCARD ALL` removes it. Bun then prepares the statement again and runs …

title: SQL › Queries in files
text: `sql.file` reads a query from a file and executes it. If the file uses placeholders like `$1` and `$2`, you can pass parameters to the query. Without parameters, the file can contain multiple commands. ```ts const result = await sql.file("query.sql", [1, 2, 3]); `sql.file` returns a lazy query like any other: Bun reads the file when you await the query. With the SQLite adapter, parameters can also be an object of named parameters (`:name`, `$name`, or `@name` placeholders), the same form `sql.unsafe` accepts below.

title: SQL › Query Execution
text: SQLite executes queries synchronously, unlike PostgreSQL, which uses asynchronous I/O. The API still returns Promises: ```ts const sqlite = new SQL("sqlite://app.db"); // Works the same as PostgreSQL, but executes synchronously under the hood const users = await sqlite`SELECT * FROM users`; // Parameters work identically const user = await sqlite`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`;

title: SQL › Query Results
text: By default, Bun's SQL client returns query results as arrays of objects, where each object represents a row with column names as keys. Two other formats are available.

title: SQL › Reserved Connections
text: `sql.reserve()` takes a connection from the pool and returns a client that wraps it, so you can run queries on an isolated connection. ```ts // Get exclusive connection from pool const reserved = await sql.reserve(); try { await reserved`INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (${"Alice"})`; } finally { // Important: Release connection back to pool await reserved.release(); } // Or using Symbol.dispose { using reserved = await sql.reserve(); await reserved`SELECT 1`; } // Automatically released When every connection is busy, `reserve()` waits until one frees up. Pass an `AbortSignal` to stop waiting: …

It also works when `DATABASE_URL` is a MySQL or MariaDB URL. …

text: Savepoints create intermediate checkpoints within a transaction, so part of it can roll back without aborting the whole thing. ```ts await sql.begin(async tx => { await tx`INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (${"Alice"})`; try { await tx.savepoint(async sp => { // This part can be rolled back separately await sp`UPDATE users SET status = active`; if (someCondition) { throw new Error("Rollback to savepoint"); } }); } catch (err) { // The savepoint rolled back, and the transaction continues } await tx`INSERT INTO audit_log (action) VALUES ('user_created')`; }); When the callback throws, Bun rolls …

title: SQL › SQLite-Specific Errors
text: SQLite errors carry SQLite's [extended result codes](https://www.sqlite.org/rescode.html#extrc) and numbers. A constraint violation reports the specific constraint, such as `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE` and `2067`, not `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT` and `19`. To match the whole family, use `error.code.startsWith("SQLITE_CONSTRAINT")` or `(error.errno & 0xff) === 19`. | Error Code | errno | Description | | ------------------------------ | ----- | ---------------------------------------------------- | | `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY` | 1555 | Duplicate primary key | | `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE` | 2067 | …

title: SQL › `sql.json`
text: PostgreSQL stores a string in a `json` or `jsonb` column as a JSON string. Pass the object itself, not `JSON.stringify(object)`: ```ts await sql`INSERT INTO settings (data) VALUES ($ theme: "dark" )`; // {"theme": "dark"} await sql`INSERT INTO settings (data) VALUES (${"dark"})`; // "dark" await sql`INSERT INTO settings (data) VALUES (${'{"theme":"dark"}'})`; // "{\"theme\":\"dark\"}", a string `sql.json(value)` stores any value as JSON, on every adapter. Use it for a number, a boolean or `null`: ```ts await sql`INSERT INTO settings (data) VALUES (${sql.json(42)})`; // 42 await sql`INSERT INTO …

title: SQL › `sql``.raw()` format
text: The `.raw()` method returns rows as arrays of `Buffer` objects. Use it for binary data or for performance. ```ts const rows = await sql`SELECT * FROM users`.raw(); console.log(rows); // [[Buffer, Buffer], [Buffer, Buffer], [Buffer, Buffer]] - On PostgreSQL, each `Buffer` holds the bytes the server sent. A prepared query gets `bool`, `int4`, `float4`, `float8`, `numeric`, `bytea`, `time`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz`, `int4[]` and `float4[]` in PostgreSQL's binary format, so a `bytea` column is its bytes. Every other type is text. All types are text on the first run of a query without parameters, …

title: SQL › `sql``.simple()`
text: The PostgreSQL wire protocol supports two types of queries: "simple" and "extended". Simple queries can contain multiple statements but don't support parameters, while extended queries (the default) support parameters but only allow one statement. To run multiple statements in a single query, use `sql``.simple()`: ```ts // Multiple statements in one query await sql` SELECT 1; SELECT 2; `.simple(); Simple queries are useful for database migrations and setup scripts. Simple queries cannot use parameters (`${value}`). If you need parameters, split your query into separate statements. These rules …

title: SQL › `sql``.values()` format
text: The `sql``.values()` method returns each row as an array of values, in the same order as the columns in your query. ```ts const rows = await sql`SELECT * FROM users`.values(); console.log(rows); The rows look like: ```ts [ ["Alice", "alice@example.com"], ["Bob", "bob@example.com"], ]; `sql``.values()` is useful when a query returns duplicate column names. With objects (the default), the last column wins because the column name is the key. With `sql``.values()`, every column is present in the array, so you can read duplicates by index.

Connections fail if server requires SSL. Default mode if none specified. | | `prefer` | Tries SSL first, falls …

Does not limit a running query | `idleTimeout` and `maxLifetime` never interrupt work. A running query, a `begin()` transaction and a reserved connection keep their connection. A connection …

title: SQL › Transactions
text: To start a new transaction, use `sql.begin`. This method works on every adapter. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, it reserves a dedicated connection from the pool. For SQLite, it begins a transaction on the single connection. Bun sends the `BEGIN` command automatically (`START TRANSACTION` on MySQL), including any optional configurations you specify. If an error occurs during the transaction, Bun issues a `ROLLBACK` and `sql.begin` rejects with the error.

title: SQL › Unhandled rejections
text: `.then()` and `.catch()` return a promise like any other. When it rejects and nothing handles the rejection, Bun reports an unhandled rejection, which ends the process unless you listen for [`unhandledRejection`](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-unhandledrejection). So does an error that your `.finally()` callback throws. A query that you only start, with `.execute()` or `.finally()`, is the exception. Its own failure is not reported, and the error is lost, when: - The query had a connection: the server refused it, or the connection was lost. - `close({ timeout: 0 })` closed the pool …

title: SQL › Unsafe Queries
text: `sql.unsafe` executes raw SQL strings. Use it with caution: it does not escape user input. Without parameters, the string can contain more than one command. ```ts // Multiple commands without parameters const result = await sql.unsafe(` SELECT ${userColumns} FROM users; SELECT ${accountColumns} FROM accounts; `); // Using parameters (only one command is allowed) const result = await sql.unsafe("SELECT " + dangerous + " FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]); The string goes to the database as written, so `sql.unsafe` and `sql.file` take the database's own placeholders: | Adapter | Placeholders | | …

title: SQL › Using With Connection Strings
text: You can also set the SSL mode in the connection string: ```ts // Using prefer mode const sql = new SQL("postgres://user:password@localhost/mydb?sslmode=prefer"); // Using verify-full mode const sql = new SQL("postgres://user:password@localhost/mydb?sslmode=verify-full");

title: SQL › When Bun reads parameters
text: Bun reads the parameters of a tagged template when it sends the query, not when it evaluates the template. Leave a `Buffer`, `TypedArray`, `Date` or object alone until the query settles, or pass a copy. ```ts const bytes = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3, 4]); const query = sql`INSERT INTO files (data) VALUES (${bytes})`; bytes.fill(0); // the query has not read `bytes` yet await query; // stores 00000000, not 01020304

title: SQL › Why not just use an existing library?
text: You can use npm packages like postgres.js, pg, and node-postgres in Bun too. They're great options. Two reasons why: 1. We think it's simpler for developers to have a database driver built into Bun. The time you spend library shopping is time you could be building your app. 2. We use some JavaScriptCore engine internals to create objects faster, in ways that would be difficult to implement in a library.

title: SQLite › `.all()`
text: Use `.all()` to run a query and get back the results as an array of objects. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const query = db.query(`select $message;`); query.all({ $message: "Hello world" }); ```txt [{ $message: "Hello world" }] Internally, this calls [`sqlite3_reset`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_reset) and repeatedly calls [`sqlite3_step`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_step) until it returns `SQLITE_DONE`.

title: SQLite › `.as(Class)` - Map query results to a class
text: Use `.as(Class)` to run a query and get back the results as instances of a class. The class's methods, getters, and setters are available on each row. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={10} class Movie { title: string; year: number; get isMarvel() { return this.title.includes("Marvel"); } } const query = db.query("SELECT title, year FROM movies").as(Movie); const movies = query.all(); const first = query.get(); console.log(movies[0].isMarvel); console.log(first.isMarvel); ```txt true true As a performance optimization, Bun does not call the class constructor or run default …

text: To bind values to a statement, pass an object to the `.all()`, `.get()`, `.run()`, or `.values()` method. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const query = db.query(`select $message;`); query.all({ $message: "Hello world" }); You can bind using positional parameters too: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query(`select ?1;`); query.all("Hello world");

Bun releases the underlying connection (and the database file handle) once the last outstanding `.prepare()` statement is finalized. To finalize **every** outstanding statement, release the connection immediately, and throw if …

See [WAL sidecar file cleanup](#wal-sidecar-file-cleanup) for a practical example. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={6} const db = new Database("mydb.sqlite"); // Ensure WAL mode is NOT persistent // this prevents WAL files from lingering after the database is closed db.fileControl(constants.SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL, 0); SQLite reads the input of `cmd` from `value` and writes its output there. `value` can be: - `number`: passed as a 32-bit integer. title: SQLite › `.finalize()`
text: Use `.finalize()` to destroy a `Statement` and free any resources associated with it. Once finalized, a `Statement` cannot be executed again. Typically, the garbage collector does this for you, but explicit finalization may be useful in performance-sensitive applications. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3} const query = db.query("SELECT title, year FROM movies"); const movies = query.all(); query.finalize();

title: SQLite › `.function()`
text: `db.function(name, fn)` defines a SQL function that calls a JavaScript function. It returns the `Database`. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={4} const db = new Database(":memory:"); db.function("add2", (a, b) => a + b); db.query("SELECT add2(12, 4) AS sum").get(); ```txt { sum: 16 } The SQL function takes as many arguments as `fn` has parameters (`fn.length`). Functions with the same name and different numbers of arguments exist side by side. A function with the same name and the same number of arguments replaces the earlier one. That includes the functions that are built …

title: SQLite › `.get()`
text: Use `.get()` to run a query and get back the first result as an object. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const query = db.query(`select $message;`); query.get({ $message: "Hello world" }); ```txt { $message: "Hello world" } Internally, this calls [`sqlite3_reset`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_reset) followed by one [`sqlite3_step`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_step) and another `sqlite3_reset`: the rows after the first are not read. If the query returns no rows, the result is `null`.

title: SQLite › Integers
text: SQLite supports signed 64-bit integers, but JavaScript only supports signed 53-bit integers or arbitrary-precision integers with `bigint`. `bigint` input is supported everywhere, but by default `bun:sqlite` returns integers as `number` types. If you need to handle integers larger than 2^53, set the `safeIntegers` option to `true` when creating a `Database` instance. The option also validates that `bigint` values passed to `bun:sqlite` do not exceed 64 bits. `bun:sqlite` binds a `number` as `INTEGER` when `Number.isSafeInteger()` is true, and as `REAL` otherwise (also `-0`).

title: SQLite › `.iterate()` (`@@iterator`)
text: Use `.iterate()` to run a query and incrementally return results. title: SQLite › Names with and without the prefix
text: The key of a named parameter can include the `$`, `:`, or `@` prefix or leave it out. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query(`select $message;`); query.all({ $message: "Hello world" }); query.all({ message: "Hello world" }); If the object has both keys, the key with the prefix wins. With `strict: true`, the key without the prefix wins.

title: SQLite › Parameters
text: Queries can contain parameters. These can be numerical (`?1`) or named (`$param` or `:param` or `@param`). Bind values to these parameters when executing the query: ```ts title="query.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query("SELECT * FROM foo WHERE bar = $bar"); const results = query.all({ $bar: "bar", }); ```txt [{ "bar": "bar" }] Numbered (positional) parameters work too: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query("SELECT ?1, ?2"); const results = query.all("hello", "goodbye"); ```txt [ { "?1": "hello", "?2": "goodbye", }, ];

title: SQLite › `.query()`
text: Use the `db.query()` method on your `Database` instance to [prepare](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/prepare.html) a SQL query. The result is a `Statement` instance that is cached on the `Database` instance. _The query is not executed._ ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query(`select "Hello world" as message`); **What does "cached" mean?** The caching refers to the **compiled prepared statement** (the SQL bytecode), not the query results. When you call `db.query()` with the same SQL string multiple times, Bun returns the same cached `Statement` object instead of …

title: SQLite › `.run()`
text: Use `.run()` to run a query and get back an object with execution metadata. This is useful for schema-modifying queries (such as `CREATE TABLE`) or bulk write operations. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const query = db.query(`create table foo (bar text);`); query.run(); ```txt { lastInsertRowid: 0, changes: 0, } Internally, this calls [`sqlite3_reset`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_reset) and repeatedly calls [`sqlite3_step`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_step) until it returns `SQLITE_DONE`. It builds no rows. The `lastInsertRowid` …

title: SQLite › `.safeIntegers()`
text: To change the setting for one `Statement`, call `.safeIntegers(true)` or `.safeIntegers(false)`. It returns the statement. Without an argument it returns the current setting. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const query = db.prepare("SELECT 9007199254741093 AS max_int"); query.safeIntegers(true).get(); // => { max_int: 9007199254741093n } query.safeIntegers(); // => true `db.query()` returns the same `Statement` for the same SQL, so the setting stays for its next caller.

title: SQLite › `safeIntegers: false` (default)
text: When `safeIntegers` is `false`, `bun:sqlite` returns integers as `number` types and rounds integers beyond 53 bits to the nearest representable `number`: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3} const db = new Database(":memory:", { safeIntegers: false }); const query = db.query(`SELECT ${BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) + 102n} as max_int`); const result = query.get(); console.log(result.max_int); ```txt 9007199254741092 A `bigint` parameter that does not fit in a signed 64-bit integer keeps its low 64 bits. For example, `2n ** 64n - 1n` is stored as `-1`.

title: SQLite › `safeIntegers: true`
text: When `safeIntegers` is `true`, `bun:sqlite` returns integers as `bigint` types: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3} const db = new Database(":memory:", { safeIntegers: true }); const query = db.query(`SELECT ${BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) + 102n} as max_int`); const result = query.get(); console.log(result.max_int); ```txt 9007199254741093n When `safeIntegers` is `true`, `bun:sqlite` throws a `RangeError` if a `bigint` value in a bound parameter does not fit in a signed 64-bit integer: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3} const db = new …

title: SQLite › `.serialize()`
text: `bun:sqlite` supports SQLite's built-in mechanism for [serializing](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/serialize.html) and [deserializing](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/deserialize.html) databases to and from memory. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const olddb = new Database("mydb.sqlite"); const contents = olddb.serialize(); // => Uint8Array const newdb = Database.deserialize(contents); Internally, `.serialize()` calls [`sqlite3_serialize`](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/serialize.html).

title: SQLite › Statements
text: A `Statement` is a _prepared query_, which means it's been parsed and compiled into an efficient binary form. It can be executed multiple times. Create a statement with the `.query` method on your `Database` instance. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query(`select "Hello world" as message`); Queries can contain parameters. These can be numerical (`?1`) or named (`$param` or `:param` or `@param`). ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const query = db.query(`SELECT ?1, ?2;`); const query = db.query(`SELECT $param1, $param2;`); A `Statement` is one SQL statement: …

title: SQLite › Strict mode
text: By default, `bun:sqlite` does not throw an error if a parameter is missing: it binds `NULL`. To instead throw an error when a parameter is missing, set `strict: true` on the `Database` constructor: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3} const strict = new Database(":memory:", { strict: true }); // throws error because of the typo: const query = strict.query("SELECT $message;").all({ messag: "Hello world" }); const notStrict = new Database(":memory:"); // does not throw error: notStrict.query("SELECT $message;").all({ messag: "Hello world" });

title: SQLite › `.toString()`
text: Calling `toString()` on a `Statement` instance prints the expanded SQL query. This is useful for debugging. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={6, 9, 12} // setup const query = db.query("SELECT $param;"); console.log(query.toString()); // => "SELECT NULL" query.run(42); console.log(query.toString()); // => "SELECT 42" query.run(365); console.log(query.toString()); // => "SELECT 365" Internally, this calls [`sqlite3_expanded_sql`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_expanded_sql). The parameters are expanded using the most recently bound values.

title: SQLite › Transactions
text: A transaction executes multiple queries _atomically_: either all of them succeed or none do. Create a transaction with the `db.transaction()` method: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={2} const insertCat = db.prepare("INSERT INTO cats (name) VALUES ($name)"); const insertCats = db.transaction(cats => { for (const cat of cats) insertCat.run(cat); }); No cats have been inserted yet. `db.transaction()` returns a new function (`insertCats`) that _wraps_ the function that executes the queries. To execute the transaction, call this function. The transaction function passes its …

title: SQLite › Update hooks
text: Set `db.onInsert`, `db.onUpdate` or `db.onDelete` to a function. SQLite calls it for each row that a statement of this `Database` inserts, updates or deletes. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={5-7} const db = new Database(":memory:"); db.run("CREATE TABLE cats (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)"); db.onInsert = (db, tableName, rowid) => { console.log(`inserted ${tableName} ${rowid}`); }; db.run("INSERT INTO cats (name) VALUES ('Salem'), ('Keanu')"); ```txt inserted cats 1 inserted cats 2 The arguments are: - `database`: the `Database`. It is also `this`. - `tableName`: the …

title: SQLite › `using` statement
text: The `using` statement closes the database connection when the block exits. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={4, 5} { using db = new Database("mydb.sqlite"); using query = db.query("select 'Hello world' as message;"); console.log(query.get()); } ```txt { message: "Hello world" }

title: SQLite › `.values()`
text: Use `values()` to run a query and get back all results as an array of arrays. ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" highlight={3, 4} const query = db.query(`select $message;`); query.values({ $message: "Hello world" }); query.values(2); ```txt [ [ "Hello world" ] ] [ [ 2 ] ] Internally, this calls [`sqlite3_reset`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_reset) and repeatedly calls [`sqlite3_step`](https://www.sqlite.org/capi3ref.html#sqlite3_step) until it returns `SQLITE_DONE`.

title: SQLite › WAL mode
text: SQLite supports [write-ahead log mode](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html) (WAL), which dramatically improves performance, especially with many concurrent readers and a single writer. We recommend enabling WAL mode for most applications. To enable WAL mode, run this pragma query at the beginning of your application: ```ts db.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" db.run("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;"); For faster commits, run `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL`. SQLite then syncs the WAL file at checkpoints instead of at every commit. A power loss can lose the last commits, but it cannot corrupt the database. …

title: SQLite › WAL sidecar file cleanup
text: When using WAL mode with a file-based database, SQLite creates two sidecar files alongside your database: a write-ahead log (`-wal`) and a shared-memory index (`-shm`). Whether SQLite removes these files automatically after `.close()` depends on your platform: - **macOS**: Bun uses the system-provided SQLite, which Apple builds with persistent WAL enabled. The `-wal` and `-shm` files **persist** after close. This is not a bug — it is how Apple configured the system SQLite. - **Linux** and **Windows**: Bun statically links its own SQLite build, which follows upstream defaults. SQLite …

title: Streams › Direct `ReadableStream`
text: Bun implements an optimized version of `ReadableStream` that avoids unnecessary queue management. With a traditional `ReadableStream`, you _enqueue_ chunks of data. The stream adds each chunk to a queue, where it sits until the stream is ready to send more data. ```ts const stream = new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { controller.enqueue("hello"); controller.enqueue("world"); controller.close(); }, }); With a direct `ReadableStream`, you write chunks of data directly to the stream. No queueing happens. The `controller` API reflects this: you call `.write()` instead of `.enqueue()`. ```ts …

title: Streams › Ending the stream
text: Call `controller.close()` (or `controller.end()`) once everything is written. Every destination flushes what it has buffered and finishes at that point. `controller.close(error)` fails the stream instead: nothing more is flushed and the consumer rejects with `error`. A destination that takes the whole body (`Bun.serve`, `fetch`, `Bun.write`, `Bun.spawn` stdin, `.text()`, and so on) calls `pull()` once. If it returns a promise, the stream stays open while that promise is pending and ends when it resolves, as if `pull()` had called `controller.close()` last; if it rejects, the stream errors with …

title: Streams › Handling backpressure
text: `controller.write()` returns the number of bytes written, or a **pending `Promise<number>`** when the destination's internal buffer is full (for example, a slow HTTP client). The chunk is accepted either way. Once the destination has gone away (for example the HTTP client disconnected), `write()` returns `0`. The promise resolves once the destination has drained, so `await`ing the result is enough: ```ts const stream = new ReadableStream({ type: "direct", async pull(controller) { for (const chunk of chunks) { await controller.write(chunk); } controller.close(); }, }); `await …

title: bun create › From a local template
text: You can define custom templates on your local file system. Put them in one of the following directories: - `$HOME/.bun-create/<name>`: global templates - `<project root>/.bun-create/<name>`: project-specific templates Set the `BUN_CREATE_DIR` environment variable to change the global template path. You can also pass the absolute path of a template folder: `bun create /path/to/template mydir`. Like a remote template, a local template is merged into an existing destination folder. title: Transpiler › `.scan()`

[Type-only](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-8.html#type-only-imports-and-export) imports and exports are ignored. ```ts example.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const transpiler = new Bun.Transpiler({ loader: "tsx", }); const code = ` const val = require('./cjs.js') import('./loader'); `; const result = transpiler.scan(code); ```json output { "exports": ["name"], "imports": [ { "kind": "import-statement", "path": "react" }, { "kind": …

title: Transpiler › `.scanImports()`
text: In performance-sensitive code, use the `.scanImports()` method to get a list of imports. It's faster than `.scan()` (especially for large files) but marginally less accurate due to its performance optimizations. ```ts example.ts icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const transpiler = new Bun.Transpiler({ loader: "tsx", }); const code = ` const val = require('./cjs.js') import('./loader'); `; const result = transpiler.scanImports(code); ```json results icon="file-json" [ { "kind": "import-statement", "path": "react" }, { "kind": "require-call", "path": "./cjs.js" }, { "kind": "dynamic-import", "path": …

title: Utils › `Bun.deepEquals()`
text: Recursively checks if two objects are equivalent. `expect().toEqual()` in `bun:test` uses this internally. ```ts const foo = { a: 1, b: 2, c: { d: 3 } }; // true Bun.deepEquals(foo, { a: 1, b: 2, c: { d: 3 } }); // false Bun.deepEquals(foo, { a: 1, b: 2, c: { d: 4 } }); Pass a third boolean parameter to enable "strict" mode. `expect().toStrictEqual()` in the test runner uses this. ```ts const a = { entries: [1, 2] }; const b = { entries: [1, 2], extra: undefined }; Bun.deepEquals(a, b); // => true Bun.deepEquals(a, b, true); // => false In strict mode, Bun considers the following unequal: …

title: Utils › `Bun.deflateSync()`
text: Compresses a `Uint8Array` using zlib's DEFLATE algorithm. ```ts const buf = Buffer.from("hello".repeat(100)); const compressed = Bun.deflateSync(buf); buf; // => Buffer(500) compressed; // => Uint8Array(12) The second argument supports the same set of configuration options as [`Bun.gzipSync`](#bun-gzipsync).

title: Utils › `Bun.env`
text: An alias for `process.env`.

title: Utils › `Bun.escapeHTML()`
text: `Bun.escapeHTML(value: string | object | number | boolean): string` Escapes the following characters from an input string: - `"` becomes `"` - `&` becomes `&` - `'` becomes `'` - `<` becomes `<` - `>` becomes `>` This function is optimized for large input. On an M1 Max, it processes 480 MB/s - 20 GB/s, depending on how much data is being escaped and whether there is non-ASCII text. Bun converts non-string types to a string before escaping.

title: Utils › `Bun.fileURLToPath()`
text: Converts a `file://` URL to an absolute path. ```ts const path = Bun.fileURLToPath(new URL("file:///foo/bar.txt")); console.log(path); // "/foo/bar.txt"

text: Decompresses a `Uint8Array` using zlib's GUNZIP algorithm. ```ts const buf = Buffer.from("hello".repeat(100)); // Buffer extends Uint8Array const compressed = Bun.gzipSync(buf); const dec = new TextDecoder(); const uncompressed = Bun.gunzipSync(compressed); dec.decode(uncompressed); // => "hellohellohello..."

text: Decompresses a `Uint8Array` using zlib's INFLATE algorithm. ```ts const buf = Buffer.from("hello".repeat(100)); const compressed = Bun.deflateSync(buf); const dec = new TextDecoder(); const decompressed = Bun.inflateSync(compressed); dec.decode(decompressed); // => "hellohellohello..."

title: Utils › `Bun.inspect()`
text: Serializes an object to a `string` exactly as `console.log` would print it. ```ts const obj = { foo: "bar" }; Bun.inspect(obj); // => '{\n foo: "bar",\n}' const arr = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]); Bun.inspect(arr); // => "Uint8Array(3) [ 1, 2, 3 ]"

title: Utils › `Bun.inspect.custom`
text: The symbol Bun uses to implement `Bun.inspect`. Override it to customize how Bun prints your objects. It is identical to `util.inspect.custom` in Node.js. ```ts class Foo { [Bun.inspect.custom]() { return "foo"; } } const foo = new Foo(); console.log(foo); // => "foo"

title: Utils › `Bun.main`
text: An absolute path to the entrypoint of the current program (the file you executed with `bun run`). ```ts script.ts Bun.main; // /path/to/script.ts Use this to determine whether a script is running directly or another script is importing it. ```ts if (import.meta.path === Bun.main) { // this script is being directly executed } else { // this file is being imported from another script } This check is analogous to the [`require.main = module` trick](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6398196/detect-if-called-through-require-or-directly-by-command-line) in Node.js.

title: Utils › `Bun.nanoseconds()`
text: Returns the number of nanoseconds since the current `bun` process started, as a `number`. Useful for high-precision timing and benchmarking. ```ts Bun.nanoseconds(); // => 7288958

title: Utils › `Bun.openInEditor()`
text: Opens a file in your default editor. Bun auto-detects your editor from the `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR` environment variables. ```ts const currentFile = import.meta.url; Bun.openInEditor(currentFile); You can override this with the `debug.editor` setting in your [`bunfig.toml`](/runtime/bunfig). ```toml bunfig.toml icon="settings" [debug] # [!code ++] editor = "code" # [!code ++] Or specify an editor with the `editor` param. You can also specify a line and column number. ```ts Bun.openInEditor(import.meta.url, { editor: "vscode", // or "subl" line: 10, column: 5, });

text: Converts an absolute path to a `file://` URL. ```ts const url = Bun.pathToFileURL("/foo/bar.txt"); console.log(url); // "file:///foo/bar.txt"

It's an advanced API; review the following examples before using it in production. ```ts test("peek", () => { const promise = Promise.resolve(true); // no await necessary! expect(peek(promise)).toBe(true); // if we peek again, it returns the same value const again = …

The timestamp is encoded using the most significant 48 bits, and the random value and counter are encoded using the remaining bits. The `timestamp` parameter defaults to the current time in milliseconds. When the …

title: Utils › `Bun.resolveSync()`
text: Resolves a file path or module specifier using Bun's internal [module resolution](/runtime/module-resolution) algorithm. The first argument is the path to resolve, and the second argument is the "root". If nothing matches, it throws an `Error`. ```ts Bun.resolveSync("./foo.ts", "/path/to/project"); // => "/path/to/project/foo.ts" Bun.resolveSync("zod", "/path/to/project"); // => "/path/to/project/node_modules/zod/index.ts" To resolve relative to the current working directory, pass `process.cwd()` or `"."` as the root. ```ts Bun.resolveSync("./foo.ts", process.cwd()); …

title: Utils › `Bun.sleep()`
text: `Bun.sleep(ms: number)` Returns a `Promise` that resolves after the given number of milliseconds. ```ts console.log("hello"); await Bun.sleep(1000); console.log("hello one second later!"); Alternatively, pass a `Date` object to receive a `Promise` that resolves at that point in time. ```ts const oneSecondInFuture = new Date(Date.now() + 1000); console.log("hello"); await Bun.sleep(oneSecondInFuture); console.log("hello one second later!");

text: `Bun.sleepSync(ms: number)` A blocking synchronous version of `Bun.sleep`. ```ts console.log("hello"); Bun.sleepSync(1000); // blocks thread for one second console.log("hello one second later!");

title: Watch Mode › `--hot` mode
text: Use `bun --hot` to enable hot reloading when executing code with Bun. Unlike `--watch` mode, Bun doesn't hard-restart the entire process. It detects code changes and updates its internal module cache with the new code. Bun's `--hot` is not the same as hot reloading in the browser. Many frameworks provide a "hot reloading" experience, where you can edit & save your frontend code (say, a React component) and see the changes reflected in the browser without refreshing the page. Bun's `--hot` is the server-side equivalent of this experience. To get hot reloading in the browser, use a framework …

title: Watch Mode › `--watch` mode
text: Watch mode works with `bun test` and `bun build`, and when running TypeScript, JSX, and JavaScript files. To run a file in `--watch` mode: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun --watch index.tsx To run your tests in `--watch` mode: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun --watch test To type check before every restart, add [`--check`](/runtime/check#watch-mode). After a type error, Bun waits for your next change instead of running the file. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun --watch --check index.tsx In `--watch` mode, Bun keeps track of all imported files and watches them for changes. Requesting `backend: "webkit"` on a non-macOS …
