title: Test configuration › concurrentTestGlob
text: Run test files matching a glob pattern with concurrent test execution enabled. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] concurrentTestGlob = "**/concurrent-*.test.ts" # Run files matching this pattern concurrently Test files matching the pattern behave as if you passed the `--concurrent` flag: every test in those files runs concurrently. Use this to migrate a test suite to concurrent execution gradually, or to run one kind of test (say, integration tests) concurrently while the rest stay sequential. The `--concurrent` CLI flag overrides this setting, forcing all tests to run …

title: Test configuration › Configuration File
text: To configure `bun test` in `bunfig.toml`, add a `[test]` section: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Options go here

title: Test configuration › Coverage Path Ignore Patterns
text: Exclude specific files or file patterns from coverage reports using glob patterns: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Single pattern coveragePathIgnorePatterns = "**/*.spec.ts" # Multiple patterns coveragePathIgnorePatterns = [ "**/*.spec.ts", "**/*.test.ts", "src/utils/**", "*.config.js", "generated/**", "vendor/**" ] Bun excludes files matching any of these patterns from coverage calculation and reporting. See [Code coverage](/test/code-coverage).

title: Test configuration › Coverage Thresholds
text: Specify the coverage threshold as a single number or as an object with per-metric thresholds: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Simple threshold - applies to lines and functions coverageThreshold = 0.8 # Detailed thresholds coverageThreshold = { lines = 0.9, functions = 0.8 } Setting a threshold makes `bun test` exit with code 1 when coverage is enabled and any file's line or function coverage is below it. Bun accepts the `statements` key but does not currently enforce it. The check applies with any coverage reporter.

title: Test configuration › Environment
text: `environment` sets the DOM that test files run with. It can be `"happy-dom"`, `"jsdom"`, or `"node"` for no DOM (the default). The package has to be installed in your project. See [DOM testing](/test/dom#test-environments). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] environment = "happy-dom" The `--environment` flag does the same thing and overrides `bunfig.toml`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --environment=happy-dom A `// @vitest-environment <name>` comment in a test file overrides both. So does a `/** @jest-environment <name> */` comment at the very top of the file.

title: Test configuration › Environment Variables
text: Set environment variables for tests with `.env` files, which Bun loads from your project root automatically. For test-specific variables, create a `.env.test` file, which `bun test` loads automatically: ```ini title=".env.test" icon="settings" NODE_ENV=test DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost:5432/test_db LOG_LEVEL=error

title: Test configuration › Examples
text: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Only run tests in the src directory root = "src" # Run tests in a specific test directory root = "tests" # Run tests in multiple specific directories (not currently supported - use patterns instead) # root = ["src", "lib"] # This syntax is not supported

title: Test configuration › Globals
text: By default, `test`, `expect` and the other globals come from `"bun:test"`. A file that imports anything from `"vitest"` gets them from `"vitest"` instead. If that file is a test file or a preload script, so do the modules it loads. Set `globals = "vitest"` to get them from `"vitest"` in every file, like `globals: true` in a Vitest project. See [what differs](/test/writing-tests#importing-from-vitest). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] globals = "vitest" # default "bun" The `--globals` flag overrides `bunfig.toml`. Write it with `=`, as in `--globals=vitest`. - With `globals = …

title: Test configuration › Install Settings Inheritance
text: `bun test` inherits network and installation configuration (such as `registry`, `cafile`, `prefer`, and `exact`) from the `[install]` section of `bunfig.toml`. This matters if your tests reach a private registry or trigger installs during the run. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [install] # These settings are inherited by bun test registry = "https://npm.company.com/" exact = true prefer = "offline" [test] # Test-specific configuration coverage = true

title: Test configuration › JUnit Reporter
text: Configure the JUnit reporter output file path directly in the config file: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reporter] junit = "path/to/junit.xml" # Output path for JUnit XML report This complements the `--reporter=junit` and `--reporter-outfile` CLI flags: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # Equivalent command line usage bun test --reporter=junit --reporter-outfile=./junit.xml

title: Test configuration › Multiple Reporters
text: You can use multiple reporters simultaneously: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # CLI approach bun test --reporter=junit --reporter-outfile=./junit.xml # Config file approach ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test.reporter] junit = "./reports/junit.xml" [test] # Also enable coverage reporting coverage = true coverageReporter = ["text", "lcov"]

title: Test configuration › Path Ignore Patterns
text: `pathIgnorePatterns` excludes files and directories from test discovery entirely, using glob patterns. Unlike `coveragePathIgnorePatterns`, which only affects coverage reports, `pathIgnorePatterns` prevents Bun from discovering matching paths and running them as tests. Use it when your project contains submodules, vendored code, or other directories with `*.test.ts` files that you don't want `bun test` to pick up. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Single pattern pathIgnorePatterns = "vendor/**" # Multiple patterns pathIgnorePatterns = [ "vendor/**", "submodules/**", …

title: Test configuration › Preload Scripts
text: The `preload` option loads scripts before the tests run: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] preload = ["./test-setup.ts", "./global-mocks.ts"] This is equivalent to using `--preload` on the command line: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --preload ./test-setup.ts --preload ./global-mocks.ts

title: Test configuration › randomize
text: Run tests in random order to identify tests with hidden dependencies: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] randomize = true

title: Test configuration › React Compiler
text: `bun test` can compile your components and hooks with Bun's built-in [React Compiler](https://react.dev/learn/react-compiler), so that your tests run what your build ships. The compiled code imports `react/compiler-runtime`, which React 19 has. This option is experimental. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] reactCompiler = true # default false Bun compiles every JavaScript and TypeScript file except test files, preload scripts and `node_modules`. It leaves alone a file or a function that has the `"use no memo"` directive, and a function that breaks the [Rules of …

title: Test configuration › rerunEach
text: Re-run each test file multiple times to identify flaky tests: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] rerunEach = 3

title: Test configuration › retry
text: Default retry count for all tests. Bun retries a failed test up to this many times. Per-test `{ retry: N }` overrides this value. Default `0` (no retries). ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] retry = 3 The `--retry` CLI flag overrides this setting.

title: Test configuration › root
text: The `root` option sets the directory Bun scans for tests, instead of the project root. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] root = "src" # Only scan for tests in the src directory

title: Test configuration › seed
text: Specify a seed for reproducible random test order. Requires `randomize = true`: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] randomize = true seed = 2444615283

title: Test configuration › Skip Test Files from Coverage
text: Exclude files matching test patterns (for example `*.test.ts`) from the coverage report: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageSkipTestFiles = true # Exclude test files from coverage reports

title: Test configuration › smol Mode
text: Enable the `--smol` memory-saving mode specifically for the test runner: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] smol = true # Reduce memory usage during test runs This is equivalent to using the `--smol` flag on the command line: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --smol The `smol` mode reduces memory usage by: - Using less memory for the JavaScript heap - Being more aggressive about garbage collection - Reducing buffer sizes where possible Use it in memory-constrained environments, such as CI runners, or for large test suites.

title: Test configuration › Sourcemap Handling
text: Bun transpiles every file, so coverage results pass through sourcemaps before they're reported. `coverageIgnoreSourcemaps` opts out of this, but the results are confusing: during transpilation, Bun may move code around and rename variables. The option is mostly useful for debugging coverage issues. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] coverageIgnoreSourcemaps = true # Don't use sourcemaps for coverage analysis When using this option, you probably want to stick a `// @bun` comment at the top of the source file to opt out of the transpilation process.

title: Test configuration › Threshold Examples
text: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] # Require 90% coverage across the board coverageThreshold = 0.9 # Different requirements for different metrics coverageThreshold = { lines = 0.85, # 85% line coverage functions = 0.90 # 90% function coverage }

title: Dates and times › Advance the clock automatically
text: With `shouldAdvanceTime: true` (`advanceTimers: true` in Jest), the fake clock advances by 20 ms every 20 real milliseconds. To use a different interval, set `advanceTimeDelta` (in Jest, pass a number as `advanceTimers`). ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true }); await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 30)); // resolves without an advance `vi.setTimerTickMode()` changes the mode while fake timers are on: - `"manual"`: only your test advances the clock. This is the default. - `"nextTimerAsync"`: every turn of the real event loop …

title: Dates and times › Choose what to fake
text: `toFake` lists the APIs to fake. `doNotFake` (`toNotFake` in Vitest) removes names from the default list. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["Date"] }); // setTimeout stays real jest.useFakeTimers({ doNotFake: ["performance"] }); // performance.now() stays real | Name | Faked by default | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- | | `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearInterval` | Yes | | `Date`, `performance`, `hrtime` | Yes | | `requestAnimationFrame`, `cancelAnimationFrame` | Yes, …

title: Dates and times › Fake timers
text: `useFakeTimers()` replaces `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout` and `clearInterval` on `globalThis` with versions that run on a fake clock. `Date`, `performance.now()` and `process.hrtime()` read the same clock. The fake clock only moves when your test advances it. `jest` and `vi` have the same functions. The clock starts at the `now` option if you pass one. Otherwise, `vi.useFakeTimers()` starts at the time you set with `setSystemTime()`, or else at what `Date.now()` returns, so a spy on `Date.now` sets the start. `jest.useFakeTimers()` starts at the real time. While the clock is …

title: Dates and times › Get mocked time with jest.now()
text: When the time is mocked (with `setSystemTime` or `useFakeTimers`), `jest.now()` returns the current mocked timestamp: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("get the current mocked time", () => { jest.useFakeTimers(); jest.setSystemTime(new Date("2020-01-01T00:00:00.000Z")); expect(Date.now()).toBe(1577836800000); // Jan 1, 2020 timestamp expect(jest.now()).toBe(1577836800000); // Same value jest.useRealTimers(); }); Use it to read the mocked time without creating a new `Date` object. `vi.getMockedSystemTime()` returns the mocked time as a `Date`, or `null` when the time isn't …

title: Dates and times › Reset the system time
text: To reset the system time, pass no arguments to `setSystemTime`: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("it was 2020, for a moment.", () => { // Set it to something! setSystemTime(new Date("2020-01-01T00:00:00.000Z")); expect(new Date().getFullYear()).toBe(2020); // reset it! setSystemTime(); expect(new Date().getFullYear()).toBeGreaterThan(2020); });

title: Dates and times › Set the time zone
text: By default, `bun test` runs in UTC (`Etc/UTC`). To change the time zone, either pass the `TZ` environment variable to `bun test`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" TZ=America/Los_Angeles bun test Or set `process.env.TZ` at runtime: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("Welcome to California!", () => { process.env.TZ = "America/Los_Angeles"; expect(new Date("2020-07-01T00:00:00.000Z").getTimezoneOffset()).toBe(420); expect(new Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone).toBe("America/Los_Angeles"); }); test("Welcome to New York!", () => { // Unlike in Jest, you can set …

title: Dates and times › setSystemTime
text: To change the system time, use `setSystemTime`: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(() => { setSystemTime(new Date("2020-01-01T00:00:00.000Z")); }); test("it is 2020", () => { expect(new Date().getFullYear()).toBe(2020); }); `setSystemTime` takes a `Date`, a timestamp in milliseconds, or a date string that `new Date()` can parse. `jest.setSystemTime` and `vi.setSystemTime` are the same function. `bun:test` also supports Jest's `useFakeTimers` and `useRealTimers`, so existing tests that use them keep working: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("just …

title: Dates and times › Timers scheduled after an `await`
text: No promise job runs before one of the functions above returns, so what a callback does after an `await` hasn't happened yet. `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, `advanceTimersToNextTimerAsync`, `runAllTimersAsync` and `runOnlyPendingTimersAsync` return a promise. Between fake timers, they let promise jobs and one turn of the real event loop run, so they pick up timers that a callback schedules after an `await`. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("a retry that waits between attempts", async () => { vi.useFakeTimers(); let attempts = 0; (async () => { while (++attempts < 3) await …

title: Dates and times › Wait for real time while fake timers are on
text: A timer function that you save before calling `useFakeTimers()` stays real. The `node:timers` and `node:timers/promises` exports stay real too. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const savedSetTimeout = setTimeout; test("waits 10 real milliseconds", async () => { vi.useFakeTimers(); await new Promise(resolve => savedSetTimeout(resolve, 10)); vi.useRealTimers(); });

title: Finding tests › Changing the Root Directory
text: By default, Bun looks for test files starting from the current working directory. Change this with the `root` option in `bunfig.toml`: ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] root = "src" # Only scan for tests in the src directory

title: Finding tests › Default Discovery Logic
text: By default, `bun test` recursively searches the project directory for files that match these patterns: - `*.test.{jsjsxtstsxmjscjsmts|cts}` - Files ending with `.test.js`, `.test.jsx`, `.test.ts`, `.test.tsx`, `.test.mjs`, `.test.cjs`, `.test.mts`, or `.test.cts` - `*_test.{jsjsxtstsxmjscjsmts|cts}` - Files ending with `_test.js`, `_test.jsx`, `_test.ts`, `_test.tsx`, `_test.mjs`, `_test.cjs`, `_test.mts`, or `_test.cts` - `*.spec.{jsjsxtstsxmjscjsmts|cts}` - Files ending with `.spec.js`, `.spec.jsx`, `.spec.ts`, `.spec.tsx`, `.spec.mjs`, `.spec.cjs`, `.spec.mts`, or `.spec.cts` - …

title: Finding tests › Exclusions
text: By default, `bun test` ignores: - `node_modules` directories - Hidden directories (those starting with a period `.`) - Files that don't have JavaScript-like extensions (based on available [loaders](/bundler/loaders))

title: Finding tests › Execution Order
text: Tests run in the following order: 1. Test files run sequentially, or across worker processes with [`--parallel`](/test/parallel) 2. Within each file, tests run sequentially in definition order

title: Finding tests › Filter by Test Name
text: To filter tests by name rather than file path, use the `-t`/`--test-name-pattern` flag with a regex pattern: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" # run all tests with "addition" in the name bun test --test-name-pattern addition `bun test` matches the pattern against the test name prefixed with the labels of all its parent `describe` blocks, separated by spaces. For example, a test defined as: ```ts title="math.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" describe("Math", () => { describe("operations", () => { test("should add correctly", () => { // ... }); }); }); For this test, `bun test` matches the …

title: Finding tests › Position Arguments as Filters
text: To filter which test files run, pass additional positional arguments to `bun test`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test <filter> <filter> ... Any test file with a path that contains one of the filters runs. Filters are substring matches, not glob patterns. For example, to run all tests in a `utils` directory: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test utils This matches files like `src/utils/string.test.ts` and `lib/utils/array_test.js`.

title: Finding tests › Specifying Exact File Paths
text: To run a specific file in the test runner, make sure the path starts with `./` or `/` to distinguish it from a filter name: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test ./test/specific-file.test.ts To run a list of files that is too long for a command line (Windows allows 32,767 characters), write one path per line to a file and pass it with `--files-from`. Every line is read as a path, with or without a leading `./`. Further paths may stand on the command line; a filter there is an error: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --files-from ./shard-1.txt

title: DOM testing › Common Issues
text: **TypeScript errors for DOM APIs**: Include the `/// <reference lib="dom" />` directive at the top of your test files. **Missing globals**: Check that the file runs in a [test environment](#test-environments), or that your preload file imports and registers `@happy-dom/global-registrator`. **React component rendering issues**: Check that `@testing-library/react` is installed and happy-dom is set up.

title: DOM testing › Custom Elements
text:
Test custom elements and web components with the same setup: ```ts title="custom-element.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" /// test("custom element", () => { // Define a custom element class MyElement extends HTMLElement { constructor() { super(); this.innerHTML = "

Custom element content

"; } } customElements.define("my-element", MyElement); // Use it in tests document.body.innerHTML = ""; const element = document.querySelector("my-element"); expect(element?.innerHTML).toBe("

Custom element content

"); });

title: DOM testing › Event Testing
text: Test DOM events and user interactions: ```ts title="events.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" /// <reference lib="dom" /> test("button click event", () => { let clicked = false; document.body.innerHTML = '<button id="test-btn">Click me</button>'; const button = document.getElementById("test-btn"); button?.addEventListener("click", () => { clicked = true; }); button?.click(); expect(clicked).toBe(true); });

title: DOM testing › Global Setup
text: For more involved setups, create a preload file that also registers global mocks: ```ts title="test-setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Register happy-dom globals GlobalRegistrator.register(); // Add any global test configuration here global.ResizeObserver = class ResizeObserver { observe() {} unobserve() {} disconnect() {} }; // Mock other APIs as needed Object.defineProperty(window, "matchMedia", { writable: true, value: jest.fn().mockImplementation(query => ({ matches: false, media: query, onchange: null, addListener: jest.fn(), removeListener: jest.fn(), addEventListener: jest.fn(), …

title: DOM testing › Options
text: `@vitest-environment-options` (or `@jest-environment-options`) takes one line of JSON. Bun passes it to happy-dom's `Window` constructor or jsdom's `JSDOM` constructor. The default URL is `http://localhost:3000`. ```ts title="dom.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" /** * @vitest-environment jsdom * @vitest-environment-options { "url": "https://example.com/" } */

title: DOM testing › Performance Considerations
text: happy-dom is fast, but for very large test suites you may want to: - Use `beforeEach` to reset the DOM state between tests - Avoid creating too many DOM elements in a single test - Use `cleanup` functions from testing libraries ```ts title="test-setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" afterEach(() => { cleanup(); document.body.innerHTML = ""; });

title: DOM testing › React Testing Library
text: Bun works with React Testing Library for testing React components. After setting up a DOM as described earlier, install and use React Testing Library normally. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add -d @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom ```ts title="component.test.tsx" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" /// <reference lib="dom" /> function Button({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { return <button>{children}</button>; } test('renders button', () => { render(<Button>Click me</Button>); expect(screen.getByRole(button)).toHaveTextContent('Click me'); });

title: DOM testing › Registering happy-dom in a preload
text: Instead of setting `environment`, you can register the globals yourself in a preload script. Install the `@happy-dom/global-registrator` package as a dev dependency. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add -d @happy-dom/global-registrator Use Bun's preload feature to register the happy-dom globals before your tests run, which makes browser APIs like `document` available in the global scope. Create a file called `happydom.ts` in the root of your project with the following code: ```ts title="happydom.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" GlobalRegistrator.register(); To preload this file before `bun …

title: DOM testing › Test environments
text: `bun test` can set up [happy-dom](https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom) or [jsdom](https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom) for you. Test files get the same globals they get in Vitest (`window`, `document`, `HTMLElement`, ...). Install the one you want as a dev dependency. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun add -d happy-dom To use it in every test file, set `environment` in `bunfig.toml` or run `bun test --environment=happy-dom`. ```toml title="bunfig.toml" icon="settings" [test] environment = "happy-dom" # or "jsdom", or "node" (the default: no DOM) To use it in one file, add the same comment …

title: DOM testing › TypeScript Support
text: Depending on your `tsconfig.json` setup, you may see a "Cannot find name document" type error in the earlier code. To load the types for `document` and other browser APIs, add the following triple-slash directive to the top of any test file. ```ts title="dom.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" /// <reference lib="dom" /> test("dom test", () => { document.body.innerHTML = `<button>My button</button>`; const button = document.querySelector("button"); expect(button?.innerText).toEqual("My button"); }); Run the test with `bun test`: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test bun test v1.3.3 …

title: DOM testing › Windows and test files
text: By default, test files share one global object and one module registry. Files with the same environment and options also share one window, so a module that read `document.body` when it was imported still has the right element in the next file. Bun restores the globals after each file, so a file that runs in `node` doesn't see `document`. With [`--isolate` or `--parallel`](/test/parallel), every file gets its own window and its own copy of every module. Use them when files in different environments import the same DOM library, because a shared module stays bound to the first window it saw. The …

title: Lifecycle hooks › API Server Setup
text: ```ts title="server-setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" let server; beforeAll(async () => { // Start test server server = await startServer({ port: 3001, env: "test", }); }); afterAll(async () => { // Stop test server await stopServer(server); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Async context
text: Everything that `runTest()` runs sees the async context `runTest()` is called in. The same goes for `runSuite()`. So a test can read an `AsyncLocalStorage` store that a hook sets: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const requestId = new AsyncLocalStorage<string>(); aroundEach(runTest => requestId.run("request-1", runTest)); test("sees the store", () => { expect(requestId.getStore()).toBe("request-1"); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Async Lifecycle Hooks
text: All lifecycle hooks support async functions. Bun waits for the promise a hook or a test returns. It also waits for any other object with a `then()` method, such as the one React's `act()` returns. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(async () => { // Async setup await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100)); console.log("Async setup complete"); }); afterAll(async () => { // Async teardown await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100)); console.log("Async teardown complete"); }); test("async test", async () => { // Test will wait for beforeAll to …

title: Lifecycle hooks › Clean Up Resources
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" afterEach(() => { // Clean up after each test document.body.innerHTML = ""; localStorage.clear(); }); afterAll(async () => { // Clean up expensive resources await closeDatabase(); await stopServer(); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Database Setup
text: ```ts title="database-setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" let connection; beforeAll(async () => { // Connect to test database connection = await createConnection({ host: "localhost", database: "test_db", }); }); afterAll(async () => { // Close database connection await closeConnection(connection); }); beforeEach(async () => { // Start with clean database for each test await clearDatabase(connection); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Error Handling
text: If a `beforeAll` hook throws, the test runner skips every test in the hook's scope: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(() => { // If this throws, all tests in this scope will be skipped throw new Error("Setup failed"); }); test("this test will be skipped", () => { // This won't run because beforeAll failed }); To log a setup failure and still fail the suite: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(async () => { try { await setupDatabase(); } catch (error) { console.error("Database setup failed:", error); throw error; // Re-throw to fail the test …

title: Lifecycle hooks › Global Setup and Teardown
text: To scope the hooks to an entire multi-file test run, define the hooks in a separate file. ```ts title="setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(() => { // global setup console.log("Global test setup"); // Initialize database connections, start servers, etc. }); afterAll(() => { // global teardown console.log("Global test teardown"); // Close database connections, stop servers, etc. }); Then use `--preload` to run the setup script before any test files. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --preload ./setup.ts To avoid typing `--preload` every time you run tests, add it to your …

title: Lifecycle hooks › Keep Hooks Simple
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: Simple, focused setup beforeEach(() => { clearLocalStorage(); resetMocks(); }); // Avoid: Complex logic in hooks beforeEach(async () => { // Too much complex logic makes tests hard to debug const data = await fetchComplexData(); await processData(data); await setupMultipleServices(data); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Mock Setup
text: ```ts title="mock-setup.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeEach(() => { // Set up common mocks mock.module("./api-client", () => ({ fetchUser: mock(() => Promise.resolve({ id: 1, name: "Test User" })), createUser: mock(() => Promise.resolve({ id: 2 })), })); }); afterEach(() => { // Clear all mocks after each test mock.clearAllMocks(); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Nested Hooks
text: You can nest hooks. They run in the following order: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(() => console.log("File beforeAll")); afterAll(() => console.log("File afterAll")); describe("outer describe", () => { beforeAll(() => console.log("Outer beforeAll")); beforeEach(() => console.log("Outer beforeEach")); afterEach(() => console.log("Outer afterEach")); afterAll(() => console.log("Outer afterAll")); describe("inner describe", () => { beforeAll(() => console.log("Inner beforeAll")); beforeEach(() => console.log("Inner beforeEach")); afterEach(() => console.log("Inner …

title: Lifecycle hooks › `onTestFinished`
text: Use `onTestFinished` to run a callback after a single test completes. The callback runs after all `afterEach` hooks. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("cleanup after test", () => { onTestFinished(() => { // runs after all afterEach hooks console.log("test finished"); }); }); Not supported in concurrent tests; use `test.serial` instead.

title: Lifecycle hooks › Per-Scope Setup and Teardown
text: Perform per-scope setup and teardown logic with `beforeAll` and `afterAll`. Where you define the hook determines its scope.

title: Lifecycle hooks › Per-Test Setup and Teardown
text: Perform per-test setup and teardown logic with `beforeEach` and `afterEach`. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeEach(() => { console.log("running test."); }); afterEach(() => { console.log("done with test."); }); // tests... test("example test", () => { // This test will have beforeEach run before it // and afterEach run after it });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Scoped to a Describe Block
text: To scope the hooks to a particular describe block: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" describe("test group", () => { beforeAll(() => { // setup for this describe block console.log("Setting up test group"); }); afterAll(() => { // teardown for this describe block console.log("Tearing down test group"); }); test("test 1", () => { // test implementation }); test("test 2", () => { // test implementation }); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Scoped to a Test File
text: To scope the hooks to an entire test file: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeAll(() => { // setup for entire file console.log("Setting up test file"); }); afterAll(() => { // teardown for entire file console.log("Tearing down test file"); }); describe("test group", () => { test("test 1", () => { // test implementation }); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Use Appropriate Scope
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: File-level setup for shared resources beforeAll(async () => { await startTestServer(); }); // Good: Test-level setup for test-specific state beforeEach(() => { user = createTestUser(); });

title: Lifecycle hooks › Wrapping Tests
text: Some setup only works as a function call around the test: a database transaction, a tracing span, an `AsyncLocalStorage` store. Use `aroundEach` for that. The hook receives a `runTest` function. It does its setup, awaits `runTest()`, then does its teardown. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" aroundEach(async runTest => { await db.transaction(runTest); }); test("inserts a user", async () => { await db.insert({ name: "Alice" }); }); `runTest()` runs the `beforeEach` hooks, the test, the `afterEach` hooks and the `onTestFinished` callbacks. The promise it returns resolves when …

title: Mocks › Advanced Spy Usage
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" class UserService { async getUser(id: string) { // Original implementation return { id, name: `User ${id}` }; } async saveUser(user: any) { // Original implementation return { ...user, saved: true }; } } const userService = new UserService(); afterEach(() => { // Restore all spies after each test jest.restoreAllMocks(); }); test("spy on service methods", async () => { // Spy without changing implementation const getUserSpy = spyOn(userService, "getUser"); const saveUserSpy = spyOn(userService, "saveUser"); // Use the service normally const …

title: Mocks › Async Mocks
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("async mock functions", async () => { const asyncMock = mock(); // Mock resolved values asyncMock.mockResolvedValueOnce("first result"); asyncMock.mockResolvedValue("default result"); expect(await asyncMock()).toBe("first result"); expect(await asyncMock()).toBe("default result"); // Mock rejected values const rejectMock = mock(); rejectMock.mockRejectedValue(new Error("Mock error")); await expect(rejectMock()).rejects.toThrow("Mock error"); });

title: Mocks › Available Properties and Methods
text: Mock functions implement the following properties and methods: | Property/Method | Description | | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `mockFn.getMockName()` | Returns the mock name | | `mockFn.getMockImplementation()` | Returns the implementation as a function | | `mockFn.mock.calls` | Array of call arguments for each invocation | | `mockFn.mock.results` | Array of return values for each invocation | | `mockFn.mock.settledResults` | Resolved or rejected value for each …

title: Mocks › Basic Function Mocks
text: Create mocks with the `mock` function. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const random = mock(() => Math.random()); test("random", () => { const val = random(); expect(val).toBeGreaterThan(0); expect(random).toHaveBeenCalled(); expect(random).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); });

title: Mocks › Basic Mock Usage
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("mock function behavior", () => { const mockFn = mock((x: number) => x * 2); // Call the mock const result1 = mockFn(5); const result2 = mockFn(10); // Verify calls expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2); expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenCalledWith(5); expect(mockFn).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith(10); // Check results expect(result1).toBe(10); expect(result2).toBe(20); // Inspect call history expect(mockFn.mock.calls).toEqual([[5], [10]]); expect(mockFn.mock.results).toEqual([ { type: "return", value: 10 }, { type: "return", value: 20 }, ]); });

title: Mocks › Cache Interaction
text: Module mocks interact with both ESM and CommonJS module caches.

title: Mocks › Classes
text: Calling a mock with `new` constructs its implementation, so you can mock or spy on a class the same way as a function. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const Dog = mock( class { name: string; constructor(name: string) { this.name = name; } speak() { return "woof"; } }, ); test("mock a class", () => { const dog = new Dog("Rex"); expect(dog.speak()).toBe("woof"); expect(Dog).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Rex"); expect(Dog.mock.instances[0]).toBe(dog); });

title: Mocks › Cleanup After Each Test File
text: When a test file ends, Bun restores any spies that are still active and clears every mock's recorded calls. Return values and implementations set with `mockReturnValue()`, `mockImplementation()` and similar methods stay until you reset the mock. A mock in a module that several test files import keeps them from one file to the next. Spies and mocks made in a `--preload` script, or in one of its `beforeAll()` hooks, aren't restored or cleared. They stay the same for every test file.

title: Mocks › Clear All Mocks
text: `mock.clearAllMocks()` resets the `.mock.calls`, `.mock.instances`, `.mock.contexts`, and `.mock.results` properties of every mock. Unlike `mock.restore()`, it does not restore the original implementation: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const random1 = mock(() => Math.random()); const random2 = mock(() => Math.random()); test("clearing all mocks", () => { random1(); random2(); expect(random1).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); expect(random2).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); mock.clearAllMocks(); expect(random1).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(0); expect(random2).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(0); // Note: …

title: Mocks › Conditional Mocking
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const shouldUseMockApi = process.env.NODE_ENV === "test"; if (shouldUseMockApi) { mock.module("./api", () => ({ fetchData: mock(async () => ({ data: "mocked" })), })); } test("conditional API usage", async () => { const { fetchData } = await import("./api"); const result = await fetchData(); if (shouldUseMockApi) { expect(result.data).toBe("mocked"); } });

title: Mocks › Differences from Vitest
text: - A `vi.mock()` call that isn't hoisted, such as one inside a function, updates a module of your own that's already imported in place. Its existing exports change, exports that only the mock has aren't added, and getters are read once. A module that only `vi.importActual()` has loaded stays the original, and the next import calls the factory. - To update a module in place, Bun calls the factory when you mock the module, not at the next import. If the factory returns a promise, an `import()` of the module doesn't wait for it. Await what `vi.mock()` returns instead. `vi.doMock()` does the same …

title: Mocks › Dynamic Mock Implementations
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("dynamic mock implementations", () => { const mockFn = mock(); // Set different implementations mockFn.mockImplementationOnce(() => "first"); mockFn.mockImplementationOnce(() => "second"); mockFn.mockImplementation(() => "default"); expect(mockFn()).toBe("first"); expect(mockFn()).toBe("second"); expect(mockFn()).toBe("default"); expect(mockFn()).toBe("default"); // Uses default implementation });

title: Mocks › ESM vs CommonJS
text: Module mocks have different implementations for ESM and CommonJS modules. For ES modules, Bun patches JavaScriptCore so it can override export values at runtime and update live bindings recursively.

title: Mocks › Factory Functions
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" function createMockUser(overrides = {}) { return { id: "mock-id", name: "Mock User", email: "mock@example.com", ...overrides, }; } const mockUserService = { getUser: mock(async (id: string) => createMockUser({ id })), createUser: mock(async (data: any) => createMockUser(data)), updateUser: mock(async (id: string, data: any) => createMockUser({ id, ...data })), };

title: Mocks › Getters and Missing Exports
text: Bun reads an export from the object the factory returned every time it's used, so getters stay live. When a mock updates a loaded module in place, each getter is read once, at that moment. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const state = vi.hoisted(() => ({ enabled: false })); vi.mock("./flags", () => ({ get enabled() { return state.enabled; }, })); test("getter", () => { expect(enabled).toBe(false); state.enabled = true; expect(enabled).toBe(true); }); You can also write to the mocked module, whether you got it from `import * as`, `import()` or `vi.importMock()`. The write …

title: Mocks › Getters and Setters
text: Pass `"get"` or `"set"` as the third argument to spy on a property's getter or setter. The spy calls the original accessor until you give it another implementation. `mockRestore()` restores the original property. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const config = { get mode() { return "production"; }, }; test("spy on a getter", () => { const mode = spyOn(config, "mode", "get").mockReturnValue("test"); expect(config.mode).toBe("test"); expect(mode).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); mode.mockRestore(); expect(config.mode).toBe("production"); }); This also works on plain properties, such …

title: Mocks › Hoisting & Preloading
text: Top-level `vi.mock()`, `vi.unmock()`, `vi.hoisted()`, `jest.mock()` and `jest.unmock()` calls are hoisted above the file's imports, as in Vitest and Jest. This way, a module is mocked before the file or anything it imports loads it. A hoisted factory can't use the file's top-level variables, because they aren't initialized yet. Declare what the factory needs with `vi.hoisted()`. A `const` or `let` that only holds strings, numbers or other primitive literals is hoisted along with the calls, as in Jest. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const mocks = vi.hoisted(() => ({ add: …

title: Mocks › Import Timing Effects
text: - **When mocking before first import**: The original module isn't evaluated, unless something still needs it, such as a factory that declares `importOriginal`, `vi.importActual()`, a mock that has neither a factory nor a `__mocks__` file, or a module in `node_modules` that imports a package you mock with `vi.mock()` - **When mocking after import**: The original module's side effects have already happened For this reason, use `vi.mock()`, `jest.mock()` or `--preload` for mocks that need to prevent side effects.

title: Mocks › Jest Compatibility
text: You can also use `jest.fn()`, as in Jest. It behaves identically. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const random = jest.fn(() => Math.random()); test("random", () => { const val = random(); expect(val).toBeGreaterThan(0); expect(random).toHaveBeenCalled(); expect(random).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); });

title: Mocks › Keep Mocks Simple
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: Simple, focused mock const mockUserApi = { getUser: mock(async id => ({ id, name: "Test User" })), }; // Avoid: Overly complex mock behavior const complexMock = mock(input => { if (input.type === "A") { return processTypeA(input); } else if (input.type === "B") { return processTypeB(input); } // ... lots of complex logic });

title: Mocks › Keeping Part of the Original Module
text: The factory is passed a function that loads the original module. Spread its result to replace only some exports. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" vi.mock("./math", async importOriginal => ({ ...(await importOriginal()), add: vi.fn(() => 42), })); test("partial mock", () => { expect(add(1, 2)).toBe(42); expect(subtract(2, 1)).toBe(1); }); Outside a factory, use `await vi.importActual("./math")` or `jest.requireActual("./math")` to load the original module. That doesn't call the factory. This also works when the mocked module is part of an import cycle. The modules that import …

title: Mocks › Lazy Evaluation
text: Bun calls the factory at the next `import` or `require()` that gets the mock. If the mock updates a loaded module in place, Bun calls it when you mock the module instead. `mock.module()`, `jest.mock()` and `jest.doMock()` do that with a loaded module, and so do some `vi.mock()` and `vi.doMock()` calls (see [Differences from Vitest](#differences-from-vitest)).

title: Mocks › Live Bindings
text: Mocked ESM modules keep live bindings, so `mock.module()`, `jest.mock()` and `jest.doMock()` update what the existing imports see. For `vi.mock()` and `vi.doMock()` it depends on the module and on who loaded it: see [Mocking a Package](#mocking-a-package) and [Differences from Vitest](#differences-from-vitest).

title: Mocks › Mock an Object with vi.mockObject()
text: `vi.mockObject(value)` returns a deep copy of `value` with every function and class replaced by a mock that returns `undefined`. Arrays become empty. Primitives and built-in objects like `Date` and `Map` are kept. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("mock an object", () => { const api = vi.mockObject({ version: 2, fetchUser: (id: string) => ({ id }), }); expect(api.fetchUser("1")).toBeUndefined(); expect(api.fetchUser).toHaveBeenCalledWith("1"); expect(api.version).toBe(2); }); With `{ spy: true }`, functions keep their implementation, and `value` is modified in place …

title: Mocks › Mock Cleanup Patterns
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" beforeEach(() => { // Set up common mocks mock.module("./logger", () => ({ log: mock(() => {}), error: mock(() => {}), warn: mock(() => {}), })); }); afterEach(() => { // Restore spies and clear call history; neither call resets the mock.module() override mock.restore(); mock.clearAllMocks(); });

title: Mocks › Mock Function Properties
text: `mock()` returns a new function decorated with additional properties. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const random = mock((multiplier: number) => multiplier * Math.random()); random(2); random(10); random.mock.calls; // [[ 2 ], [ 10 ]] random.mock.results; // [ // { type: "return", value: 0.6533907460954099 }, // { type: "return", value: 0.6452713933037312 } // ]

title: Mocks › Mocking a Package
text: `vi.mock()` and `vi.doMock()` mock a package for your own code only, as in Vitest. A module inside `node_modules` that imports the package gets the real one. `jest.mock()` and `mock.module()` mock it for every importer, as in Jest. The exception is a `.js` file that uses `import` or `export` in a package without `"type": "module"`. Node would read it as CommonJS, so Vitest loads it like your own code, and it gets the mock. ```ts vi.mock("dep", () => ({ default: fake })); // a library that requires "dep" still gets the real "dep" jest.mock("dep", () => fake); // the library gets the fake too If …

title: Mocks › Mocking External Dependencies
text: ```ts title="database.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Mock external database library mock.module("pg", () => ({ Client: mock(function () { return { connect: mock(async () => {}), query: mock(async (sql: string) => ({ rows: [{ id: 1, name: "Test User" }], })), end: mock(async () => {}), }; }), })); test("database operations", async () => { const { Database } = await import("./database"); const db = new Database(); const users = await db.getUsers(); expect(users).toHaveLength(1); expect(users[0].name).toBe("Test User"); });

title: Mocks › Mocking Without a Factory
text: You can call `vi.mock(path)` and `jest.mock(path)` without a factory. `mock.module()` always needs one. - If a `__mocks__` directory has a file with the same name, Bun loads that file instead. For a file, that's `__mocks__/<file>` in the same directory. title: Mocks › Module Mocks Are Removed After Each Test File
text: Module mocks are removed when the test file ends. The next file gets the real module, and modules that imported the mock are re-evaluated. So is a module that made a mock, so a helper that calls `vi.mock()` mocks for every test file that imports it. Other modules stay cached between files. Mocks made in a `--preload` script apply to every test file. A test file can mock a module that the preload script already mocked. With `vi.mock()` and `vi.doMock()`, only the modules the test file imports get the file's mock. Modules the preload script imported keep what they imported, as in Vitest. With …

title: Mocks › When to Use Preload
text: Mocking a module that's already been imported updates the module cache, so anything that imports it gets the mocked version. Bun has already evaluated the original module, though, so its side effects have already happened. To prevent the original module from being evaluated at all, mock it before it's imported, with a factory that doesn't declare `importOriginal` (see [Import Timing Effects](#import-timing-effects)). Use `vi.mock()` or `jest.mock()`, which are hoisted, or mock it in a `--preload` script.

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › `--isolate`
text: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun test --isolate Runs each test file in a fresh JavaScript global object inside the same process. Between files Bun: - creates a new `globalThis` (so properties a file stuck on `globalThis`, patched built-ins, and module-level state are gone), - clears the ESM and CommonJS module registries (every file re-evaluates its imports), - closes servers, sockets, file watchers and subprocesses the file left open, cancels its timers, and restores fake timers, - re-runs `--preload` scripts in the new global. Isolating every file is how Jest and Vitest behave by default. …

JIT-compiled code belongs to a global object, so with `--isolate` every file starts over in the interpreter. With `--isolate=modules`, a file reuses the code that was compiled for earlier files. | | `--isolate` | `--isolate=modules` | | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------- | | Modules, module mocks, `--preload` scripts | new per file | new per file | | The window of a [DOM …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › `--parallel`
text: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun test --parallel # one worker per CPU core bun test --parallel=4 # exactly 4 workers The main `bun test` process becomes a coordinator. It discovers test files as usual, then starts worker processes and hands each one file at a time. Results stream back as each test finishes, so the output looks the same as a serial run. The coordinator prints each file's results together under its filename, and never interleaves `console.log` output from a test with another file's. ```txt bun test v1.4.0 8x PARALLEL src/router.test.ts: ✓ matches static routes [0.31ms] ✓ …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › Balancing with `--timings`
text: File count is a poor proxy for duration: one shard can end up with all the slow integration tests. Give `bun test` a record of how long each file takes and it cuts shards by total time instead, keeping neighbouring files (which share imports) together: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" # Record durations (any run can do this; --parallel is fine) bun test --timings=.bun-test-timings.json --update-timings # Use them bun test --shard=2/8 --parallel --timings=.bun-test-timings.json The file is plain JSON, slowest first, so it doubles as a "what's slow" report: ```json title=".bun-test-timings.json" …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › Concurrent tests within a file
text: `--parallel` spreads _files_ across cores. Within one file tests still run one at a time unless you opt in to concurrency, which lets `async` tests overlap while one is waiting on I/O: ```ts title="api.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test.concurrent("GET /users", async () => { const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/users`); expect(res.status).toBe(200); }); test.concurrent("GET /posts", async () => { const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/posts`); expect(res.status).toBe(200); }); // runs after the concurrent group, alone test.serial("resets the database", async () => { await resetDb(); }); - …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › Every file is isolated (unless you opt out)
text: `--parallel` implies [`--isolate`](#--isolate): each file runs in a fresh global object even when two files land on the same worker. Tests that pass with `--parallel` don't depend on state leaked by an earlier file. `--parallel --no-isolate` turns that off: each worker keeps a single global and module registry for all the files it is handed, exactly like a serial `bun test` does for the whole suite. Each worker evaluates imports (and `--preload` modules) once instead of once per file, which is the fastest way to run a large suite of small files. The price is that a file can observe whatever an …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › How files are distributed
text: The coordinator sorts files by path and splits them into one contiguous chunk per worker, so files in the same directory, which usually import the same modules, mostly land in the same process (a chunk boundary can fall inside a directory, and stolen files move). When a worker drains its chunk it steals the back half of the largest remaining chunk from another worker. With [`--timings`](#balancing-with---timings) the coordinator cuts the chunks by recorded duration instead of file count, each worker starts its slowest file first, and an idle worker steals the slowest not-yet-started file from …

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › One timings file per shard
text: You can pass `--timings` more than once. Bun reads the files as one table and skips paths that don't exist yet. `--update-timings` writes to the **first** path. Under `--shard` that output contains only the files the shard ran, so the shards' outputs are disjoint. Read together on the next run, they add up to the whole suite with no merge step. [Large codebases](/test/index#large-codebases) on the main page has the full CI workflow.

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › Splitting a suite across CI machines with `--shard`
text: ```sh terminal icon="terminal" bun test --shard=1/3 # machine 1 bun test --shard=2/3 # machine 2 bun test --shard=3/3 # machine 3 Every machine sorts the discovered test files by path and takes a deterministic slice, so together the shards cover each file exactly once with no coordination. Without `--timings`, file `i` of the sorted list goes to shard `(i mod n) + 1` — balanced by file count, not by how long files take.

title: Parallel & isolated test runs › When `--parallel` helps, and when it doesn't
text: `--parallel` pays off when the suite is dominated by test execution — I/O waits, real computation, subprocesses, many files. It costs something too: every file re-evaluates its imports in a fresh global (see [`--isolate`](#--isolate)), and each worker is a separate process with its own JIT warm-up. For a suite of very fast files that all import the same large module graph, plain `bun test` (one process, one shared module registry) can be faster. Try both; Bun prints the numbers at the end of every run.

title: Test Reporters › Inspector Protocol for Testing

title: Runtime behavior › Single Process
text: The test runner runs all tests in a single process by default. This provides: - **Faster startup** - No need to spawn multiple processes - **Shared memory** - Efficient resource usage - **Simpler debugging** - All tests in one process However, this means: - Tests share global state (use lifecycle hooks to clean up) - One test crash can affect others - No true parallelization of individual tests

title: Runtime behavior › Test Isolation
text: Since tests run in the same process, ensure proper cleanup: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" afterEach(() => { // Clean up global state global.myGlobalVar = undefined; delete process.env.TEST_VAR; // Restore mocked functions if needed jest.restoreAllMocks(); });

title: Runtime behavior › Test Timeouts
text: Each test has a default timeout of 5000ms (5 seconds). Tests that exceed it fail.

title: Runtime behavior › Timers
text: Like Node.js, Bun makes a `setTimeout()` delay under 1 ms wait for 1 ms. In `bun test` it doesn't wait: when the event loop has nothing else to do, `setTimeout(callback, 0)` runs at once. Messages and immediates that are already queued run first, and so does a timer that was due before it, as in Node.js. Testing Library and user-event await such a timer after every step, so in a test that clicks and types those milliseconds add up. `setInterval()` keeps its minimum of 1 ms.

title: Runtime behavior › TZ (Timezone)
text: `bun test` uses UTC (`Etc/UTC`) as the time zone unless the `TZ` environment variable overrides it. This keeps date and time behavior consistent across machines. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("timezone is UTC by default", () => { const date = new Date(); expect(date.getTimezoneOffset()).toBe(0); }); To test with a specific time zone: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" TZ=America/New_York bun test

title: Runtime behavior › Unhandled Errors
text: `bun test` tracks unhandled promise rejections and errors that occur between tests. If any occur, `bun test` exits with a non-zero code even when no test failed. In both examples below, the error happens while the file is loading, and the file's tests still run. This helps catch errors in asynchronous code that might otherwise go unnoticed: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("test 1", () => { expect(true).toBe(true); }); // This error happens outside any test queueMicrotask(() => { throw new Error("Unhandled error"); }); test("test 2", () => { expect(true).toBe(true); }); …

title: Runtime behavior › Unsettled Top-Level Await
text: There's no timeout while a test file is loading. If a top-level `await` or `import` is still pending and nothing left on the event loop could settle it, `bun test` fails the file, prints the modules that are stuck, and moves on to the next file. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" await new Promise(() => {}); ```txt error: "/path/to/test.ts" never finished loading note: the event loop is empty, so nothing can settle it anymore note: unsettled top-level await in "/path/to/test.ts" The same applies to `--preload` scripts, async `describe()` callbacks, and tests or hooks with a …

title: Runtime behavior › Watch Mode
text: With the `--watch` flag, the test runner watches for file changes and re-runs tests. ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --watch

title: Snapshots › Array Snapshots
text: Arrays are also well-suited for snapshot testing: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("array snapshot", () => { const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map(n => n * 2); expect(numbers).toMatchSnapshot(); });

title: Snapshots › Basic Snapshots
text: Write snapshot tests with the `.toMatchSnapshot()` matcher: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("snap", () => { expect("foo").toMatchSnapshot(); }); The first time this test runs, Bun serializes the argument to `expect` and writes it to a snapshot file in a `__snapshots__` directory alongside the test file.

title: Snapshots › Complex Objects
text: Snapshots work well with complex nested objects: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("complex object snapshot", () => { const user = { id: 1, name: "John Doe", email: "john@example.com", profile: { age: 30, preferences: { theme: "dark", notifications: true, }, }, tags: ["developer", "javascript", "bun"], }; expect(user).toMatchSnapshot(); });

title: Snapshots › Custom Serializers
text: Use `expect.addSnapshotSerializer()` to change how snapshot matchers print certain values. It applies to those values at any depth in a snapshot: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" expect.addSnapshotSerializer({ test: value => value instanceof Money, serialize: value => `${value.amount} ${value.currency}`, }); test("price", () => { expect({ price: new Money(5, "EUR") }).toMatchInlineSnapshot(` { "price": 5 EUR, } `); }); A serializer is a [`pretty-format` plugin](https://github.com/jestjs/jest/tree/main/packages/pretty-format#writing-plugins), so serializers written for Jest …

title: Snapshots › Error Snapshots
text: You can also snapshot error messages with `.toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot()` and `.toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot()`: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("error snapshot", () => { expect(() => { throw new Error("Something went wrong"); }).toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot(); expect(() => { throw new Error("Another error"); }).toThrowErrorMatchingInlineSnapshot(); }); After running, the inline version becomes: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("error snapshot", () => { expect(() => { throw new Error("Something went wrong"); …

title: Snapshots › File Snapshots
text: `.toMatchFileSnapshot()` compares a value with a snapshot stored in its own file. The file can have the right extension, so you can open it like any other file. The path is relative to the test file. ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("renders the page", async () => { await expect(render(page)).toMatchFileSnapshot("./snapshots/page.html"); }); - A string is compared with the file's contents as is. - Any other value is printed first. Bun always prints it the way Vitest does ([`pretty-format`](#snapshots-from-jest-and-vitest)), even when `test` is imported from `"bun:test"`. …

title: Snapshots › Function Output Snapshots
text: Snapshot the output of functions: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" function generateReport(data: any[]) { return { total: data.length, summary: data.map(item => ({ id: item.id, name: item.name })), timestamp: "2024-01-01", // Fixed for testing }; } test("report generation", () => { const data = [ { id: 1, name: "Alice", age: 30 }, { id: 2, name: "Bob", age: 25 }, ]; expect(generateReport(data)).toMatchSnapshot(); });

title: Snapshots › Group Related Snapshots
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" describe("Button component", () => { test("primary variant", () => { expect(render(<Button variant="primary">Click</Button>)) .toMatchSnapshot(); }); test("secondary variant", () => { expect(render(<Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>)) .toMatchSnapshot(); }); test("disabled state", () => { expect(render(<Button disabled>Disabled</Button>)) .toMatchSnapshot(); }); });

title: Snapshots › Handle Dynamic Data
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: Normalize dynamic data test("API response format", () => { const response = { data: { id: 1, name: "Test" }, timestamp: Date.now(), requestId: generateId(), }; expect({ ...response, timestamp: "TIMESTAMP", requestId: "REQUEST_ID", }).toMatchSnapshot(); }); // Or use property matchers test("API response with matchers", () => { const response = getApiResponse(); expect(response).toMatchSnapshot({ timestamp: expect.any(Number), requestId: expect.any(String), }); });

title: Snapshots › Inline Snapshots
text: For smaller values, use `.toMatchInlineSnapshot()`. Bun stores inline snapshots directly in your test file: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("inline snapshot", () => { // First run: snapshot will be inserted automatically expect({ hello: "world" }).toMatchInlineSnapshot(); }); After the first run, Bun automatically updates your test file: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("inline snapshot", () => { expect({ hello: "world" }).toMatchInlineSnapshot(` { "hello": "world", } `); });

title: Snapshots › Keep Snapshots Small
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: Focused snapshots test("user name formatting", () => { const formatted = formatUserName("john", "doe"); expect(formatted).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"John Doe"`); }); // Avoid: Huge snapshots that are hard to review test("entire page render", () => { const page = renderEntirePage(); expect(page).toMatchSnapshot(); // This could be thousands of lines });

title: Snapshots › Organizing Large Snapshot Files
text: For large projects, consider organizing tests to keep snapshot files manageable: ```text title="directory structure" icon="file-directory" tests/ ├── components/ │ ├── Button.test.tsx │ └── __snapshots__/ │ └── Button.test.tsx.snap ├── utils/ │ ├── formatters.test.ts │ └── __snapshots__/ │ └── formatters.test.ts.snap

title: Snapshots › Platform Differences
text: Be aware of platform-specific differences: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Paths might differ between Windows/Unix test("file operations", () => { const result = processFile("./test.txt"); expect({ ...result, path: result.path.replace(/\\/g, "/"), // Normalize paths }).toMatchSnapshot(); });

title: Snapshots › Property Matchers
text: For values that change between test runs (like timestamps or IDs), use property matchers: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("snapshot with dynamic values", () => { const user = { id: Math.random(), // This changes every run name: "John", createdAt: new Date().toISOString(), // This also changes }; expect(user).toMatchSnapshot({ id: expect.any(Number), createdAt: expect.any(String), }); }); The snapshot file stores: ```txt title="snapshot file" icon="file-code" exports[`snapshot with dynamic values 1`] = ` { "createdAt": Any<String>, "id": Any<Number>, "name": "John", } `;

title: Snapshots › React Component Snapshots
text: Snapshots work well for React components: ```tsx title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" function Button({ children, variant = "primary" }) { return <button className={`btn btn-${variant}`}>{children}</button>; } test("Button component snapshots", () => { const { container: primary } = render(<Button>Click me</Button>); const { container: secondary } = render(<Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>); expect(primary.innerHTML).toMatchSnapshot(); expect(secondary.innerHTML).toMatchSnapshot(); });

title: Snapshots › Reviewing Snapshot Changes
text: When snapshots change, carefully review them: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" # See what changed git diff __snapshots__/ # Update if changes are intentional bun test --update-snapshots # Commit the updated snapshots git add __snapshots__/ git commit -m "Update snapshots after UI changes"

title: Snapshots › Snapshot Failures
text: When snapshots fail, Bun shows a diff: ```diff title="diff" icon="file-code" { - "name": "John", + "name": "Jane", } - Expected - 1 + Received + 1 Common causes: - Intentional changes (update with `--update-snapshots`) - Unintentional changes (fix the code) - Dynamic data (use property matchers) - Environment differences (normalize the data)

title: Snapshots › Snapshot Files
text: After the first run, Bun creates: ```text title="directory structure" icon="file-directory" your-project/ ├── snap.test.ts └── __snapshots__/ └── snap.test.ts.snap The snapshot file contains: ```ts title="__snapshots__/snap.test.ts.snap" icon="file-code" // Bun Snapshot v1, https://bun.sh/docs/test/snapshots exports[`snap 1`] = `"foo"`; On future runs, Bun compares the argument against the snapshot on disk.

title: Snapshots › Snapshots from Jest and Vitest
text: Bun reads and writes each snapshot file in the format of the runner that created it. The file's first line names that runner. `.snap` files from a Jest or Vitest project keep passing, and both runners can still read them after Bun adds or updates entries. | First line | Keys | Values | `toThrowErrorMatchingSnapshot()` | | ----------------------- | ----------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------- | | `// Bun Snapshot v1` | `outer inner 1` | Bun's format | the error message | | `// Jest Snapshot v1` | `outer inner 1` | `pretty-format` | the error message | | `// Vitest …

title: Snapshots › Updating Snapshots
text: Regenerate snapshots with: ```bash terminal icon="terminal" bun test --update-snapshots Do this when you've intentionally changed the output. In CI environments, Bun does not write new snapshots unless you pass this flag.

title: Snapshots › Use Descriptive Test Names
text: ```ts title="test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Good: Clear what the snapshot represents test("formats currency with USD symbol", () => { expect(formatCurrency(99.99)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"$99.99"`); }); // Avoid: Unclear what's being tested test("format test", () => { expect(format(99.99)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"$99.99"`); });

title: Snapshots › Using Inline Snapshots
text: 1. Write your test with `.toMatchInlineSnapshot()` 2. Run the test once 3. Bun automatically updates your test file with the snapshot 4. On subsequent runs, Bun compares the value against the inline snapshot

title: Writing tests › Argument Passing
text: How Bun passes arguments to your test function depends on the structure of your test cases: - If a table row is an array (like `[1, 2, 3]`), Bun passes each element as an individual argument - If a row is not an array (like an object), Bun passes it as a single argument ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Array items passed as individual arguments test.each([ [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 9], ])("add(%i, %i) = %i", (a, b, expected) => { expect(a + b).toBe(expected); }); // Object items passed as a single argument test.each([ { a: 1, b: 2, expected: 3 }, { a: 4, b: 5, expected: 9 …

title: Writing tests › Assertion Counting
text: Bun supports verifying that a specific number of assertions were called during a test:

title: Writing tests › Async Tests
text: Tests can be async. ```ts title="math.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("2 * 2", async () => { const result = await Promise.resolve(2 * 2); expect(result).toEqual(4); }); Alternatively, use the `done` callback to signal completion. If your test function takes a `done` parameter, you must call it or the test hangs. ```ts title="math.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("2 * 2", done => { Promise.resolve(2 * 2).then(result => { expect(result).toEqual(4); done(); }); });

text: | Status | Matcher | | ------ | ------------------ | | ✅ | `.not` | | ✅ | `.toBe()` | | ✅ | `.toEqual()` | | ✅ | `.toBeNull()` | | ✅ | `.toBeUndefined()` | | ✅ | `.toBeNaN()` | | ✅ | `.toBeDefined()` | | ✅ | `.toBeFalsy()` | | ✅ | `.toBeTruthy()` | | ✅ | `.toStrictEqual()` |

title: Writing tests › Basic Usage
text: To define a test: ```ts title="math.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("2 + 2", () => { expect(2 + 2).toBe(4); });

title: Writing tests › Combining modifiers
text: You can chain modifiers in any order. Repeating a modifier, as in `test.skip.skip`, has no effect. `skip` wins over `todo`, and `todo` wins over `failing`. ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test.skipIf(isWindows).skipIf(isCI)("skipped on Windows and in CI", () => {}); test.skipIf(isWindows).failing("skipped on Windows, expected to fail elsewhere", () => { expect(0.1 + 0.2).toBe(0.3); });

title: Writing tests › Conditional Tests for Describe Blocks
text: The conditional modifiers `.if()`, `.skipIf()`, and `.todoIf()` also work on `describe` blocks, affecting all tests in the suite: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const isMacOS = process.platform === "darwin"; // Only runs the entire suite on macOS describe.if(isMacOS)("macOS-specific features", () => { test("feature A", () => { // only runs on macOS }); test("feature B", () => { // only runs on macOS }); }); // Skips the entire suite on Windows describe.skipIf(process.platform === "win32")("Unix features", () => { test("feature C", () => { // skipped on Windows }); …

title: Writing tests › Custom Equality
text: Use `expect.addEqualityTesters()` to teach `toEqual()`, `toStrictEqual()`, `toMatchObject()`, `toHaveBeenCalledWith()`, and the other deep-equality matchers how to compare your own types. A tester returns `true` or `false`, or `undefined` if it doesn't handle the two values. ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" function areVolumesEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown) { if (a instanceof Volume && b instanceof Volume) return a.equals(b); return undefined; } expect.addEqualityTesters([areVolumesEqual]); test("1 L is 1000 mL", () => { expect({ size: new Volume(1, "L") }).toEqual({ …

title: Writing tests › Examples
text: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Basic specifiers test.each([ ["hello", 123], ["world", 456], ])("string: %s, number: %i", (str, num) => { // "string: hello, number: 123" // "string: world, number: 456" }); // %p for pretty-format output test.each([ [{ name: "Alice" }, { a: 1, b: 2 }], [{ name: "Bob" }, { x: 5, y: 10 }], ])("user %p with data %p", (user, data) => { // 'user { name: "Alice" } with data { a: 1, b: 2 }' // 'user { name: "Bob" } with data { x: 5, y: 10 }' }); // %# for index test.each(["apple", "banana"])("fruit #%# is %s", fruit => { // "fruit #0 is …

title: Writing tests › expect.assertions(count)
text: Use `expect.assertions(count)` to verify that a specific number of assertions are called during a test: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("exactly two assertions", () => { expect.assertions(2); // Will fail if not exactly 2 assertions are called expect(1 + 1).toBe(2); expect("hello").toContain("ell"); }); `expect.assertions(count)` helps ensure all your assertions run, especially in complex async code with multiple code paths.

title: Writing tests › expect.hasAssertions()
text: Use `expect.hasAssertions()` to verify that at least one assertion is called during a test: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("async work calls assertions", async () => { expect.hasAssertions(); // Will fail if no assertions are called const data = await fetchData(); expect(data).toBeDefined(); }); `expect.hasAssertions()` is especially useful in async tests, to make sure your assertions run.

title: Writing tests › expectTypeOf
text: These functions are no-ops at runtime. Run [`bun check`](/runtime/check) or `bun test --check` to verify the type assertions. The `expectTypeOf` function provides type-level assertions that TypeScript's type checker verifies. To test your types: 1. Write your type assertions using `expectTypeOf` 2. Run `bun check` to check that your types are correct ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" // Basic type assertions expectTypeOf<string>().toEqualTypeOf<string>(); expectTypeOf(123).toBeNumber(); expectTypeOf("hello").toBeString(); // Object type matching expectTypeOf({ a: 1, b: …

title: Writing tests › Fixtures
text: `test.extend()` returns a new `test` function with fixtures. A fixture is a value that's set up before a test and torn down after it. Tests get fixtures by destructuring the callback's first parameter. ```ts title="server.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" const test = base.extend<{ server: Bun.Server<undefined>; url: string }>({ server: async ({}, use) => { const server = Bun.serve({ port: 0, fetch: () => new Response("ok") }); // setup await use(server); // the test runs here await server.stop(); // teardown }, url: async ({ server }, use) => { await use(server.url.href); }, }); …

For example, `%s` prints `1` for `1` and `null` for `null`. Objects and arrays are printed on one line. …

title: Writing tests › Polling
text: `expect.poll()` calls a function, awaits its result, and runs the matcher on it. It retries until the matcher passes. The matcher returns a promise: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("the queue drains", async () => { await expect.poll(() => queue.length).toBe(0); await expect.poll(() => fetchStatus(), { interval: 10, timeout: 500, message: "status" }).toBe("ready"); }); | Option | Default | Description | | ---------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `interval` | `50` | Milliseconds between attempts | | `timeout` | …

title: Writing tests › Promises
text: `.resolves` and `.rejects` run the matcher on the value a promise resolves to or rejects with. They also accept a thenable or a function that returns a promise. The matcher returns a promise, so `await` it: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("promises", async () => { await expect(Promise.resolve(42)).resolves.toBe(42); await expect(fetchUser("invalid-id")).rejects.toThrow("User not found"); await expect(() => fetchUser("invalid-id")).rejects.toThrow("User not found"); }); If you don't `await` a matcher, the test still waits for it before ending, and a failure still …

title: Writing tests › Soft Assertions
text: `expect.soft()` doesn't throw when a matcher fails. The test keeps running and is marked as failed at the end: ```ts title="example.test.ts" icon="/icons/typescript.svg" test("response", async () => { const response = await fetch(url); expect.soft(response.status).toBe(200); expect.soft(response.headers.get("content-type")).toBe("text/html"); // checked even if the status is wrong }); `expect.soft()` works with `.not`, `.resolves`, `.rejects`, and custom matchers. Outside a test, or in a concurrent test after its first `await`, a failed matcher throws as usual.

text: | Status | Matcher | | ------ | --------------------- | | ✅ | `.toContain()` | | ✅ | `.toHaveLength()` | | ✅ | `.toMatch()` | | ✅ | `.toContainEqual()` | | ✅ | `.stringContaining()` | | ✅ | `.stringMatching()` | | ✅ | `.arrayContaining()` | `expect.stringMatching()` takes a regular expression. A string is the source of one, as in `new RegExp(string)`. To look for a literal string, use `expect.stringContaining()`.
